kamelets.name: avro-deserialize-action
kamelets.title: Avro Deserialize Action
kamelets.summary: Turns each message of Avro binary data back into a JSON object, using the Avro schema the data was written with.
kamelets.description:
Turns each message of Avro binary data back into a JSON object, using the Avro schema the data was written with.

Use it to read records that arrive in Avro, a compact binary format described by a schema, for example from a Kafka topic, and work on them as JSON. To turn JSON into Avro, use `avro-serialize-action`; for Protobuf, use `protobuf-deserialize-action`.

Input: Avro binary data, as bytes, without the schema in it, such as `avro-serialize-action` writes.

Output: the body is parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`) with one field for each field of the schema. The `Content-Type` header is removed. Put `json-serialize-action` after this action to get JSON text.

Good to know: Avro data does not say which schema it was written with, so the schema must be the one the writer used. When `schema` is not set, the schema found by an earlier `resolve-pojo-schema-action` is used.

kamelets.name: avro-serialize-action
kamelets.title: Avro Serialize Action
kamelets.summary: Turns each message, a JSON object, into Avro binary data that follows the Avro schema you give.
kamelets.description:
Turns each message, a JSON object, into Avro binary data that follows the Avro schema you give.

Use it to send records in Avro, a compact binary format described by a schema, to a system that expects it, such as a Kafka topic whose readers decode Avro. To turn Avro back into JSON, use `avro-deserialize-action`; for Protobuf, use `protobuf-serialize-action`.

Input: parsed JSON (a Map or a Jackson `JsonNode`) whose fields match the schema. JSON text fails: put `json-deserialize-action` before this action to parse it.

Output: the body is the Avro binary data, as bytes, and the `Content-Type` header is set to `application/avro`.

Good to know: the schema is not written into the data, so whoever reads it needs the same schema. A message fails when it lacks a field of the schema, has a field the schema does not know, or has a value of the wrong type. When `schema` is not set, the schema found by an earlier `resolve-pojo-schema-action` is used.

kamelets.name: aws-bedrock-agent-runtime-sink
kamelets.title: AWS Bedrock Agent Runtime Sink
kamelets.summary: Answers the question in each message from the documents of an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, or finds the passages of the documents that match it, or passes it to a Bedrock agent.
kamelets.description:
Answers the question in each message from the documents of an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, or finds the passages of the documents that match it, or passes it to a Bedrock agent.

Use it to build a question-and-answer service or a chatbot over your own documents, such as manuals, policies or FAQs, loaded into a Bedrock knowledge base. Set `operation` to `retrieve` to get only the passages that match the question, for example to show them as search results or to give them to a model of your own. Set it to `invokeAgent` to ask a Bedrock agent that you have set up in the Bedrock console. To load new documents into the knowledge base, use `aws-bedrock-agent-sink`; to call a model without a knowledge base, use `aws-bedrock-text-sink`.

Input: the body is the question, as text. The optional `CamelAwsBedrockAgentRuntimeSessionId` header continues an earlier conversation, with `retrieveAndGenerate` and `invokeAgent`: set it to the session ID of an earlier answer.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards depends on `operation`. With `retrieveAndGenerate`, the default, and with `invokeAgent`, it is the answer, as text. The `CamelAwsBedrockAgentRuntimeSessionId` header holds the ID of the session, and the `CamelAwsBedrockAgentRuntimeCitations` header the passages of the documents the answer is based on, as objects of the AWS SDK for Java. With `retrieve`, the body is a List of the passages found, each an object of the AWS SDK for Java with the text of the passage (`content.text`), its `score` and the `location` of its document. The `CamelAwsBedrockAgentRuntimeRetrievedResults` header holds the same List.

Good to know: `retrieveAndGenerate` needs `modelId` and `knowledgeBaseId`, `retrieve` needs `knowledgeBaseId`, and `invokeAgent` needs `agentId` and `agentAliasId`; without them, `retrieve` and `invokeAgent` fail before they call Bedrock. The passages from `retrieve` are not JSON, and turned into JSON as they are, each is an empty object: take the parts you need in the next step, such as `$\{body[0].content.text}` in a Simple expression. With `invokeAgent` and no session ID, each message starts a new session. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-bedrock-agent-sink
kamelets.title: AWS Bedrock Agent Sink
kamelets.summary: Starts, lists or looks up the ingestion jobs of an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, which load the documents of a data source, such as an S3 bucket, into the knowledge base.
kamelets.description:
Starts, lists or looks up the ingestion jobs of an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, which load the documents of a data source, such as an S3 bucket, into the knowledge base.

Use it to refresh a knowledge base after its documents changed, for example to start an ingestion job when new files arrive in the bucket of the data source, or every night from `timer-source`, and to check how the job went. To ask questions of the knowledge base, use `aws-bedrock-agent-runtime-sink`.

Input: the body is not used. For `getIngestionJob`, the `CamelAwsBedrockAgentIngestionJobId` header is the ID of the job to look up, and is required.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards depends on the operation: for `startIngestionJob` the ID of the new job, as text; for `listIngestionJobs` a List of job summaries; for `getIngestionJob` the job, an object of the AWS SDK for Java, with its status, such as `IN_PROGRESS`, `COMPLETE` or `FAILED`, also in the `CamelAwsBedrockAgentIngestionJobStatus` header.

Good to know: an ingestion job runs in the background, and `startIngestionJob` returns at once; to follow it, copy the ID from the body into the `CamelAwsBedrockAgentIngestionJobId` header and use `getIngestionJob`. The operation, the knowledge base and the data source come only from the options; headers cannot change them. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-bedrock-text-sink
kamelets.title: AWS Bedrock Text Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends a prompt to a text model in Amazon Bedrock, such as Amazon Titan or Anthropic Claude, for each message, and gives the answer of the model.
kamelets.description:
Sends a prompt to a text model in Amazon Bedrock, such as Amazon Titan or Anthropic Claude, for each message, and gives the answer of the model.

Use it to summarize, classify, translate or write text with a large language model, for example to summarize support tickets or draft replies. To answer questions from your own documents in a Bedrock knowledge base, use `aws-bedrock-agent-runtime-sink`.

Input: the body is the request of the model, as JSON text in the format of the chosen model, not the bare prompt. For Amazon Titan, for example `{"inputText":"Summarize: ...","textGenerationConfig":{"maxTokenCount":500}}`. For Claude 3, the Messages format, for example `{"anthropic_version":"bedrock-2023-05-31","max_tokens":500,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Summarize: ..."}]}`.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the answer, in a form that depends on the model: for Titan the response as JSON text, with the generated text in `results`; for Claude 3 the response as parsed JSON, with the generated text in `content`; for the older Claude models only the generated text, as text.

Good to know: the request and response formats are those of the model provider, described for each model in the Amazon Bedrock documentation; a body in another format fails. Each message is one call of the model. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-cloudtrail-source
kamelets.title: AWS Cloudtrail Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the events that AWS CloudTrail records in an AWS account, such as API calls and console sign-ins, one message per event.
kamelets.description:
Reads the events that AWS CloudTrail records in an AWS account, such as API calls and console sign-ins, one message per event.

Use it to react to activity in an AWS account, for example to raise an alert when a secret is read, a security group is changed or someone signs in to the console. Set `eventSource` to read the events of one AWS service only.

Output: the body is the CloudTrail record of the event, as JSON text. The headers give the ID, the name (such as `GetSecretValue`), the source (such as `secretsmanager.amazonaws.com`) and the user name of the event.

Good to know: it looks up the management events that CloudTrail keeps for the region, and reads the events that happen after it starts. It remembers where it is only while it runs: the events that happen while it is stopped are not read. Nothing is removed from CloudTrail. An event can be looked up only some minutes after it happened, and sometimes after a newer event: every `lookBackInterval` it looks up the last `lookBackWindow` again, and reads the events it missed. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-cloudwatch-sink
kamelets.title: AWS CloudWatch Metrics Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends one data point of a custom metric to Amazon CloudWatch for each message, with the name, the value and the unit of the metric taken from headers or options.
kamelets.description:
Sends one data point of a custom metric to Amazon CloudWatch for each message, with the name, the value and the unit of the metric taken from headers or options.

Use it to record business or technical numbers from an integration, such as orders processed, items in stock or processing time, and to graph them or set alarms on them in CloudWatch.

Input: the body is not used. The `metric-name` header (or `ce-metricname`) is the name of the metric; it is required unless the `metricName` option is set. The optional `metric-value` header (or `ce-metricvalue`) is the value, a number; when it is not set, the value is `metricValue`, or 1. The optional `metric-unit` header (or `ce-metricunit`) is the unit, such as `Count`, `Seconds`, `Bytes` or `Percent`; when it is not set, the unit is `metricUnit`, or `Count`. A header wins over the option. The optional `metric-dimension-name` and `metric-dimension-value` headers (or `ce-metricdimensionname` and `ce-metricdimensionvalue`) add one dimension, such as `Region` and `eu`. The optional `metric-timestamp` header (or `ce-metrictimestamp`) is the time of the data point.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: a message without a metric name, when `metricName` is not set either, fails, and so does a value that is not a number or a unit that CloudWatch does not know. Set the options to send the same metric for every message, for example `metricName` `OrdersProcessed` to count the messages. The time in `metric-timestamp` must be a Java `Instant` or `Date`: text is ignored, and then the data point gets the time it is sent. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-comprehend-sink
kamelets.title: AWS Comprehend Sink
kamelets.summary: Analyzes the text of each message with Amazon Comprehend, for example to detect its language, its sentiment, or the people, places and personal data it mentions.
kamelets.description:
Analyzes the text of each message with Amazon Comprehend, for example to detect its language, its sentiment, or the people, places and personal data it mentions.

Use it to sort customer feedback by sentiment, route support tickets by language, or find personal data in text before it is stored.

Input: the body is the text to analyze.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is what was found, as objects of the AWS SDK for Java (not JSON text): a List for most operations, such as the languages with their scores for `detectDominantLanguage` or the entities for `detectEntities`, and the sentiment with its scores for `detectSentiment`. Headers give the main result: `CamelAwsComprehendDetectedLanguage` with its score, or `CamelAwsComprehendDetectedSentiment` with its scores.

Good to know: every operation except `detectDominantLanguage` needs `languageCode`, and a message fails without it. `classifyDocument` needs `endpointArn`. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-ddb-sink
kamelets.title: AWS DynamoDB Sink
kamelets.summary: Writes each message as an item into an Amazon DynamoDB table: it creates or replaces, updates or deletes the item, depending on the operation.
kamelets.description:
Writes each message as an item into an Amazon DynamoDB table: it creates or replaces, updates or deletes the item, depending on the operation.

Use it to store events or records, such as orders, sensor readings or user profiles, as items of a DynamoDB table, or to delete items. To receive the changes made to a table, use `aws-ddb-streams-source`.

Input: the body is a JSON object, as JSON text, whose fields are the attributes of the item, such as `{"id":"A-1","customer":"Alice","total":42}`; it must hold the key attributes of the table. Text becomes a string attribute, a number a number, true or false a boolean, an object a map, and a list a set of strings or of numbers. With `DeleteItem` the body only needs the key. With `UpdateItem` the body holds a `key` object with the key attributes and an `item` object with the attributes to set, such as `{"key":{"id":"A-1"},"item":{"status":"shipped"}}`. The optional `CamelAwsDdbOperation` header chooses the operation for one message.

Output: the body is unchanged. The `CamelAwsDdbAttributes` header holds the attributes of the item before the change (`PutItem`, `DeleteItem`) or after it (`UpdateItem`).

Good to know: `PutItem`, the default, replaces the whole item that has the same key, so the attributes missing from the body are lost; use `UpdateItem` to change some attributes only. A body without the key of the table fails. Do not choose the operation with an `operation` field in the body: depending on the Camel version it is ignored, and the item is then replaced as with `PutItem`, or the message fails. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-ddb-streams-source
kamelets.title: AWS DynamoDB Streams Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the changes made to the items of an Amazon DynamoDB table from its stream, one message per inserted, modified or removed item.
kamelets.description:
Receives the changes made to the items of an Amazon DynamoDB table from its stream, one message per inserted, modified or removed item.

Use it to react when data changes in a table, for example to copy new orders to another system, keep a search index or a cache up to date, or record an audit trail. To write items into a table, use `aws-ddb-sink`.

Output: the body is a JSON object, as JSON text, that describes one change: `eventName` is `INSERT`, `MODIFY` or `REMOVE`, and `dynamodb` holds the key of the item (`keys`) and, depending on the view type of the stream, the item before (`oldImage`) and after (`newImage`) the change, with the type of each attribute. The headers give the ID and the name of the event.

Good to know: DynamoDB Streams must be enabled on the table, with the view type that holds the images you need, such as new and old images. By default it reads only the changes made after it starts, up to 100 in one poll; set `maxResultsPerRequest` to read fewer at a time. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-ec2-sink
kamelets.title: AWS EC2 Sink
kamelets.summary: Asks Amazon EC2 for the status of virtual machines (instances), such as whether they run and pass their health checks, each time a message arrives, or starts, stops or reboots them.
kamelets.description:
Asks Amazon EC2 for the status of virtual machines (instances), such as whether they run and pass their health checks, each time a message arrives, or starts, stops or reboots them.

Use it to check regularly that your EC2 instances are running and healthy, for example every few minutes from `timer-source`, and raise an alert when a check fails, or to start and stop test machines on a schedule.

Input: the body is not used. The `instanceIds` header (or `ce-instanceids`) is a comma-separated list of the IDs of the instances, such as `i-0abc123,i-0def456`. For the status, it is optional; without it, the status of all the running instances of the region is returned. To start, stop or reboot, it is required.

Output: the body is the answer of AWS, an object of the AWS SDK for Java (not JSON text). By default, a `DescribeInstanceStatusResponse`, with for each instance its ID, availability zone, state (such as `running`) and the results of the instance and system status checks. When there are more results than fit, the `CamelAwsEC2NextToken` header holds the token of the next page. `describeInstances` gives a `DescribeInstancesResponse`, and `startInstances` and `stopInstances` a `StartInstancesResponse` or `StopInstancesResponse` with the previous and the new state of each instance, such as `stopped` and `pending`. `rebootInstances` leaves the body as it was.

Good to know: by default it only reads, and never starts, stops or changes an instance; `operation` chooses another action. It cannot create or terminate instances. With Camel 4.23, the `instanceIds` header is ignored: the status of all the instances is returned, and start, stop and reboot reach no instance. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-eventbridge-sink
kamelets.title: AWS Eventbridge Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message as an event to an Amazon EventBridge event bus, where rules route it to targets such as Lambda functions, SQS queues or Step Functions.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message as an event to an Amazon EventBridge event bus, where rules route it to targets such as Lambda functions, SQS queues or Step Functions.

Use it to publish business events, such as `Order Shipped`, for other applications and AWS services to react to through EventBridge rules.

Input: the body is the detail of the event, as JSON text that holds a JSON object, such as `{"orderId": "A-1"}`. The `detail-type` header (or `ce-detail-type`) is the detail type, such as `Order Shipped`; the `event-source` header (or `ce-event-source`, or `ce-source`) is the source, such as `com.example.shop`; and the `resources-arn` header (or `ce-resources-arn`) is the ARN (Amazon Resource Name) of the resource the event is about, or several separated by commas. Each header falls back on its option: `detailType`, `eventSource` and `resourcesArn`.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the response of EventBridge, and the `CamelAwsEventbridgeFailedEntryCount` header is 1 when EventBridge rejected the event, 0 otherwise.

Good to know: a message fails when it has no detail type, no source or no resource ARN, from a header or an option. `eventSourcePrefix` is put before every source. An event that EventBridge rejects, such as one whose body is not a JSON object, is not delivered; depending on the Camel version the message then fails, or it only sets `CamelAwsEventbridgeFailedEntryCount` to 1. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-kinesis-firehose-sink
kamelets.title: AWS Kinesis Firehose Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message as a record to an Amazon Data Firehose (Kinesis Data Firehose) delivery stream, which delivers the records in batches to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch or another service.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message as a record to an Amazon Data Firehose (Kinesis Data Firehose) delivery stream, which delivers the records in batches to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch or another service.

Use it to load events or logs into S3 or a data warehouse without writing code that reads them, with Firehose doing the batching. To feed a Kinesis data stream that your own applications read, use `aws-kinesis-sink`.

Input: the body becomes the data of the record, as text, bytes or a stream. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. Firehose writes the records one after the other, without anything between them: end each record with a line break if the files must have one record per line. Headers are not used.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelAwsKinesisFirehoseRecordId` header gives the ID of the record.

Good to know: the delivery stream must exist and take Direct PUT as its source; a message for a delivery stream that does not exist fails. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-kinesis-sink
kamelets.title: AWS Kinesis Sink
kamelets.summary: Writes each message as a record to an Amazon Kinesis data stream.
kamelets.description:
Writes each message as a record to an Amazon Kinesis data stream.

Use it to feed a stream of events, such as clicks, logs or sensor readings, to the applications that read the stream, for example with `aws-kinesis-source`. To deliver data to S3 or a data warehouse without writing a reader, use `aws-kinesis-firehose-sink`.

Input: the body becomes the data of the record, as text, bytes or a stream. The optional `partition` header (or `ce-partition`) is the partition key: the records with the same key go to the same shard, in order. Without it, the key is a unique ID, so the records spread over the shards. The optional `sequence-number` header (or `ce-sequencenumber`) is the sequence number of the record that must come before this one, for a strict order within a partition key.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelAwsKinesisSequenceNumber` and `CamelAwsKinesisShardId` headers give the sequence number and the shard of the record.

Good to know: the stream must exist. The other headers are not sent: a Kinesis record has only data and a partition key. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-kinesis-source
kamelets.title: AWS Kinesis Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the records of an Amazon Kinesis data stream, one message per record.
kamelets.description:
Reads the records of an Amazon Kinesis data stream, one message per record.

Use it to process a stream of events that other applications write to Kinesis, such as clicks, logs or readings from devices, for example with `aws-kinesis-sink`.

Output: the body is the data of the record, as bytes. The headers give the partition key, the sequence number, the shard ID and the arrival time of the record.

Good to know: by default it reads the stream from its oldest record, and again from the oldest record each time the integration starts: it does not remember where it stopped, so records are read again after a restart. Set `iteratorType` to `LATEST` to read only the records written after it started; the records written while it was stopped are then not read. `iteratorType` can also start at a sequence number or at a time, again on each start. Records are not removed: Kinesis keeps them for the retention period of the stream. It reads all the shards of the stream, up to 1000 records from each in one poll: set `shardId` to read one shard only, and `maxResultsPerRequest` to read fewer records in one poll. When the stream is resharded, it goes on with the new shards; with `shardClosed` set to `fail`, every poll also fails with an error in the log, but the records are still read. With `useKclConsumers` it reads through the Kinesis Client Library instead, which keeps where it stopped in a DynamoDB table named after `applicationName`, or after the stream, and does not use `iteratorType`, `shardId`, `maxResultsPerRequest` or `shardClosed`; the body is then a `ByteBuffer` rather than bytes. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid. With `useKclConsumers`, the calls of the KCL to DynamoDB and CloudWatch go straight to AWS, without the proxy and without `uriEndpointOverride`.

kamelets.name: aws-lambda-sink
kamelets.title: AWS Lambda Sink
kamelets.summary: Calls an AWS Lambda function for each message, with the body as the event of the function, and waits for its result.
kamelets.description:
Calls an AWS Lambda function for each message, with the body as the event of the function, and waits for its result.

Use it to run your own serverless code on each message, such as enriching an order, checking a document or calling another API, without running a server for it.

Input: the body is the event given to the function, as JSON text, such as `{"orderId":"A-1"}`. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is what the function returned, as text (JSON text for most functions). The `CamelAwsLambdaStatusCode` header holds the status code of the call.

Good to know: an error raised inside the function does not fail the message: the body is then the error that the function reported, and the `CamelAwsLambdaFunctionError` header is set, for example to `Unhandled`. A function that does not exist fails the message. Each call waits until the function ends; the function cannot be called asynchronously (invocation type `Event`). Set `operation` to read the settings, versions or aliases of the function instead of calling it, or to publish a new version; the body afterwards is then the answer of AWS, an object of the AWS SDK for Java, such as a `GetFunctionConfigurationResponse` (not JSON text). To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-polly-sink
kamelets.title: AWS Polly Sink
kamelets.summary: Turns the text of each message into speech with Amazon Polly, and gives the audio, such as an MP3 file.
kamelets.description:
Turns the text of each message into speech with Amazon Polly, and gives the audio, such as an MP3 file.

Use it to create voice messages, audio versions of articles or spoken announcements from text. Write the audio to a file or a bucket as the next step, for example with `aws-s3-sink`.

Input: the body is the text to speak, as plain text, or as SSML when `textType` is `SSML`. The voice comes from `voiceId`, or when that is not set from the `CamelAwsPollyVoiceId` header; one of them is required.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the audio, as a stream in the format of `outputFormat`, and the `CamelAwsPollyContentType` header holds its content type, such as `audio/mpeg`.

Good to know: the stream can be read only once, so write it to a file or a bucket right away. A voice that is not available with the chosen `engine` fails the message. To change how words are pronounced, such as an abbreviation or a product name, store a pronunciation lexicon in Polly and name it in `lexiconNames`. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-redshift-sink
kamelets.title: AWS Redshift Sink
kamelets.summary: Runs an SQL statement, such as an INSERT, on an Amazon Redshift database for each message, with the values taken from the JSON body.
kamelets.description:
Runs an SQL statement, such as an INSERT, on an Amazon Redshift database for each message, with the values taken from the JSON body.

Use it to load events or records, such as orders or page views, into a table of a Redshift data warehouse, or to update rows when something changes. To read rows from Redshift, use `aws-redshift-source`.

Input: the body is a JSON object, as JSON text, such as `{"username":"alice","city":"Rome"}`. Each `:#name` in `query` takes the value of the field with that name, else of the header with that name. The statement runs once per message.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the JSON object parsed as a Map, and the `CamelSqlUpdateCount` header holds the number of rows changed.

Good to know: a body that is not a JSON object fails, and so does a body that lacks a field named in `query` when no header has that name either. It logs in with a database user and password, not with AWS keys, and connects with the Amazon Redshift JDBC driver, which uses TLS by default. Other settings of the driver go in `connectionProperties`.

kamelets.name: aws-redshift-source
kamelets.title: AWS Redshift Source
kamelets.summary: Runs an SQL query on an Amazon Redshift database at regular intervals, and sends each row of the result as a message.
kamelets.description:
Runs an SQL query on an Amazon Redshift database at regular intervals, and sends each row of the result as a message.

Use it to pick up records from a Redshift data warehouse, such as new orders or daily figures, and pass them on to another system. To write to Redshift, use `aws-redshift-sink`.

Output: one message per row. The body is the row as a JSON object, in JSON text, with the column names as field names, such as `{"id":1,"username":"alice","city":"Rome"}`. The `Content-Type` header is `application/json`.

Good to know: the query runs again every `delay` milliseconds, and returns the same rows each time unless they change; set `consumedQuery` to mark or delete each row once it has been sent. It logs in with a database user and password, not with AWS keys, and connects with the Amazon Redshift JDBC driver, which uses TLS by default. Other settings of the driver go in `connectionProperties`.

kamelets.name: aws-s3-event-based-source
kamelets.title: AWS S3 Event Based Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the events of an Amazon S3 bucket, such as a new or a deleted file, from the Amazon SQS queue that Amazon EventBridge sends them to, one message per event.
kamelets.description:
Receives the events of an Amazon S3 bucket, such as a new or a deleted file, from the Amazon SQS queue that Amazon EventBridge sends them to, one message per event.

Use it to react to new files in a bucket as soon as they arrive, without listing the bucket again and again, for example to process uploaded documents or imported data files. To read the files of a bucket by polling it, use `aws-s3-source`.

Output: the body is the EventBridge event, as JSON text: `detail-type` says what happened (such as `Object Created` or `Object Deleted`), `detail.bucket.name` is the bucket and `detail.object.key` the key of the file. With `getObject` set to true, the event of a file uploaded with a simple upload (PutObject) carries the content of the file instead, as a stream, with the `CamelAwsS3ProducedBucketName` and `CamelAwsS3ProducedKey` headers; the other events then come as parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`).

Good to know: it needs a setup in AWS. In the properties of the bucket, turn on sending events to Amazon EventBridge; then create an EventBridge rule for the events of source `aws.s3` and that bucket, with the queue as its target. Each event is deleted from the queue once it has been processed, unless `deleteAfterRead` is false; an event that fails stays in the queue and is received again when its visibility timeout (`visibilityTimeout`) ends. The files stay in the bucket. `getObject` skips files created by a multipart upload or a copy, and never connects through `uriEndpointOverride`. It logs in to the queue and, with `getObject`, to the bucket with `accessKey` and `secretKey`, or without keys, through the IAM role or the AWS profile of the environment, with `useDefaultCredentialsProvider` or `useProfileCredentialsProvider`. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-s3-sink
kamelets.title: AWS S3 Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file (object) to an Amazon S3 bucket, under a key (file name) taken from a header, the `keyName` option, or a generated ID.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file (object) to an Amazon S3 bucket, under a key (file name) taken from a header, the `keyName` option, or a generated ID.

Use it to store data in S3 for other systems or for archiving, such as exported records, received documents or events. To collect many small messages into a few large files, use `aws-s3-streaming-upload-sink`.

Input: the body is the content of the file, as text, bytes, a stream or a file. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The optional `file` header (or `ce-file`) is the key, the path of the file in the bucket, such as `orders/order-1.json`. Without it, and without `keyName`, the key is a generated unique ID. The optional `CamelAwsS3ContentType` header sets the content type of the file; the `Content-Type` header is not used, and without it the file is stored as `application/octet-stream`.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelAwsS3Key` and `CamelAwsS3ETag` headers give the key and the ETag of the uploaded file.

Good to know: a file with the same key is replaced without warning, unless `conditionalWritesEnabled` is true: then the upload of a key that exists already fails. When `keyName` is set, the `file` header is ignored and every message replaces the same file. To copy files from `aws-s3-source` under their own names, set the `file` header from its `CamelAwsS3Key` header first. It also works with S3-compatible storage, such as MinIO, through `overrideEndpoint`, `uriEndpointOverride` and `forcePathStyle`. To encrypt the files with a key of AWS KMS, as a bucket policy may require, set `useAwsKMS` and `awsKMSKeyId`; `storageClass` sets their storage class. One upload takes at most 5 GB; for larger files, set `multiPartUpload` to true, and each file of `partSize` or more is uploaded in parts. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-s3-source
kamelets.title: AWS S3 Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files (objects) in an Amazon S3 bucket, one message per file, and by default deletes each file once it has been read.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files (objects) in an Amazon S3 bucket, one message per file, and by default deletes each file once it has been read.

Use it to process files that another system drops into a bucket, such as uploaded documents, exported reports or log files. To react to new files through S3 event notifications instead of reading the bucket over and over, use `aws-s3-event-based-source`.

Output: the body is the content of the file, as bytes. The headers give the bucket name, the key (the path of the file in the bucket), the content type and the ETag of the file.

Good to know: files are deleted from the bucket after they are read, unless `deleteAfterRead` is set to false; then the same files are read again on every poll. `moveAfterRead` moves them to another bucket instead. It also works with S3-compatible storage, such as MinIO, through `overrideEndpoint` and `uriEndpointOverride`. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-s3-streaming-upload-sink
kamelets.title: AWS S3 Streaming upload Sink
kamelets.summary: Writes many messages into a few large files in an Amazon S3 bucket, adding each message to the current file and starting a new file after a number of messages or bytes.
kamelets.description:
Writes many messages into a few large files in an Amazon S3 bucket, adding each message to the current file and starting a new file after a number of messages or bytes.

Use it to store a stream of small records, such as log lines, events or sensor readings, as a few large files instead of one file per message. To upload one file per message, use `aws-s3-sink`.

Input: the body is added to the end of the current file as it is, as text, bytes or a stream. Nothing is put between two messages: end each message with a line break if the file must have one record per line. The names of the files come from `keyName`, not from headers.

Output: the message is unchanged. The message that completes a file gets the `CamelAwsS3ETag` header of that file.

Good to know: a file is uploaded when it has `batchMessageNumber` messages or `batchSize` bytes, or when `streamingUploadTimeout` has passed; until then it is not in the bucket. With the default `namingStrategy` of `progressive`, the first file is named `keyName`, such as `logs/app.log`, and the next ones `logs/app-1.log`, `logs/app-2.log` and so on. With `restartingPolicy` set to `override`, a new run starts again from `keyName` and replaces the files of the earlier run. To encrypt the files with a key of AWS KMS, as a bucket policy may require, set `useAwsKMS` and `awsKMSKeyId`; `storageClass` sets their storage class. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-secrets-manager-sink
kamelets.title: AWS Secrets Manager Sink
kamelets.summary: Creates a secret in AWS Secrets Manager for each message, with the body as its value, or changes or reads the value of an existing secret.
kamelets.description:
Creates a secret in AWS Secrets Manager for each message, with the body as its value, or changes or reads the value of an existing secret.

Use it to store passwords, API keys or certificates that another system generates, so that your applications can read them from Secrets Manager, to rotate such a value, or to read one inside a route.

Input: the body is the value of the secret, as text, for example a password, or several values as a JSON object in JSON text. With `operation` set to `getSecret`, the body is not used. For `createSecret`, the name of the new secret comes from the `secret-name` header, else from the `ce-secret-name` header; without either, the ID of the message is used as the name. `updateSecret` and `getSecret` work on the secret in `secretId`.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the answer of AWS, a `CreateSecretResponse` object of the AWS SDK for Java with the ARN, the name and the version ID of the new secret; for `updateSecret`, an `UpdateSecretResponse` with the ARN, the name and the new version ID. For `getSecret`, the body is the value of the secret, as text, or as bytes for a binary secret, and the `CamelAwsSecretsManagerSecretVersionId` header holds the ID of its version.

Good to know: by default it only creates secrets, and a message for a name that already exists fails. Set `operation` to `updateSecret` to change the value of the existing secret in `secretId`, or to `getSecret` to read it; both fail when `secretId` is not set or the secret does not exist. A message without a name header creates a secret with a generated name, such as `4D678616B8AFAA1-0000000000000002`. With `binaryPayload`, the body is stored as the binary value of the secret instead of as text. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-ses-sink
kamelets.title: AWS SES Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message as a plain-text email through Amazon SES (Simple Email Service), to the addresses in the `to` header or the `to` option.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message as a plain-text email through Amazon SES (Simple Email Service), to the addresses in the `to` header or the `to` option.

Use it to send notifications, alerts or confirmations by email from an integration, such as an order confirmation or an alert when a job fails.

Input: the body is the text of the email, as plain text. The `to` header (or `ce-to`) gives one or more recipient addresses, separated by commas; it is required unless the `to` option is set. The optional `subject` header (or `ce-subject`) is the subject; without it and without the `subject` option, the subject is a generated ID. The optional `reply-to-addresses` header (or `ce-reply-to-addresses`) is a comma-separated list of addresses that replies go to. Each of these headers takes precedence over the option of the same purpose.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelAwsSesMessageId` header gives the ID that SES gave the email.

Good to know: a message without a `to` header fails, unless the `to` option is set. The `cc`, `bcc`, `returnPath` and `configurationSet` options apply to every email. The `from` address, and `returnPath` when it is set, must be verified in SES, and while the SES account is in the sandbox, the recipients must be verified too. A `configurationSet` that does not exist in SES makes every email fail. To reach a local stand-in of AWS, use `overrideEndpoint` and `uriEndpointOverride`. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-sns-fifo-sink
kamelets.title: AWS SNS FIFO Sink
kamelets.summary: Publishes each message to an Amazon SNS FIFO topic, which delivers the messages of a group in order, and without duplicates, to the SQS FIFO queues subscribed to it.
kamelets.description:
Publishes each message to an Amazon SNS FIFO topic, which delivers the messages of a group in order, and without duplicates, to the SQS FIFO queues subscribed to it.

Use it to fan out ordered updates, such as the changes of one order or one account, to several FIFO queues at once. For a standard topic use `aws-sns-sink`.

Input: the body becomes the text of the notification, as text. The optional `group` header (or `ce-group`) is the message group ID, such as a customer ID: the messages of one group are delivered in order. Without it, each message is a group of its own. The optional `subject` header (or `ce-subject`) is the subject; it takes precedence over the `subject` option. The other headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent as SNS message attributes.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelAwsSnsMessageId` header gives the ID of the published message.

Good to know: the name of the topic ends in `.fifo`. With `contentBasedDeduplication` false, the default, each message gets a unique deduplication ID, so SNS drops only a message sent twice by a retry; set it to true to drop messages with the same body, which the topic must allow. With `messageStructure` set to `json`, the body is a JSON object with a text for each kind of subscriber. `serverSideEncryptionEnabled` and `kmsMasterKeyId` apply only to a topic that `autoCreateTopic` creates. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-sns-sink
kamelets.title: AWS SNS Sink
kamelets.summary: Publishes each message to an Amazon SNS topic, which delivers it to every subscriber of the topic, such as SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP addresses, email addresses or phone numbers.
kamelets.description:
Publishes each message to an Amazon SNS topic, which delivers it to every subscriber of the topic, such as SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP addresses, email addresses or phone numbers.

Use it to fan out an event to many receivers at once, or to send notifications such as alerts by email or SMS through a topic. For a FIFO topic use `aws-sns-fifo-sink`; to send to a single queue use `aws-sqs-sink`.

Input: the body becomes the text of the notification, as text. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The optional `subject` header (or `ce-subject`) is the subject, which email subscribers see as the subject line; it takes precedence over the `subject` option. The other headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent as SNS message attributes.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelAwsSnsMessageId` header gives the ID of the published message.

Good to know: with `messageStructure` set to `json`, the body is a JSON object with a text for each kind of subscriber. `serverSideEncryptionEnabled` and `kmsMasterKeyId` apply only to a topic that `autoCreateTopic` creates. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-sqs-batch-sink
kamelets.title: AWS SQS Batch Sink
kamelets.summary: Splits the text of each message at a separator and sends the parts as separate SQS messages to an Amazon SQS queue, in one batch call.
kamelets.description:
Splits the text of each message at a separator and sends the parts as separate SQS messages to an Amazon SQS queue, in one batch call.

Use it to send many small items that arrive together, such as a comma-separated list of IDs, as one SQS message each, with fewer calls to AWS. To send each message as one SQS message, use `aws-sqs-sink`.

Input: the body is text that `batchSeparator` splits, such as `one,two,three` with a separator of `,`; each part becomes the body of one SQS message.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the response of SQS, and the `CamelAwsSqsSuccessfulMessageCount` and `CamelAwsSqsFailedMessageCount` headers say how many parts were sent and how many failed.

Good to know: unless `queueURL`, `queueOwnerAWSAccountId` or an ARN in `queueNameOrArn` gives the address of the queue, the queue is looked up by listing the queues, which needs the `sqs:ListQueues` permission besides `sqs:SendMessage`. `delaySeconds` keeps each message hidden for a while after it is sent. `serverSideEncryptionEnabled` with `kmsMasterKeyId` changes the queue itself when the integration starts, so that SQS encrypts its messages with that KMS key. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-sqs-fifo-sink
kamelets.title: AWS SQS FIFO Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message to an Amazon SQS FIFO queue, which delivers the messages of a group in the order they were sent and drops duplicates.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message to an Amazon SQS FIFO queue, which delivers the messages of a group in the order they were sent and drops duplicates.

Use it to queue messages whose order matters, such as the updates of one order or one account, which must be processed in the order they happened. For a standard queue use `aws-sqs-sink`.

Input: the body becomes the body of the SQS message, as text. The optional `group` header (or `ce-group`) is the message group ID, such as a customer ID: the messages of one group are delivered in order. Without it, each message is a group of its own, so there is no order between messages.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelAwsSqsMessageId` header gives the ID of the SQS message.

Good to know: the name of the queue ends in `.fifo`. With `contentBasedDeduplication` false, the default, each message gets a unique deduplication ID, so SQS drops only a message sent twice by a retry; set it to true to drop messages with the same body, which the queue must allow. Unless `queueURL`, `queueOwnerAWSAccountId` or an ARN in `queueNameOrArn` gives the address of the queue, the queue is looked up by listing the queues, which needs the `sqs:ListQueues` permission besides `sqs:SendMessage`. A FIFO queue does not take a delay for each message, so this Kamelet has no `delaySeconds`. `serverSideEncryptionEnabled` with `kmsMasterKeyId` changes the queue itself when the integration starts, so that SQS encrypts its messages with that KMS key. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-sqs-sink
kamelets.title: AWS SQS Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message as an SQS message to an Amazon SQS (Simple Queue Service) queue.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message as an SQS message to an Amazon SQS (Simple Queue Service) queue.

Use it to hand work to other systems that read the queue, such as orders to process or jobs to run, and to buffer it when they are slow or down. For a FIFO queue use `aws-sqs-fifo-sink`, to send many parts in one call use `aws-sqs-batch-sink`, and to notify many receivers at once use `aws-sns-sink`.

Input: the body becomes the body of the SQS message, as text; bytes and streams are read as text. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The other headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent as SQS message attributes.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelAwsSqsMessageId` header gives the ID of the SQS message.

Good to know: unless `queueURL`, `queueOwnerAWSAccountId` or an ARN in `queueNameOrArn` gives the address of the queue, the queue is looked up by listing the queues, which needs the `sqs:ListQueues` permission besides `sqs:SendMessage`. `delaySeconds` keeps each message hidden for a while after it is sent. `serverSideEncryptionEnabled` with `kmsMasterKeyId` changes the queue itself when the integration starts, so that SQS encrypts its messages with that KMS key. To reach a local stand-in of AWS, use `overrideEndpoint` and `uriEndpointOverride`. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-sqs-source
kamelets.title: AWS SQS Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the messages of an Amazon SQS queue, one message each, and by default deletes each message from the queue once it has been processed.
kamelets.description:
Receives the messages of an Amazon SQS queue, one message each, and by default deletes each message from the queue once it has been processed.

Use it to process work that other systems put in a queue, such as orders, jobs or notifications, or the events that SNS, S3 or EventBridge send to a queue. For the events of an S3 bucket, `aws-s3-event-based-source` can also fetch the files.

Output: the body is the body of the SQS message, as text. The headers give the message ID (`CamelAwsSqsMessageId`), the receipt handle and the MD5 checksum of the body. The message attributes, which the sender sets on a message, are read only when `messageAttributeNames` names them, and the system attributes of SQS, such as `SentTimestamp`, only when `attributeNames` names them. Each attribute that is read becomes a header of the same name, except a message attribute whose name starts with `Camel`.

Good to know: a message is deleted only after it has been processed without error; a message that fails stays in the queue and is received again when its visibility timeout ends. With `deleteAfterRead` set to false, the messages stay in the queue and are received again and again. A message that takes longer to process than the visibility timeout is received a second time, by this or another reader: set `extendMessageVisibility` to keep it hidden for as long as it is processed. By default one message is processed at a time; `concurrentConsumers` processes several in parallel. Without `queueURL`, `queueOwnerAWSAccountId` or an ARN in `queueNameOrArn`, the queue is looked up by listing the queues, which needs the `sqs:ListQueues` permission. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-timestream-query-sink
kamelets.title: AWS Timestream Query Sink
kamelets.summary: Runs an SQL query on Amazon Timestream, the time series database of AWS, for each message, with the query taken from a header.
kamelets.description:
Runs an SQL query on Amazon Timestream, the time series database of AWS, for each message, with the query taken from a header.

Use it to read time series data, such as sensor readings or application metrics, for example every hour from `timer-source`, to build a report or check a threshold.

Input: the body is not used. The `query` header (or `ce-query`) is the SQL query to run, such as `SELECT * FROM "sensors"."readings" WHERE time > ago(1h)`; it is required.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the answer of AWS, a `QueryResponse` object of the AWS SDK for Java (not JSON text), with the columns and the rows of the first page of the result.

Good to know: the query is run as it is written in the header, so never build it from untrusted data. Only the first page of a large result is returned. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: aws-translate-action
kamelets.title: AWS Translate Action
kamelets.summary: Translates the text of each message from one language into another with Amazon Translate.
kamelets.description:
Translates the text of each message from one language into another with Amazon Translate.

Use it to translate customer messages, support tickets or product descriptions, for example from Italian into English before they are analyzed or stored, also when the messages come in several languages.

Input: the body is the text to translate.

Output: the body is the translated text.

Good to know: the target language is fixed by `targetLanguage`. The source language is fixed by `sourceLanguage`, or, with `autodetectSourceLanguage`, Amazon Translate detects it in each message. Only the listed language codes can be chosen, although Amazon Translate knows more languages. With `terminologyNames`, your own translations of terms, such as product and brand names, are applied. To reach AWS through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and set `proxyProtocol` to `HTTP` for a proxy that takes plain HTTP, such as Squid.

kamelets.name: azure-cosmosdb-sink
kamelets.title: Azure CosmosDB Sink
kamelets.summary: Creates or replaces an item (a JSON document) in a container of Azure Cosmos DB for each message, from the JSON object in the body.
kamelets.description:
Creates or replaces an item (a JSON document) in a container of Azure Cosmos DB for each message, from the JSON object in the body.

Use it to store orders, events or profiles as JSON documents in Cosmos DB. To receive the changes made to a container, use `azure-cosmosdb-source`.

Input: the body is one item as JSON text: a JSON object with an `id` field, such as `{"id": "1001", "region": "EU"}`. A Map fails: turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The partition key value of the item comes from the `itemPartitionKey` option or, when the option is not set, from the `itemPartitionKey` header (or `ce-itemPartitionKey`) of each message.

Output: the body afterwards is the item as it was created, as a Map, with the fields that Cosmos DB adds.

Good to know: a message without a partition key value fails. With `operation` `createItem`, the default, an item whose `id` already exists in the same partition fails; with `upsertItem`, it replaces the existing item. The database and the container must exist, unless `createDatabaseIfNotExists` and `createContainerIfNotExists` are true; a new container needs `containerPartitionKeyPath`.

kamelets.name: azure-cosmosdb-source
kamelets.title: Azure CosmosDB Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the items created or changed in a container of Azure Cosmos DB, through its change feed, as a JSON array per batch.
kamelets.description:
Receives the items created or changed in a container of Azure Cosmos DB, through its change feed, as a JSON array per batch.

Use it to react to new or updated documents, for example to copy them to a search index, a cache or Kafka. To create items, use `azure-cosmosdb-sink`.

Output: the body is a JSON array of the items of one batch, as bytes, each item with the fields that Cosmos DB adds, such as `_etag`.

Good to know: it reads only the changes made after it first starts, unless `startFromBeginning` is true, and it does not see deleted items. It keeps its position in a lease container, `camel-lease` in the database `databaseName` unless set otherwise, which must exist unless `createLeaseContainerIfNotExists` is true. Two integrations that read the same container with the same lease container share one position, and each change goes to only one of them, unless each has its own `leasePrefix`. It checks for new changes every 5 seconds unless `feedPollDelay` is set. Set `hostName` so that after a crash, the integration continues at once instead of after up to a minute.

kamelets.name: azure-eventhubs-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Eventhubs Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message as an event to an event hub in Azure Event Hubs, the Azure service for event streams.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message as an event to an event hub in Azure Event Hubs, the Azure service for event streams.

Use it to publish events, such as clicks, sensor readings or changes, for stream processing or for other applications to read. To receive them, use `azure-eventhubs-source`.

Input: the body becomes the body of the event: text, bytes or a stream. A Map fails: turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. A List is sent as one event per element. The optional `partition-id` header (or `ce-partition-id`) is the partition to send to, such as `0`; without it, and without `partitionKey`, Event Hubs chooses one.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: log in with `sharedAccessName` and `sharedAccessKey`, with `connectionString`, or with `credentialType` `AZURE_IDENTITY`. Set `namespaceName` and `eventhubName` unless `connectionString` is set. The shared access policy needs the Send right. With `partitionKey` set, a message with a `partition-id` or `ce-partition-id` header fails.

kamelets.name: azure-eventhubs-source
kamelets.title: Azure Eventhubs Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the events of an event hub in Azure Event Hubs, one message per event, and saves how far it has read in an Azure Storage blob container.
kamelets.description:
Receives the events of an event hub in Azure Event Hubs, one message per event, and saves how far it has read in an Azure Storage blob container.

Use it to process event streams, such as telemetry or changes, that other applications send to Event Hubs. To send events, use `azure-eventhubs-sink`.

Output: the body is the body of the event, as bytes. The headers give its partition (`CamelAzureEventHubsPartitionId`), offset, sequence number and the time it was enqueued, and `CamelAzureEventHubsMetadata` holds the custom properties of the event.

Good to know: log in with `sharedAccessName` and `sharedAccessKey`, with `connectionString`, or with `credentialType` `AZURE_IDENTITY`. Set `namespaceName` and `eventhubName` unless `connectionString` is set. When no position has been saved yet, it starts with the events that arrive after it starts, not the older ones. It reads as the `$Default` consumer group, or as the one in `consumerGroupName`, and each consumer group has its own saved position. For each partition, it saves its position (a checkpoint) in `blobContainerName` after `checkpointBatchSize` events (500 when not set), or `checkpointBatchTimeout` milliseconds (5000 when not set) after the first event since the last checkpoint, whichever comes first. The events read after the last checkpoint are read again after a restart.

kamelets.name: azure-functions-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Function Sink
kamelets.summary: Calls a function in Azure Functions over HTTP for each message, with the message as the body of the request.
kamelets.description:
Calls a function in Azure Functions over HTTP for each message, with the message as the body of the request.

Use it to run your own serverless code on each message, such as an enrichment, a notification or a calculation. For any other web service, use `http-sink`.

Input: the body is sent as the request body, as text, bytes or a stream. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The `Content-Type` header is sent as the content type of the request, and the other headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent as HTTP headers.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the response of the function, and the `CamelHttpResponseCode` header its status code.

Good to know: a response with a status code outside 200 to 299 fails the message. The `key` is sent as the `code` query parameter of the request, or, when `keyInHeader` is true, in the `x-functions-key` header, which keeps it out of the address of the request that error messages show.

kamelets.name: azure-servicebus-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Servicebus Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message to a queue or a topic in Azure Service Bus, the Azure message broker.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message to a queue or a topic in Azure Service Bus, the Azure message broker.

Use it to hand work or events to other applications through Service Bus, such as orders to process, or notifications for all the subscribers of a topic, now or after a delay. For simple storage queues, use `azure-storage-queue-sink`.

Input: the body is sent as text: text, bytes or a stream are read as text, so bytes that are not UTF-8 text, such as an image, are damaged. With `binary` set to `true`, the body is sent as bytes, exactly as they are, and text as its UTF-8 bytes. A Map is sent as its text form, so turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`; with `binary`, a Map cannot be sent at all. A List is sent as one message per element. The optional `CamelAzureServiceBusApplicationProperties` header, a Map, sets the custom properties of the message.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: the shared access policy of the connection string needs the Send right.

A queue created with sessions enabled accepts only messages with a session ID: without one, the send fails. A topic accepts them, but each of its subscriptions with sessions enabled moves them to its dead-letter queue. Set `sessionId` to send every message with that session ID; a reader of the queue or subscription then receives the messages of the session in the order they were sent. The session ID is fixed for the Kamelet: the `CamelAzureServiceBusSessionId` header is not read, so messages that must go to different sessions need one sink for each session ID.

Set `scheduledEnqueueDelay` to have Service Bus hold each message for that many seconds before readers can receive it, for example to send a reminder. The delay is the same for every message, and counts from the clock of the integration.

To log in with an Azure identity instead of a connection string, set `credentialType` to `AZURE_IDENTITY` and `fullyQualifiedNamespace`, and leave `connectionString` unset.

kamelets.name: azure-servicebus-source
kamelets.title: Azure Servicebus Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the messages of a queue, or of a topic subscription, in Azure Service Bus, one message each.
kamelets.description:
Receives the messages of a queue, or of a topic subscription, in Azure Service Bus, one message each.

Use it to process work or events that other applications send through Service Bus, one at a time or several at once, including a queue with sessions, or to read the messages that Service Bus has dead-lettered. To read new blobs from Event Grid events that arrive in a Service Bus queue, use `azure-storage-blob-event-based-source`.

Output: the body is the body of the Service Bus message, as bytes. The headers give its ID (`CamelAzureServiceBusMessageId`), its custom properties (`CamelAzureServiceBusApplicationProperties`, a Map), its content type, correlation ID, subject, enqueued time and delivery count, its session ID (`CamelAzureServiceBusSessionId`) when it was sent with one, and, for a dead-lettered message, why it was dead-lettered (`CamelAzureServiceBusDeadLetterReason` and `CamelAzureServiceBusDeadLetterErrorDescription`).

Good to know: with the default `serviceBusReceiveMode` of `PEEK_LOCK`, a message is removed only once it has been processed; a message whose processing fails is given back and received again, until Service Bus moves it to the dead-letter queue after the maximum delivery count (10 by default). With `enableDeadLettering` set to `true`, it is moved to the dead-letter queue straight away instead, with the exception as the reason, such as `java.lang.IllegalStateException: Invalid order`. With `RECEIVE_AND_DELETE`, a message is removed as soon as it is received, so a failure loses it. For a topic, set `serviceBusType` to `topic` and `subscriptionName`.

The messages are processed one at a time, in the order they arrive, unless a step of the integration works asynchronously, such as a delay. With `maxConcurrentCalls` set above 1, that many are processed at the same time, in no particular order.

A queue or subscription created with sessions enabled can be read only with `sessionEnabled` set to `true`: without it, the integration starts but receives nothing, and logs a warning from Service Bus every few seconds (`It is not possible for an entity that requires sessions to create a non-sessionful message receiver`). With sessions, the messages of one session are received in the order they were sent, and the next one only once the previous one has been processed, unless a step of the integration works asynchronously, such as a delay. A message whose processing fails is received again before the next one of its session, unless `enableDeadLettering` moves it to the dead-letter queue. `maxConcurrentSessions` sessions, 1 by default, are read at the same time; the messages of different sessions have no order between them. `maxConcurrentCalls` counts for each session: above 1, the messages of one session are processed at the same time too, and lose their order.

To read the dead-letter queue, set `subQueue` to `DEAD_LETTER_QUEUE`, and leave `sessionEnabled` unset even when the queue has sessions, because the dead-letter queue has none. A dead-lettered message whose processing fails is not moved anywhere else: it is given back and received again straight away, over and over, and holds up the dead letters behind it.

To log in with an Azure identity instead of a connection string, set `credentialType` to `AZURE_IDENTITY` and `fullyQualifiedNamespace`, and leave `connectionString` unset.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-blob-append-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Blob Append Sink
kamelets.summary: Adds each message at the end of an append blob in Azure Blob Storage, named after the `file` header, and creates the blob when it does not exist yet.
kamelets.description:
Adds each message at the end of an append blob in Azure Blob Storage, named after the `file` header, and creates the blob when it does not exist yet.

Use it to collect log lines, audit records or CSV rows from many messages into one growing blob. To write each message as a blob of its own, use `azure-storage-blob-sink`.

Input: the body is the data to add: text, bytes or a stream. It is added as it is, so end each line with a line break yourself. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The `file` header (or `ce-file`) is the name of the blob, such as `logs/app.log`. Without it, each message goes to a new blob with a generated unique name.

Output: the body afterwards is `true`, and headers such as `CamelAzureStorageBlobAppendOffset` and `CamelAzureStorageBlobCommittedBlockCount` describe the append.

Good to know: the container must exist: a missing container fails the message. A name that is already used by a block blob, such as one written by `azure-storage-blob-sink`, fails the message too.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-blob-event-based-source
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Blob Event-based Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the Event Grid events of an Azure Storage account from a Service Bus queue or topic, and can read the content of each new blob in a container.
kamelets.description:
Receives the Event Grid events of an Azure Storage account from a Service Bus queue or topic, and can read the content of each new blob in a container.

Use it to react quickly to new blobs, such as uploaded files, without reading the container over and over. It needs an Event Grid subscription on the storage account that sends the events, in the Event Grid schema, to a Service Bus queue, or to a topic so that other applications can receive the same events from subscriptions of their own. To read the container on a timer instead, use `azure-storage-blob-source`.

Output: when `getBlob` is false, the default, the body is the Event Grid event as JSON (an Azure `BinaryData`, which converts to text or bytes). When `getBlob` is true, the body of a `Microsoft.Storage.BlobCreated` event for a blob of `containerName` is the content of that blob, as a stream of bytes; the other events are passed on as parsed JSON (a Jackson JSON node).

Good to know: with the default `serviceBusReceiveMode` of `RECEIVE_AND_DELETE`, an event is removed from the queue, or from the subscription of the topic, as soon as it is received, so an event whose processing fails is lost. With `getBlob`, only blobs at the top of the container can be read: an event for a blob in a virtual folder, such as `in/a.txt`, fails. Events are processed one at a time, in order, unless `maxConcurrentCalls` is set.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-blob-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Blob Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file (a block blob) to a container in Azure Blob Storage, named after the `file` header.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file (a block blob) to a container in Azure Blob Storage, named after the `file` header.

Use it to store documents, exports or event payloads in Azure, for other applications or for archiving. To add each message at the end of one growing blob, such as a log, use `azure-storage-blob-append-sink`.

Input: the body is the content of the blob: text, bytes or a stream. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The optional `file` header (or `ce-file`) is the name of the blob, such as `reports/2026-05.csv`; a `/` in it puts the blob in a virtual folder. Without it, the blob gets a generated unique name.

Output: the body afterwards is `true`, and headers such as `CamelAzureStorageBlobETag` and `CamelAzureStorageBlobLastModified` describe the uploaded blob.

Good to know: a blob with the same name is replaced. The container must exist: a missing container fails the message. The name comes only from `file` or `ce-file`: to copy blobs from `azure-storage-blob-source` and keep their names, set `file` from its `CamelAzureStorageBlobBlobName` header first.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-blob-source
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Blob Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files (blobs) in a container of Azure Blob Storage, one message per blob, and can delete each blob, or move it to another container, once it has been read.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files (blobs) in a container of Azure Blob Storage, one message per blob, and can delete each blob, or move it to another container, once it has been read.

Use it to process files that another system drops into a container, such as uploaded documents, exported reports or log files. To react to new blobs through Event Grid events instead of reading the container over and over, use `azure-storage-blob-event-based-source`.

Output: the body is the content of the blob, as a stream of bytes. The headers give the name of the blob (`CamelAzureStorageBlobBlobName`, with its folder path), its type, content type, size, ETag and last-modified time.

Good to know: blobs are kept after they are read, so the same blobs are read again on every poll, every 500 milliseconds by default; set `deleteAfterRead` to true to delete each blob once it has been processed, or `moveAfterRead` to move it to another container. It reads all the blobs of the container, those in virtual folders too, unless `prefix` or `regex` narrows them down. With `deleteAfterRead`, the blob deleted is the one named in the `CamelAzureStorageBlobBlobName` header when processing ends, so do not change that header.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-datalake-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Blob Data Lake Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file to a file system in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, named after the `file` header.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file to a file system in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, named after the `file` header.

Use it to land data for analytics, such as exports, events or reports, in a data lake. For plain blob containers, use `azure-storage-blob-sink`.

Input: the body is the content of the file: text, bytes or a stream. A Map fails: turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The optional `file` header (or `ce-file`) is the name of the file, such as `sales-2026-05.csv`. Without it, the file gets a generated unique name.

Output: the body afterwards is `true`.

Good to know: the file is written at the top of the file system, or in `directoryName`. By default it logs in as an app registration, with `clientId`, `clientSecret` and `tenantId`, so that app needs a role on the account that allows writing, such as Storage Blob Data Contributor. It can log in with an account key (`accountKey`) or a SAS token (`sasSignature`) instead.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-datalake-source
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Blob Data Lake Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files in a file system of Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, one message per file, on every poll.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files in a file system of Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, one message per file, on every poll.

Use it to process files that land in a data lake, such as exports or reports. For plain blob containers, use `azure-storage-blob-source`, which can also delete what it reads.

Output: the body is the content of the file, as a stream of bytes. The `CamelAzureStorageDataLakeFileName` header is the name of the file, and other headers give its size, content type, ETag and last-modified time.

Good to know: it neither deletes nor moves the files, so it reads all of them again on every poll, every 500 milliseconds by default. It reads the files at the top of the file system, or of `directoryName`; the files in directories below are read only when `recursive` is true. `regex` keeps only the files whose path matches, and `fileName` reads one file. Log in as an app registration with `clientId`, `clientSecret` and `tenantId` (the default), or with an account key (`accountKey`) or a SAS token (`sasSignature`).

kamelets.name: azure-storage-files-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Files Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file to a directory of a file share in Azure Files, named after the `file` header.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file to a directory of a file share in Azure Files, named after the `file` header.

Use it to drop files where applications or people that mount the share can read them, such as reports or exports. For blob containers, use `azure-storage-blob-sink`.

Input: the body is the content of the file: text, bytes or a stream. A Map fails: turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The optional `file` header (or `ce-file`) is the name of the file; only its last part is used, so `reports/2026/data.csv` is written as `data.csv` in `directoryName`. Without it, the file gets a generated unique name.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: a file with the same name is replaced, unless `fileExist` says otherwise. Missing directories are created.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-files-source
kamelets.title: Azure Storage File Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files in a directory of a file share in Azure Files, one message per file, and can delete each file once it has been read.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files in a directory of a file share in Azure Files, one message per file, and can delete each file once it has been read.

Use it to process files that people or applications put on a share, such as scanned documents or exports. For blob containers, use `azure-storage-blob-source`.

Output: the body is the content of the file, which converts to text, bytes or a stream. The `CamelFileName` header is the path of the file from `directoryName`, `CamelFileNameOnly` its name, and `CamelFileLength` and `CamelFileLastModified` its size and last-modified time.

Good to know: files are kept after they are read, so the same files are read again on every poll, every 500 milliseconds by default. To read each file only once, set `deleteAfterRead` to true to delete it, set `move` to a directory such as `.done` to move it, or set `noop` to true to leave it in place and remember the files read, in memory or, with `idempotentRepository`, across restarts. Subdirectories are read only when `recursive` is true. `include` and `antInclude` read only the files whose names match.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-queue-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Queue Sink
kamelets.summary: Adds each message to a queue in Azure Queue Storage, as the text of a queue message.
kamelets.description:
Adds each message to a queue in Azure Queue Storage, as the text of a queue message.

Use it to hand work to another application or worker that reads the queue, such as orders to process or jobs to run. For a message broker with topics and dead-letter queues, use `azure-servicebus-sink`.

Input: the body is the text of the queue message: text or bytes. A Map is sent as its text form, so turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The optional `expiration` header (or `ce-expiration`) sets how long the message stays in the queue, as an ISO-8601 duration such as `PT1H` (one hour) or `P2D` (two days); without it, the message expires after 7 days.
