Output: the body afterwards is `true`, and headers such as `CamelAzureStorageQueueMessageId` and `CamelAzureStorageQueueExpirationTime` describe the message sent.

Good to know: the queue must exist, or a message fails, unless `createQueue` is true. A message can be held back for a while before readers see it, with `visibilityTimeout`. An `expiration` that is a plain number, such as `600`, fails the message.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-queue-source
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Queue Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the messages of a queue in Azure Queue Storage, one message each, and deletes each message from the queue once it has been processed.
kamelets.description:
Receives the messages of a queue in Azure Queue Storage, one message each, and deletes each message from the queue once it has been processed.

Use it to process work that other applications put in a storage queue, such as orders or jobs. For Service Bus queues and topics, use `azure-servicebus-source`.

Output: the body is the text of the queue message (as a stream). The headers give its ID (`CamelAzureStorageQueueMessageId`), the times it was inserted and expires, its pop receipt, and how many times it has been received (`CamelAzureStorageQueueDequeueCount`).

Good to know: a received message is hidden from other readers while it is processed. When the processing fails, it stays in the queue and is received again once that time is over, 30 seconds by default (`visibilityTimeout`), with a higher dequeue count. The queue is checked for new messages every 500 milliseconds, unless `delay` says otherwise.

kamelets.name: cassandra-sink
kamelets.title: Cassandra Sink
kamelets.summary: Runs a CQL statement, such as an INSERT, in an Apache Cassandra keyspace for each message, with the values of its `?` markers taken from the JSON array in the body.
kamelets.description:
Runs a CQL statement, such as an INSERT, in an Apache Cassandra keyspace for each message, with the values of its `?` markers taken from the JSON array in the body.

Use it to store events or records as rows of a Cassandra table, for example each reading of a sensor or each order that arrives on a Kafka topic.

Input: the body is a JSON array, as text, with one value for each `?` in `query`, in the same order: for `INSERT INTO accounts (id, username, city) VALUES (?, ?, ?)` the body `[1,"oscerd","Rome"]`. With `jsonPayload` set to false, the body is used as it is, as the one value of a statement with a single `?`.

Output: the body afterwards is an empty List for an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE.

Good to know: with `jsonPayload` true, the default, a message fails when its body is not a JSON array, such as a JSON object. The values are sent apart from the statement, so the content of a message cannot change it. `ANY`, the default `consistencyLevel`, is the weakest level: a write counts as done even before a replica has stored it. When the datacenter of the cluster is not called `datacenter1`, set `datacenter` to its name, or the Kamelet fails to start with `No node was available to execute the query`. The Kamelet connects without TLS, so a cluster that accepts only TLS connections refuses it.

kamelets.name: ceph-event-based-source
kamelets.title: Ceph Event Based Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the bucket notifications that a Ceph Object Gateway sends to a Kafka topic, one message per event, such as a file added to or deleted from a bucket.
kamelets.description:
Receives the bucket notifications that a Ceph Object Gateway sends to a Kafka topic, one message per event, such as a file added to or deleted from a bucket.

Use it to react as soon as a file is uploaded to or removed from a Ceph bucket, without reading the bucket over and over. Set `getObject` to true to receive the content of each new file. To read and remove the files of a bucket instead, use `ceph-source`.

Output: the body is the notification as JSON text, unchanged: a `Records` array that gives the event name (such as `ObjectCreated:Put`), the bucket name and the key of the file. The headers `ceph-event-id`, `ceph-opaque-data`, `ceph-object-metadata` and `ceph-object-tags` give the fields Ceph adds to the event; metadata and tags are a List of entries with a `key` and a `val`. Each header is also set with a `ce-` name, such as `ce-cepheventid`. With `getObject` true, the body of an `ObjectCreated` event is the content of the file instead, as a stream, with its content type in `CamelAwsS3ContentType`, and the other events come out as parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`), not as text.

Good to know: the notification and its Kafka topic are set up on the Ceph side; this Kamelet only reads the topic. A record that is not a Ceph notification (without a `Records` array) fails. `saslAuthType` has no default and must be set; `NONE` connects to Kafka with no login and no TLS. Without `consumerGroup`, each start uses a new group, so with the default `autoOffsetReset` of `latest` the events sent while it was stopped are not read.

kamelets.name: ceph-sink
kamelets.title: Ceph Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file (object) to a bucket of a Ceph Object Gateway, the S3-compatible storage of Ceph.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file (object) to a bucket of a Ceph Object Gateway, the S3-compatible storage of Ceph.

Use it to store data in Ceph, such as reports, exports, images or received messages to keep as an archive. For MinIO use `minio-sink`, and for Amazon S3 use `aws-s3-sink`.

Input: the body is the content of the file, as text, bytes or a stream. The key (the name of the file in the bucket) comes from the optional `file` header, or the `ce-file` header; when neither is set it is `keyName`, or a generated unique name when `keyName` is not set either.

Output: the body is unchanged.

Good to know: a file with the same key is overwritten, so with `keyName` set and no `file` header each message replaces the previous one. The bucket is addressed as part of the host name (such as `my-bucket.ceph.example.com`) unless `cephUrl` uses an IP address; set `forcePathStyle` to true when the DNS of the gateway has no wildcard name for its buckets.

kamelets.name: ceph-source
kamelets.title: Ceph Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files (objects) in a bucket of a Ceph Object Gateway, one message per file, and by default deletes each file once it has been read.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files (objects) in a bucket of a Ceph Object Gateway, one message per file, and by default deletes each file once it has been read.

Use it to process files that another system drops into a Ceph bucket, such as uploaded documents, exported reports or log files. To react to the bucket notifications of Ceph instead of reading the bucket over and over, use `ceph-event-based-source`.

Output: the body is the content of the file, as bytes. The headers give the bucket name, the key (the path of the file in the bucket, `CamelAwsS3Key`), the content type and the ETag of the file.

Good to know: files are deleted from the bucket after they are read, unless `deleteAfterRead` is set to false; then the same files are read again on every poll. Files in folders are read too. The bucket is addressed as part of the host name (such as `my-bucket.ceph.example.com`) unless `cephUrl` uses an IP address; set `forcePathStyle` to true when the DNS of the gateway has no wildcard name for its buckets.

kamelets.name: couchbase-sink
kamelets.title: Couchbase Sink
kamelets.summary: Stores each message as a document in a Couchbase bucket, or deletes a document, under a document ID that the Kamelet counts up or that a header gives.
kamelets.description:
Stores each message as a document in a Couchbase bucket, or deletes a document, under a document ID that the Kamelet counts up or that a header gives.

Use it to save events, orders or other records as JSON documents in Couchbase, for example each message that arrives on a Kafka topic, or to delete the documents that messages name. To read documents, use `couchbase-source`.

Input: the body is the document. JSON text is stored as a JSON document; other text is stored as a JSON string. With `autoStartId` true, the default, the documents get the IDs `1`, `2`, `3` and so on, counted from `startingId`, and the `CamelCouchbaseId` header is ignored. With `autoStartId` false, the `CamelCouchbaseId` header is the ID; a message without it uses `key`, and fails when `key` is not set either. With `operation` `CCB_DEL`, the body is not used.

Output: the body afterwards is `true`. After a delete, it is the result of Couchbase as text, such as `MutationResult{cas=0x18e92f09b4bf0000, ...}`.

Good to know: a document that already has the ID is replaced. The count starts again at `startingId` each time the integration starts, so with `autoStartId` true a restart overwrites the documents stored before. Set `autoStartId` to false and give each message its own ID to avoid that. The documents go to the default collection of the bucket unless `collection` is set, in `scope`; a collection that does not exist makes each message wait and fail with `AmbiguousTimeoutException` (10 seconds by default, see `retryAttempts`). The connection is not encrypted, also with `protocol` set to `https`.

kamelets.name: couchbase-source
kamelets.title: Couchbase Source
kamelets.summary: Runs a SQL++ (N1QL) query on a Couchbase bucket again and again, and sends each document or row it finds as a message, as JSON text.
kamelets.description:
Runs a SQL++ (N1QL) query on a Couchbase bucket again and again, and sends each document or row it finds as a message, as JSON text.

Use it to pass the documents of a Couchbase bucket on to another system, for example to copy them to a search index or a data warehouse. To store documents, use `couchbase-sink`.

Output: the body is one result row as JSON text. Without `statement`, the query reads all the documents of the default collection, and a row is `{"<bucket>":<the document>,"__id":"<document ID>"}`. With `collection` set, it reads that collection of `scope`, and a row is `{"<collection>":<the document>,"__id":"<document ID>"}`. The `CamelCouchbaseId` header holds the ID of the document.

Good to know: the query runs again every `delay` milliseconds and, unless `processedStrategy` is `delete`, nothing marks a document as read, so the same documents are sent on every run. With `delete`, each document is deleted once its message has been processed. A `statement` must name the document ID `__id` (`SELECT META().id AS __id, ...`), or its rows are skipped. With `fullDocument` set to true, the body is an object of the Couchbase SDK instead of JSON text. The connection is not encrypted, also with `protocol` set to `https`.

kamelets.name: counter-source
kamelets.title: Counter Source
kamelets.summary: Sends a message with a number that counts up by one, such as 1, 2, 3, at a regular interval.
kamelets.description:
Sends a message with a number that counts up by one, such as 1, 2, 3, at a regular interval.

Use it to try out a sink or an action with messages that are each different and easy to follow, or to make ordered test data. For the same fixed message every time use `timer-source`, and for a calendar schedule such as "every weekday at 9:00" use `cron-source`.

Output: the body is the number, as an Integer (a whole number, not text). The `Content-Type` header is `text/plain`.

Good to know: it keeps sending until the integration is stopped, unless `numbers` is set. The count starts again from `start` when the integration restarts.

kamelets.name: cron-source
kamelets.title: Cron Source
kamelets.summary: Sends the same fixed message on a calendar schedule, written as a cron expression, such as every weekday at 9:00.
kamelets.description:
Sends the same fixed message on a calendar schedule, written as a cron expression, such as every weekday at 9:00.

Use it to start a flow at set times, such as a report every morning or a clean-up every night. For a message every few seconds or minutes, `timer-source` is simpler, and for a message that counts up use `counter-source`.

Output: the body is the `message` option as text, the same on every message. Headers about the schedule are set too, such as `fireTime` (the time of this message) and `nextFireTime`.

Good to know: the times are in the time zone of the machine it runs on. It keeps sending until the integration is stopped.

kamelets.name: crypto-decrypt-action
kamelets.title: Crypto Decrypt Action
kamelets.summary: Decrypts the body of each message that `crypto-encrypt-action` encrypted, with the same algorithm and secret key.
kamelets.description:
Decrypts the body of each message that `crypto-encrypt-action` encrypted, with the same algorithm and secret key.

Use it to get back the original data that was encrypted with `crypto-encrypt-action`, for example after reading it from storage or receiving it from another system.

Input: the encrypted data exactly as `crypto-encrypt-action` produced it, as bytes or a stream. If it was encoded on the way, for example in Base64, decode it first.

Output: the body is the original data, as bytes (a stream). The headers are kept.

Good to know: data that was changed, or a different `algorithm`, `mode` or `key` than when encrypting, fails the message with "Message authentication failed". The key is a secret; keep it in a vault or a secret, not in plain configuration.

kamelets.name: crypto-encrypt-action
kamelets.title: Crypto Encrypt Action
kamelets.summary: Encrypts the body of each message with a secret key, such as an AES key, for `crypto-decrypt-action` to decrypt later with the same key.
kamelets.description:
Encrypts the body of each message with a secret key, such as an AES key, for `crypto-decrypt-action` to decrypt later with the same key.

Use it to protect sensitive data, such as personal or payment details, before it is stored or sent through a system you do not fully trust, and decrypt it later with `crypto-decrypt-action` and the same `algorithm` and `key`.

Input: text or bytes.

Output: the body is the encrypted data, as bytes (a stream), a little longer than the input. It is not text: to send it where only text fits, encode it, for example in Base64. The headers are kept.

Good to know: the key is a secret; anyone who has it can decrypt the data, so keep it in a vault or a secret, not in plain configuration. The encrypted data carries a check value, so `crypto-decrypt-action` fails on data that was changed or decrypted with another key. A key of the wrong length fails each message, not the start. Set `mode` to `CBC`: without it, AES encrypts in ECB mode, where equal parts of the data give equal encrypted bytes. Data encrypted without `mode` is decrypted only without `mode`, so set it on both actions at the same time.

kamelets.name: data-type-action
kamelets.title: Data Type Action
kamelets.summary: Converts the body of each message into the data type you name, such as plain text, bytes, JSON, Avro or Protobuf, and sets the `Content-Type` header to match.
kamelets.description:
Converts the body of each message into the data type you name, such as plain text, bytes, JSON, Avro or Protobuf, and sets the `Content-Type` header to match.

Use it to give the next step the kind of body it needs, such as bytes for a sink that writes files, or to turn JSON into Avro binary data after `resolve-pojo-schema-action` has found the schema. A data type is a name for a kind of body together with the conversion into it; `camel catalog transformer` lists the names.

Input: `text-plain` and `application-octet-stream` take any text; `application-json` and `application-x-struct` take JSON text; `avro-binary` and `protobuf-binary` take a JSON object, as JSON text or a Jackson `JsonNode` but not a Map; `avro-x-struct` and `protobuf-x-struct` take Avro or Protobuf binary data.

Output: `text-plain` gives text (`Content-Type` `text/plain`); `application-octet-stream` bytes (`application/octet-stream`); `application-json` JSON text as bytes (`application/json`); the `x-struct` ones parsed JSON, a Jackson `JsonNode` (`application/x-struct`); `avro-binary` and `protobuf-binary` binary data (`avro/binary`, `protobuf/binary`). `application-cloudevents+json` wraps the body, under `data`, in a CloudEvents JSON envelope.

Good to know: a name that does not exist makes every message fail, and so do the Avro and Protobuf data types without a schema from an earlier `resolve-pojo-schema-action`. With `text-plain`, a Map becomes text such as `{id=1, name=Ann}`, not JSON.

kamelets.name: databricks-sink
kamelets.title: Databricks Sink
kamelets.summary: Runs an SQL statement, such as an INSERT, on a Databricks SQL warehouse or cluster for each message, with values taken from the fields of the JSON object in the body.
kamelets.description:
Runs an SQL statement, such as an INSERT, on a Databricks SQL warehouse or cluster for each message, with values taken from the fields of the JSON object in the body.

Use it to store records from another system as rows of a table, such as each order that arrives on a Kafka topic, or to update or delete rows. To read rows, use `databricks-source`.

Input: the body is one JSON object, as text, such as `{"username":"oscerd","city":"Rome"}`. In `query`, write `:#username` where the value of the field `username` goes. When the object has no field of that name, the header of that name is used instead. Fields that `query` does not name are ignored.

Output: the body afterwards is the JSON object as a Map, and the `CamelSqlUpdateCount` header holds the number of rows the statement changed. When `query` is a SELECT, the body is instead a List of the rows found, each a Map, and the `CamelSqlRowCount` header holds their number.

Good to know: a message fails when its body is not a JSON object (a JSON array or plain text, for example), or when it has no value for a parameter of `query`. The values are sent to the database apart from the SQL text, so the content of a message cannot change the statement. Do not write `?` in `query`, not even in a quoted string: the Kamelet then fails to start.

kamelets.name: databricks-source
kamelets.title: Databricks Source
kamelets.summary: Runs an SQL query on a Databricks SQL warehouse or cluster again and again, and sends each row it returns as a message, as a JSON object.
kamelets.description:
Runs an SQL query on a Databricks SQL warehouse or cluster again and again, and sends each row it returns as a message, as a JSON object.

Use it to pick up the rows that another application adds to a table, such as new orders or events, and pass them on to another system. To write rows, use `databricks-sink`.

Output: the body is one row as JSON text, an object with the column names as keys, such as `{"id":1,"username":"oscerd","city":"Rome"}`. The `Content-Type` header is `application/json`.

Good to know: the query runs again `delay` milliseconds after the previous run, so the same rows are sent again and again, unless `consumedQuery` marks or deletes each row once it is sent and `query` leaves such rows out: for example `SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE processed = false` with `UPDATE accounts SET processed = true WHERE id = :#id`. When the next step fails for a row, `consumedQuery` is not run for it, and the row is read again. A query that finds no rows sends nothing. `query` cannot contain `?`. The format of date and time columns in the JSON depends on the Camel version.

kamelets.name: delay-action
kamelets.title: Delay Action
kamelets.summary: Holds each message for a fixed time, such as one second, before passing it on.
kamelets.description:
Holds each message for a fixed time, such as one second, before passing it on.

Use it to slow down a flow, for example to give another system time to finish its work before the next step, or to space out the calls of a test. To limit how many messages pass per second or per minute, rather than holding each one, use `throttle-action`.

Input: any message.

Output: the same message, unchanged, after the wait.

kamelets.name: dns-dig-action
kamelets.title: DNS DIG Action
kamelets.summary: Asks the DNS for the records of one kind, such as A or MX, of a name, and gives the answer as text, in the format of the `dig` tool.
kamelets.description:
Asks the DNS for the records of one kind, such as A or MX, of a name, and gives the answer as text, in the format of the `dig` tool.

Use it to see the records of a domain, such as its mail (MX) records, for example to check a DNS change. To get only the IP address of a name, use `dns-ip-action`, and to get its address records as JSON, use `dns-lookup-action`.

Input: the name to look up, taken from the `domain-name` header, else from the `ce-domainname` header, else from the body as text. The kind of record comes from the `dns-type` header, else from the `ce-dnstype` header, else it is `A` (the IPv4 addresses).

Output: the body is the whole answer as text, as the `dig` command shows it: the question, the records found, and the status, such as `NOERROR`.

Good to know: a name the DNS does not know does not fail the message: the answer has the status `NXDOMAIN` and no records. The Kamelet has no options; it asks the DNS servers of the machine it runs on.

kamelets.name: dns-ip-action
kamelets.title: DNS IP Action
kamelets.summary: Finds the IP address of a host name, such as `apache.org`, and gives it as text.
kamelets.description:
Finds the IP address of a host name, such as `apache.org`, and gives it as text.

Use it to turn a host name into an address for a later step, or to check that a name can be resolved. To see all the address records of a name with how long they may be cached, use `dns-lookup-action`, and to ask for other kinds of record, such as mail (MX) records, use `dns-dig-action`.

Input: the name to look up, taken from the `domain` header, else from the `ce-domain` header, else from the body as text.

Output: the body is one IP address, as text, such as `151.101.2.132`.

Good to know: when a name has several addresses, only one of them is given. A name the DNS does not know fails the message with an unknown host error. The headers are `domain` and `ce-domain`, not `domain-name` as for `dns-lookup-action` and `dns-dig-action`. The Kamelet has no options; it uses the name resolution of the machine it runs on.

kamelets.name: dns-lookup-action
kamelets.title: DNS Lookup Action
kamelets.summary: Asks the DNS for the address records of a host name, such as `apache.org`, and gives them as JSON.
kamelets.description:
Asks the DNS for the address records of a host name, such as `apache.org`, and gives them as JSON.

Use it to check that a name exists in the DNS, or to see its records and how long they may be cached, for example to monitor a domain. To get the IP address of a name, use `dns-ip-action` instead, and to ask for other kinds of record, such as mail (MX) records, use `dns-dig-action`.

Input: the name to look up, taken from the `domain-name` header, else from the `ce-domainname` header, else from the body as text.

Output: the body is a JSON array with one entry per record found. Each entry has the type, the class and the time to live of the record.

Good to know: a name the DNS does not know fails the message with "host not found". The Kamelet has no options; it asks the DNS servers of the machine it runs on.

kamelets.name: docling-convert-action
kamelets.title: Docling Convert Action
kamelets.summary: Turns each document, such as a PDF, an office document or an HTML page, into Markdown, HTML or plain text with Docling, keeping its headings, lists and tables.
kamelets.description:
Turns each document, such as a PDF, an office document or an HTML page, into Markdown, HTML or plain text with Docling, keeping its headings, lists and tables.

Use it to get well-structured text out of documents before an AI step, for example in front of `langchain4j-ingest-sink` to load them into a vector store. For plain text without a Docling server, use `tika-extract-text-action`.

Input: the document, as bytes, a stream, a file or text. The header named in `documentIdHeader` (by default `CamelLangChain4jIngestDocumentId`) is the id of the document, if any; it is kept for `langchain4j-ingest-sink` further on.

Output: the body is the document as Markdown, as text, or as HTML or plain text with `operation`. The headers of the message are kept.

Good to know: to use a Docling Serve server, which is the usual setup, set both `useDoclingServe` to true and `doclingServeUrl`; otherwise it runs the `docling` command-line program, which must be installed on the machine of the integration. A server started with an API key needs `authenticationScheme` set to `API_KEY` and the key in `authenticationToken`. A conversion that takes longer than `processTimeout`, 30 seconds when it is not set, fails the message; the first conversion after a Docling Serve server starts, and a large PDF on a server without a GPU, can take longer than that. The text in images, such as scanned pages, is read with OCR unless `enableOcr` is false. With `maxDocumentSize`, a larger document fails the message without being sent.

kamelets.name: drop-field-action
kamelets.title: Drop Field Action
kamelets.summary: Removes one field, chosen by its name, from each message that is a JSON object.
kamelets.description:
Removes one field, chosen by its name, from each message that is a JSON object.

Use it to take out a field that the next system does not accept or should not see, such as an internal ID or a password. To remove several fields, or to keep only some, use `replace-field-action`; to keep the field but hide its value, use `mask-field-action`.

Input: a JSON object, as JSON text or as parsed JSON (a Map or a Jackson `JsonNode`). Only the fields at the top level of the object are looked at. A JSON array is passed on unchanged; a body that is not JSON fails.

Output: the same object without the field. When the `Content-Type` header is `application/json`, the body is JSON text again; otherwise it is parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`), which `json-serialize-action` turns into JSON text.

Good to know: a message without the field is passed on unchanged. A field of the same name inside a nested object is not removed.

kamelets.name: drop-header-action
kamelets.title: Drop Header Action
kamelets.summary: Removes one header, given by its name, from each message.
kamelets.description:
Removes one header, given by its name, from each message.

Use it to remove a header that the next step must not see, for example an `Authorization` header with a secret, or a header that would change what a sink does. To remove several headers at once by a pattern, such as all the headers whose names start with `Camel`, use `drop-headers-action`.

Input: any message.

Output: the same body, and the same headers without the one named by `name`. A message without that header passes on unchanged.

Good to know: the name is not case-sensitive: `FOO` also removes the header `foo`.

kamelets.name: drop-headers-action
kamelets.title: Drop Headers Action
kamelets.summary: Removes from each message all the headers whose names match a pattern, such as `Camel*`.
kamelets.description:
Removes from each message all the headers whose names match a pattern, such as `Camel*`.

Use it to remove the internal `Camel*` headers that came with a message from outside before it reaches a sink, or to clear many headers at once before a message goes to another system. To remove a single header by its name, `drop-header-action` is enough.

Input: any message.

Output: the same body, without the headers that match `pattern`. The headers that match `excludePattern` are kept.

Good to know: a pattern is compared with each header name first as an exact name, then as a wildcard when it ends with `*` (`x-*` matches every name that starts with `x-`), and then as a Java regular expression, such as `x-(one|two)`. None of these comparisons is case-sensitive.

kamelets.name: elasticsearch-index-sink
kamelets.title: ElasticSearch Index Sink
kamelets.summary: Stores each message, a JSON object, as a document in an index of Elasticsearch, so that it can be searched.
kamelets.description:
Stores each message, a JSON object, as a document in an index of Elasticsearch, so that it can be searched.

Use it to make records searchable, such as orders, log entries or products, or to feed dashboards in Kibana. For OpenSearch, use `opensearch-index-sink`.

Input: the body is the document, as JSON text, such as `{"order": 42, "status": "shipped"}`. The optional `indexId` header (or `ce-indexid`) is the id of the document: a document with the same id is replaced. Without it, Elasticsearch makes up a new id, so each message adds a new document. The optional `indexName` header (or `ce-indexname`) is the index to write to, instead of the `indexName` option.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the id of the document, as text.

Good to know: a body that is not JSON fails the message, and so does a message with no index, from the option or the header. It connects with TLS by default (`enableSSL`). For a cluster whose certificate is self-signed, or signed by a private certificate authority (CA), give the certificate of that CA in `certificate`; without it, the message fails with `PKIX path building failed`. When Elasticsearch does not answer, the message fails after 30 seconds; `connectionTimeout` and `socketTimeout` change that.

kamelets.name: exec-sink
kamelets.title: Exec Sink
kamelets.summary: Runs a program or command on the machine where the integration runs, once for each message, with the body as its standard input.
kamelets.description:
Runs a program or command on the machine where the integration runs, once for each message, with the body as its standard input.

Use it to hand each message to an existing script or command-line tool, for example a script that imports a file or a tool that converts data, and to use what the program prints in the next step.

Input: the body is written to the standard input of the program, when it is text, bytes, a stream or a file. Another body, or no body, runs the program without input.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is what the program printed on its standard output, as a stream, or no body when it printed nothing. The `CamelExecExitValue` header is the exit code of the program, and `CamelExecStderr` what it printed on its standard error.

Good to know: this Kamelet runs programs by design, with the rights of the integration, so never place it after a source of untrusted messages. `executable` is only the name or path of the program, and its arguments go in `args`. Only the options decide what runs: `CamelExecCommand*` headers on the message are ignored. The program is started directly, not through a shell, so `*`, `$HOME`, `|`, `>` and `;` in the arguments are passed on as they are. A program that ends with an error exit code does not fail the message; check `CamelExecExitValue`, or list the exit codes that mean success in `exitValues`. A program that is not found, or a `workingDir` that does not exist, fails the message. A program that runs longer than `commandTimeout` is stopped.

kamelets.name: extract-field-action
kamelets.title: Extract Field Action
kamelets.summary: Replaces the body of each message that is a JSON object with the value of one of its fields, or copies that value into a header.
kamelets.description:
Replaces the body of each message that is a JSON object with the value of one of its fields, or copies that value into a header.

Use it to keep only the part of a message you need, such as the `payload` of an event or the `email` of a customer, or, with `headerOutput`, to have that value in a header for a later step while the body stays as it is. To do the opposite, and wrap a body in a field, use `hoist-field-action`.

Input: a JSON object, as JSON text or as parsed JSON (a Map or a Jackson `JsonNode`). The field must be at the top level of the object. A JSON array, or a body that is not JSON, fails.

Output: the body is the value of the field. When the `Content-Type` header is `application/json`, it is JSON text, so a text value keeps its quotes (`"Ann"`) unless `trimField` is true; otherwise it is the value itself, such as the text `Ann`. When `headerOutput` is true, the value goes into the header `CamelKameletsExtractFieldName`, or the header named by `headerOutputName`, and the body is left as it was.

Good to know: when the object does not have the field, the body or the header is empty (the JSON text `null` when the `Content-Type` header is `application/json`); the message does not fail.

kamelets.name: fhir-sink
kamelets.title: FHIR Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message, a FHIR resource such as a Patient or an Observation, to a FHIR server of healthcare data, to create, update, delete or validate it there.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message, a FHIR resource such as a Patient or an Observation, to a FHIR server of healthcare data, to create, update, delete or validate it there.

Use it to write healthcare records into a FHIR server, for example to create a Patient for each new admission, or to update an Observation that a device measured. To read resources from a FHIR server, use `fhir-source`.

Input: the body is the FHIR resource, as JSON text, or as XML text with `encoding` set to `XML`, such as `{"resourceType": "Patient", "name": [{"family": "Doe"}]}`. It is sent with the operation set by `apiName` and `methodName`, which must be one that takes a resource: `CREATE` with `resource`, `UPDATE` with `resource`, `DELETE` with `resource`, or `VALIDATE` with `resource`.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the outcome of the operation, as a Java object of the HAPI FHIR library, with the id of the resource; it is not JSON.

Good to know: a body that is not a valid FHIR resource of the chosen `fhirVersion` fails the message. Operations that do not take a resource, such as `READ` or `SEARCH`, fail. Before the first message, it reads the capability statement of the server at `/metadata`, unless `validationMode` is `NEVER`. A server that does not answer within `connectionTimeout` and `socketTimeout`, 10 seconds each when they are not set, fails the message.

kamelets.name: fhir-source
kamelets.title: FHIR Source
kamelets.summary: Runs the same search on a FHIR server of healthcare data over and over, by default for all the Patient resources, and sends each search result, a FHIR Bundle, as one message.
kamelets.description:
Runs the same search on a FHIR server of healthcare data over and over, by default for all the Patient resources, and sends each search result, a FHIR Bundle, as one message.

Use it to copy healthcare records, such as patients or observations, from a FHIR server into another system, or to check a FHIR server on a schedule. To create or update resources on a FHIR server, use `fhir-sink`.

Output: the body is a FHIR Bundle of type `searchset`, as JSON text, with the number of resources found (`total`) and the resources themselves under `entry`. The `Content-Type` header is `application/fhir+json`.

Good to know: a new search starts about every half second unless `delay` is set, and every search returns all the matching resources again, not only the new ones; add a filter such as `_lastUpdated` to `url` to narrow it. Log in with `username` and `password`, or with `accessToken`, or leave them out for a server without login; when both kinds are set, both are sent.

kamelets.name: file-watch-source
kamelets.title: File Watch Source
kamelets.summary: Sends a message each time a file in a local directory is created, changed or deleted, with the kind of change and the path of the file.
kamelets.description:
Sends a message each time a file in a local directory is created, changed or deleted, with the kind of change and the path of the file.

Use it to react to files that another program writes into a directory on the same machine, for example to start processing when a new export appears, or to keep track of the changes in a folder. To read files from a remote server instead, use `ftp-source`, `sftp-source` or `aws-s3-source`.

Output: the body is the file that changed, which the next step can read as text or bytes; a deleted file or a directory has no content to read. The `CamelFileEventType` header is `CREATE`, `MODIFY` or `DELETE`, `CamelFileName` is the path of the file relative to the watched directory, and `CamelFileAbsolutePath` is its full path.

Good to know: it watches the subdirectories too, new ones included, unless `recursive` is false. To send only the changes of some files, set `antInclude`. It never changes or deletes the files. Only changes made while it runs are sent, not the files that are already there when it starts. The path must be a directory, not a single file; it is created when it does not exist. On Kubernetes, mount the directory into the pod as a volume.

kamelets.name: freemarker-template-action
kamelets.title: Freemarker Template Action
kamelets.summary: Builds a new message body from a FreeMarker template, filling in values from the incoming message.
kamelets.description:
Builds a new message body from a FreeMarker template, filling in values from the incoming message.

Use it to turn data into text for people or for another system, such as an email, a report or a small XML or JSON document, when you already have FreeMarker templates or need its loops and conditions. For simple templates, `mustache-template-action` is an alternative; to reshape JSON into other JSON, `jslt-action` is often simpler.

Input: any body. The template sees the body as `$\{body}` and a header as `${headers.name}`, for example `Dear ${headers.customer}, your order $\{body} has shipped.`

Output: the body is the text the template produced. The headers are kept.

Good to know: a value the template uses that is missing, such as a header that is not set, fails the message; give a default with `${headers.customer!""}`. A template file that cannot be found fails the message too. The template is loaded from a file, the classpath or a URL given by the `template` option; it cannot come from the message.

kamelets.name: ftp-sink
kamelets.title: FTP Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file to a directory on an FTP server.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file to a directory on an FTP server.

Use it to deliver exports, reports or data files to a partner or a legacy system that receives files over FTP. For an encrypted connection use `ftps-sink`, and for a server you reach with SSH use `sftp-sink`.

Input: the body is the content of the file, as text, bytes or a stream. The name of the file comes from the `file` header, or from `ce-file` when `file` is not set; any directory in it is dropped, so `reports/data.csv` is written as `data.csv`. Without these headers, `CamelFileName` is used as it is, subdirectories included, and without any of them a unique name is generated.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelFileNameProduced` header is set to the path of the file on the server.

Good to know: a file with the same name is replaced, unless `fileExist` says otherwise. A file is uploaded under its real name from the start, so a reader that polls the directory can pick it up half-written. To prevent that, set `tempPrefix` to upload it under a temporary name and rename it once it is complete, or `doneFileName` to write an empty done file next to it once it is complete. The connection and the login are not encrypted. A file name that points outside `directoryName` fails the message. Files are sent in ASCII (text) mode unless `binary` is true.

kamelets.name: ftp-source
kamelets.title: FTP Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files in a directory on an FTP server, one message per file, and by default leaves them on the server.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files in a directory on an FTP server, one message per file, and by default leaves them on the server.

Use it to collect the files that a partner or a legacy system drops on an FTP server, such as orders, invoices or exports. For an encrypted connection use `ftps-source`, and for a server you reach with SSH use `sftp-source`.

Output: the body is the content of the file, as a stream. The `file` and `ce-file` headers hold the name of the file, with its path below `directoryName` when `recursive` is true, such as `2026/orders.csv`. `CamelFileName` holds the same name, and `CamelFileLength` the size of the file in bytes.

Good to know: files are not deleted or moved after they are read, unless `delete` is true or `move` is set. A file is read only once while the integration runs (`idempotent`), but the files left on the server are all read again after a restart; to read each file only once, also across restarts, set `move` to a directory such as `.done`, set `delete` to true, or keep the list of the files read in a file with `idempotentRepository`. To read only some of the files, set `include`, `exclude` or `antInclude`. To leave a file alone while another program is still writing it, set `readLock`. The connection and the login are not encrypted. Files are transferred in ASCII (text) mode unless `binary` is true.

kamelets.name: ftps-sink
kamelets.title: FTPS Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file to a directory on an FTPS server, which is FTP with TLS encryption.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file to a directory on an FTPS server, which is FTP with TLS encryption.

Use it to deliver exports, reports or data files to a partner or a legacy system that receives files over FTPS. For a server without TLS use `ftp-sink`, and for a server you reach with SSH use `sftp-sink`.

Input: the body is the content of the file, as text, bytes or a stream. The name of the file comes from the `file` header, or from `ce-file` when `file` is not set; any directory in it is dropped, so `reports/data.csv` is written as `data.csv`. Without these headers, `CamelFileName` is used as it is, subdirectories included, and without any of them a unique name is generated.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelFileNameProduced` header is set to the path of the file on the server.

Good to know: a file with the same name is replaced, unless `fileExist` says otherwise. A file is uploaded under its real name from the start, so a reader that polls the directory can pick it up half-written. To prevent that, set `tempPrefix` to upload it under a temporary name and rename it once it is complete, or `doneFileName` to write an empty done file next to it once it is complete. By default it uses explicit TLS: it connects to the normal FTP port, usually 21, and then switches to TLS. For a server that uses implicit TLS, usually on port 990, set `implicit` to true. A file name that points outside `directoryName` fails the message. Files are sent in ASCII (text) mode unless `binary` is true.

kamelets.name: ftps-source
kamelets.title: FTPS Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files in a directory on an FTPS server (FTP with TLS encryption), one message per file, and by default leaves them on the server.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files in a directory on an FTPS server (FTP with TLS encryption), one message per file, and by default leaves them on the server.

Use it to collect the files that a partner or a legacy system drops on an FTPS server, such as orders, invoices or exports. For a server without TLS use `ftp-source`, and for a server you reach with SSH use `sftp-source`.

Output: the body is the content of the file, as a stream. The `file` and `ce-file` headers hold the name of the file, with its path below `directoryName` when `recursive` is true, such as `2026/orders.csv`. `CamelFileName` holds the same name, and `CamelFileLength` the size of the file in bytes.

Good to know: files are not deleted or moved after they are read, unless `delete` is true or `move` is set. A file is read only once while the integration runs (`idempotent`), but the files left on the server are all read again after a restart; to read each file only once, also across restarts, set `move` to a directory such as `.done`, set `delete` to true, or keep the list of the files read in a file with `idempotentRepository`. To read only some of the files, set `include`, `exclude` or `antInclude`. To leave a file alone while another program is still writing it, set `readLock`. By default it uses explicit TLS: it connects to the normal FTP port, usually 21, and then switches to TLS. For a server that uses implicit TLS, usually on port 990, set `implicit` to true. Files are transferred in ASCII (text) mode unless `binary` is true.

kamelets.name: github-commit-source
kamelets.title: GitHub Commit Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each new commit on a branch of a GitHub repository, one message per commit, oldest first, by asking the GitHub API for new commits.
kamelets.description:
Receives each new commit on a branch of a GitHub repository, one message per commit, oldest first, by asking the GitHub API for new commits.

Use it to start a flow when code is pushed, for example to post the commit message to a chat channel or to trigger a build or a deployment.

Output: the body is the commit message as JSON text, that is a quoted JSON string such as `"Fix the login page"`. The `CamelGitHubCommitSha` header gives the SHA of the commit, `CamelGitHubCommitUrl` its web address, and `CamelGitHubCommitAuthor` and `CamelGitHubCommitCommitter` the names of its author and committer.

Good to know: with the default `startingSha` of `last`, only the commits made after the start are sent. It works with github.com, not with GitHub Enterprise Server. It asks GitHub for new commits once a minute by default (`delay`), and every request counts against the API rate limit of the token.

kamelets.name: github-event-source
kamelets.title: GitHub Event Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the activity of a GitHub repository, such as pushes, issues, pull requests and stars, one message per event, by asking the GitHub API for new events.
kamelets.description:
Receives the activity of a GitHub repository, such as pushes, issues, pull requests and stars, one message per event, by asking the GitHub API for new events.

Use it to follow everything that happens in a repository in one flow, for example to log it or to count it. To receive only commits, pull requests, comments on pull requests or tags, use `github-commit-source`, `github-pullrequest-source`, `github-pullrequest-comment-source` or `github-tag-source`.

Output: the body is the type of the event as JSON text, that is a quoted JSON string such as `"PUSH"`, `"PULL_REQUEST"` or `"ISSUES"`. The details of the event are only in the `CamelGitHubEventPayload` header, as a Java object.

Good to know: when it starts, it first sends the recent events that GitHub still lists for the repository, not only the new ones. It works with github.com, not with GitHub Enterprise Server. It asks GitHub for new events once a minute by default (`delay`), and every request counts against the API rate limit of the token.

kamelets.name: github-pullrequest-comment-source
kamelets.title: GitHub Pull Request Comments Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each new comment written on the open pull requests of a GitHub repository, one message per comment, by asking the GitHub API for new comments.
kamelets.description:
Receives each new comment written on the open pull requests of a GitHub repository, one message per comment, by asking the GitHub API for new comments.

Use it to react to the discussion on pull requests, for example to answer a command written in a comment, such as `/retest`, or to forward the comments to a chat channel. To receive the pull requests themselves, use `github-pullrequest-source`.

Output: the body is the comment as JSON text. The `CamelGitHubPullRequest` header gives the number of the pull request it was written on.

Good to know: only the comments written after the start are sent, and only on pull requests that are still open. These are the comments of the conversation of a pull request, not the review comments on lines of code. It works with github.com, not with GitHub Enterprise Server. Once a minute by default (`delay`), it asks GitHub for the open pull requests and for the comments of each of them, and every request counts against the API rate limit of the token.

kamelets.name: github-pullrequest-source
kamelets.title: GitHub Pull Request Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each new pull request opened in a GitHub repository, one message per pull request, by asking the GitHub API for new open pull requests.
kamelets.description:
Receives each new pull request opened in a GitHub repository, one message per pull request, by asking the GitHub API for new open pull requests.

Use it to react when someone proposes a change, for example to announce the pull request in a chat channel, open a review ticket or start a check. To receive the comments on pull requests, use `github-pullrequest-comment-source`.

Output: the body is the pull request as JSON text. The `CamelGitHubPullRequest` header gives its number, and `CamelGitHubPullRequestHeadCommitSha` the SHA of its latest commit.

Good to know: only the pull requests opened after the start are sent, once each; updates, merges and closes are not. It works with github.com, not with GitHub Enterprise Server. It asks GitHub for new pull requests once a minute by default (`delay`), and every request counts against the API rate limit of the token.

kamelets.name: github-tag-source
kamelets.title: GitHub Tag Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each new tag created in a GitHub repository, one message per tag, by asking the GitHub API for the tags of the repository.
kamelets.description:
Receives each new tag created in a GitHub repository, one message per tag, by asking the GitHub API for the tags of the repository.

Use it to react to a new version, for example to announce a release, update a changelog or start a deployment. To receive every commit instead, use `github-commit-source`.

Output: the body is the tag as JSON text.

Good to know: only the tags created after the start are sent; the tags that exist when it starts are skipped. It works with github.com, not with GitHub Enterprise Server. It asks GitHub for the tags once a minute by default (`delay`), and every request counts against the API rate limit of the token.

kamelets.name: google-bigquery-sink
kamelets.title: Google Big Query Sink
kamelets.summary: Inserts each message as one or more rows into a table in Google BigQuery.
kamelets.description:
Inserts each message as one or more rows into a table in Google BigQuery.

Use it to load events or records into BigQuery for analytics and reports, such as orders, page views or sensor readings, as they happen.

Input: the body is JSON text: a JSON object for one row, or a JSON array of objects for several rows. The names of the fields are the names of the columns of the table, such as `{"id": 1, "item": "book"}`.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the parsed JSON: a Map for one row, or a List of Maps.

Good to know: the table must exist with its columns. A message with a field that is not a column of the table, or with a body that is not JSON, fails, and none of its rows are inserted. A message that is sent again, for example after a failure, adds its rows again, unless `useAsInsertId` names a field that identifies each row.

kamelets.name: google-calendar-source
kamelets.title: Google Calendar Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the events of a Google Calendar, such as meetings and appointments, one message per event, by asking the calendar for events at a regular interval.
kamelets.description:
Receives the events of a Google Calendar, such as meetings and appointments, one message per event, by asking the calendar for events at a regular interval.

Use it to act on calendar entries, for example to send a reminder before a meeting, copy new appointments into another system, or notify a team when a booking is made.

Output: the body is the event as JSON text, with the fields of the Google Calendar API such as `id`, `summary`, `start` and `attendees`. The `CamelGoogleCalendarEventId` header gives the ID of the event.

Good to know: by default it only receives the events that have not ended yet at the time of the poll (`consumeFromNow`). Each poll asks for one page of up to `maxResults` events (10 by default), the events that changed least recently first, so the same events can come again on every poll. With `considerLastUpdate` set to true, each poll reads all the pages, and after the first poll only the events that changed since the last one received. With `syncFlow` set to true, each poll after the first asks only for the events that are new or changed since the previous one; do not combine it with `query` or `considerLastUpdate`. It logs in to Google either with OAuth (an OAuth client of a Google Cloud project, and an access token and a refresh token of a Google account that may read the calendar), or with the key of a service account in `serviceAccountKey`, which reads the calendars shared with it, or the calendar of the user in `delegate`.

kamelets.name: google-mail-source
kamelets.title: Google Mail Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the emails of a Gmail mailbox that match a search, by default the unread ones, one message per email, and marks each email as read once it has been processed.
kamelets.description:
Receives the emails of a Gmail mailbox that match a search, by default the unread ones, one message per email, and marks each email as read once it has been processed.

Use it to act on incoming email, for example to open a ticket for each email sent to a support address, or to collect orders or invoices that arrive by mail.

Output: the body is the text of the email (its first part with content, such as the plain text part) as JSON text, that is the text in double quotes with JSON escapes. The headers give the subject (`CamelGoogleMailStreamSubject`), the sender (`CamelGoogleMailStreamFrom`), the recipients (`CamelGoogleMailStreamTo`, `CamelGoogleMailStreamCc`, `CamelGoogleMailStreamBcc`) and the Gmail ID of the email (`CamelGoogleMailId`). With `raw` set to true, the body is the whole email instead, with its attachments, encoded in base64url, as JSON text, and only the Gmail ID is set as a header.

Good to know: it reads the emails that match `query`, by default the unread ones. With `markAsRead` set to false and the default query, the same emails are read again on every poll. An email whose processing fails is marked as unread again. Each poll reads up to `maxResults` emails, 10 by default. It logs in to Google either with OAuth (an OAuth client of a Google Cloud project, and an access token and a refresh token of the Gmail account), or with the key of a service account in `serviceAccountKey` together with `scopes`, which reads the mailbox of the user in `delegate`.

kamelets.name: google-pubsub-sink
kamelets.title: Google Pubsub Sink
kamelets.summary: Publishes each message to a topic in Google Cloud Pub/Sub.
kamelets.description:
Publishes each message to a topic in Google Cloud Pub/Sub.

Use it to send events or data to other applications that read the topic through a subscription, such as orders, sensor readings or notifications. To read messages from a subscription, use `google-pubsub-source`.

Input: the body becomes the data of the Pub/Sub message, as text (sent as UTF-8) or bytes. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent as attributes of the Pub/Sub message.

Output: the message is unchanged, with the ID that Pub/Sub gave the published message in the `CamelGooglePubsubMessageId` header.

Good to know: the topic must exist; a message sent to a topic that does not exist fails. Without `serviceAccountKey`, it logs in with the Application Default Credentials of the environment where it runs. Pub/Sub delivers the messages in any order. To have the messages with the same `CamelGooglePubsubOrderingKey` header delivered in the order they were published, set `messageOrderingEnabled` to true and `pubsubEndpoint` to a regional endpoint, and enable message ordering on the subscription. A message with that header fails when `messageOrderingEnabled` is not true.

kamelets.name: google-pubsub-source
kamelets.title: Google Pubsub Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the messages of a Google Cloud Pub/Sub subscription, one message per Pub/Sub message, and acknowledges each one once it has been processed.
kamelets.description:
Receives the messages of a Google Cloud Pub/Sub subscription, one message per Pub/Sub message, and acknowledges each one once it has been processed.

Use it to react to events that other applications publish to a Pub/Sub topic, such as orders, uploads or alerts. To publish messages, use `google-pubsub-sink`. To react to new files in a Cloud Storage bucket through Pub/Sub notifications, use `google-storage-event-based-source`.

Output: the body is the data of the Pub/Sub message, as bytes. The `CamelGooglePubsubMessageId` and `CamelGooglePubsubPublishTime` headers give the ID and the publish time of the message, `CamelGooglePubsubAttributes` gives its attributes as a Map, and each attribute is also set as a header of its own.

Good to know: the subscription must already exist; for one that does not, it logs an error and receives nothing. A message whose processing fails is not acknowledged, so Pub/Sub delivers it again. With `ackMode` `NONE`, the route acknowledges each message itself, through the `CamelGooglePubsubAcknowledge` header. On a subscription with a dead-letter topic, `maxDeliveryAttempts` stops a message that keeps failing from being processed again. Without `serviceAccountKey`, it logs in with the Application Default Credentials of the environment where it runs.

kamelets.name: google-sheets-sink
kamelets.title: Google Sheets Sink
kamelets.summary: Writes each message as one or more rows to a Google Sheets spreadsheet, either appended after the last row or written over a given range of cells.
kamelets.description:
Writes each message as one or more rows to a Google Sheets spreadsheet, either appended after the last row or written over a given range of cells.

Use it to collect data in a spreadsheet that people can read and share, such as form submissions, orders or daily figures. To read the rows of a spreadsheet, use `google-sheets-source`.

Input: the body is JSON text: a JSON object for one row, or a JSON array of objects for several rows. The keys are the column letters of the cells to write, such as `{"A": "Alice", "B": 3}`, or the names set in `columnNames`. Only the columns of `range` are written, so set `range` to cover them, such as `A:B`.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the response of Google Sheets, which says which cells were written.

Good to know: without `range`, only column `A` is written. With the default `operation` of `append`, the rows are added after the last row of the table found in `range`; with `update`, they overwrite the cells of `range`. It logs in to Google either with OAuth (an OAuth client of a Google Cloud project, and an access token and a refresh token of the Google account that owns or may edit the spreadsheet), or with the key of a service account in `serviceAccountKey` together with `scopes`; share the spreadsheet with the email address of the service account as an editor, or set `delegate`.

kamelets.name: google-sheets-source
kamelets.title: Google Sheets Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the cells of a Google Sheets spreadsheet again and again, at a regular interval, and sends each row of the range as a message.
kamelets.description:
Reads the cells of a Google Sheets spreadsheet again and again, at a regular interval, and sends each row of the range as a message.

Use it to feed the content of a spreadsheet that people maintain, such as a price list, a contact list or a list of tasks, to another system on a schedule. To write rows to a spreadsheet, use `google-sheets-sink`.

Output: with `range` set, the body is one row as JSON text, a JSON array of the values of the row (or of one column, with `majorDimension` set to `COLUMNS`), such as `["Alice","3"]`; with `splitResults` set to false, it is the whole range as JSON text, with the rows in its `values` field. Without `range`, the body is the description of the spreadsheet (its sheets and properties) as JSON text, not its cells. The `CamelGoogleSheets.spreadsheetId` and `CamelGoogleSheets.range` headers repeat the options.

Good to know: every poll reads the whole range again, by default every 500 milliseconds, so the same rows come again and again until `repeatCount` is reached; it does not track which rows are new. It logs in to Google either with OAuth (an OAuth client of a Google Cloud project, and an access token and a refresh token of a Google account that may read the spreadsheet), or with the key of a service account in `serviceAccountKey` together with `scopes`; share the spreadsheet with the email address of the service account, or set `delegate`.

kamelets.name: google-storage-event-based-source
kamelets.title: Google Storage Event-based Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the change notifications of a Google Cloud Storage bucket from a Pub/Sub subscription, one message per change, and can download each new file.
kamelets.description:
Receives the change notifications of a Google Cloud Storage bucket from a Pub/Sub subscription, one message per change, and can download each new file.

Use it to react as soon as a file is uploaded to, changed in or deleted from a bucket, without reading the whole bucket over and over. It needs a Pub/Sub notification on the bucket, created for example with `gcloud storage buckets notifications create gs://my-bucket --topic=my-topic`, and a subscription on that topic. To read and delete the files of a bucket instead, use `google-storage-source`.

Output: by default, the body is the notification as JSON text (bytes): the metadata of the file, such as its name, size and content type. The `eventType` header says what happened (`OBJECT_FINALIZE` for a new or replaced file, `OBJECT_DELETE` for a deleted one), and the `objectId` and `bucketId` headers give the name of the file and of its bucket. With `getObject` set to true, the body of a new file in `bucketNameOrArn` is the content of the file, as bytes, with the `CamelGoogleCloudStorage...` headers of the file.

Good to know: every notification of the subscription comes out, also for other events and other buckets; `bucketNameOrArn` is only used to choose which new files to download. Downloading does not delete the file. A notification whose processing fails is not acknowledged, so Pub/Sub delivers it again. With `ackMode` `NONE`, the route acknowledges each notification itself, through the `CamelGooglePubsubAcknowledge` header. On a subscription with a dead-letter topic, `maxDeliveryAttempts` stops a notification that keeps failing from being processed again.

kamelets.name: google-storage-sink
kamelets.title: Google Storage Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file (object) to a Google Cloud Storage bucket.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file (object) to a Google Cloud Storage bucket.

Use it to store data for later use or for other systems, such as exported reports, archived events or files received from another system. To read the files of a bucket, use `google-storage-source`.

Input: the body is the content of the file, as text, bytes, a stream or a file. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The optional `file` header (or `ce-file`) is the name of the file in the bucket, with its folders, such as `reports/2024-06-01.csv`; without it, the file gets a generated unique name.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards describes the uploaded file (its bucket, name, size and generation), not its content, and the `CamelGoogleCloudStorageObjectName` header holds the name of the file.

Good to know: a file with the same name is overwritten. With `objectName`, every message overwrites the same file. The bucket must exist, unless `autoCreateBucket` is true; a bucket it creates is in `storageLocation`, `US-EAST1` when that is not set. Without `serviceAccountKey`, it logs in with the Application Default Credentials of the environment where it runs, or with Workload Identity Federation when `useWorkloadIdentityFederation` is true.

kamelets.name: google-storage-source
kamelets.title: Google Storage Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files (objects) in a Google Cloud Storage bucket, one message per file, and by default deletes each file once it has been read.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files (objects) in a Google Cloud Storage bucket, one message per file, and by default deletes each file once it has been read.

Use it to process files that another system drops into a bucket, such as uploaded documents, exported reports or log files. To react to new files through Pub/Sub notifications instead of reading the bucket over and over, use `google-storage-event-based-source`.

Output: the body is the content of the file, as a stream. The headers give the bucket name (`CamelGoogleCloudStorageBucketName`), the object name, that is the path of the file in the bucket (`CamelGoogleCloudStorageObjectName`), the content type and the ETag of the file.

Good to know: files are deleted from the bucket after they are read, unless `deleteAfterRead` is set to false; then the same files are read again on every poll, about twice a second, or every `delay` milliseconds. With `moveAfterRead`, they are copied to `destinationBucket` first. A file whose processing fails is not deleted or moved, and is read again on the next poll. Without `serviceAccountKey`, it logs in with the Application Default Credentials of the environment where it runs, or with Workload Identity Federation when `useWorkloadIdentityFederation` is true.

kamelets.name: google-vertexai-sink
kamelets.title: Google Vertex AI Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message as a prompt to a generative AI model in Google Vertex AI, such as Gemini, and replaces the body with the answer of the model.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message as a prompt to a generative AI model in Google Vertex AI, such as Gemini, and replaces the body with the answer of the model.

Use it to summarize, classify, translate or answer questions about text as it flows, for example to summarize support tickets or extract the topic of an email. To call a partner model of the Model Garden instead, such as Claude of Anthropic, set `operation` to `rawPredict` and `publisher`.

Input: the body is the prompt, as text; bytes and streams are read as text. The optional `CamelGoogleVertexAIPrompt` header gives the prompt instead of the body. With `rawPredict`, the header is not used: the body is the prompt as text, or a JSON request in the format of the publisher, such as the Messages API of Anthropic, which is sent as it is, with `anthropic_version` added for Anthropic.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the answer of the model, as text, for the default `generateText` operation; with `jsonMode` set to true, it is JSON text. The `CamelGoogleVertexAIFinishReason` header says why the model stopped, and the token counts are in the `CamelGoogleVertexAIPromptTokenCount`, `CamelGoogleVertexAICandidatesTokenCount` and `CamelGoogleVertexAITotalTokenCount` headers. With `rawPredict` and the publisher `anthropic`, the body afterwards is the text of the answer, and the `CamelGoogleVertexAIRawResponse` header has the whole answer as JSON text; with another publisher, the body is the answer of the model as JSON text.

Good to know: with a prompt as text and the publisher `anthropic`, `rawPredict` also sends `temperature`, `topP` and `topK`, as 0.7, 0.95 and 40 when they are not set, and `maxOutputTokens` as `max_tokens`, 1024 when it is not set. Send a JSON request as the body to choose the fields of the request yourself.

kamelets.name: graphql-sink
kamelets.title: GraphQL Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends a GraphQL query or mutation, from the body of each message or from a file, to a GraphQL server with an HTTP POST, and gives back the answer of the server.
kamelets.description:
Sends a GraphQL query or mutation, from the body of each message or from a file, to a GraphQL server with an HTTP POST, and gives back the answer of the server.

Use it to create or change data through a GraphQL API with a mutation, for example to add a record for each event, or to fetch data with a query. It can also run a stored query from `queryFile` each time a message arrives.

Input: the body is the GraphQL query or mutation itself, as text, such as `{ books { title } }`. A body that is not text, such as a Map, fails the message. With `queryFile`, the query comes from that file instead, and the body is not sent, except that a Map body is sent as the variables of the query when `variables` is not set. The other headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent as HTTP headers.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the answer of the server, as JSON text with its `data` and `errors`.

Good to know: GraphQL errors in the answer do not fail the message, but an HTTP status outside 200 to 299 does. Without `queryFile`, the body is run as a query, so only send it messages from a source you trust. When the query defines several operations, `operationName` picks the one to run. To go through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` to its host and port; a proxy that asks for a login is not supported. Headers on the message cannot change where the request is sent.

kamelets.name: has-header-filter-action
kamelets.title: Has Header Filter Action
kamelets.summary: Keeps only the messages that have a given header, optionally with a given value, and drops all others.
kamelets.description:
Keeps only the messages that have a given header, optionally with a given value, and drops all others.

Use it to pass on only the messages that carry a marker, such as a `priority` header, or only those of one kind, such as the events whose `type` header is `order`. To match the value of a header against a pattern, use `header-matches-filter-action`, and to keep or drop messages by the content of a JSON body, use `predicate-filter-action`.

Input: any message. The header named by `name` is read.

Output: the same message, unchanged, when it has the header and, when `value` is set, when the header has exactly that value. Otherwise the message is dropped and nothing is sent on.

Good to know: the comparison with `value` is case-sensitive: `order` does not match `Order`. A header with an empty value counts as present when `value` is not set.

kamelets.name: header-matches-filter-action
kamelets.title: Header Matches Filter Action
kamelets.summary: Keeps only the messages whose value of a given header matches a regular expression, and drops all others.
kamelets.description:
Keeps only the messages whose value of a given header matches a regular expression, and drops all others.

Use it to pass on only some messages, for example only the events whose `type` header has the form `order-` followed by a number, or only the messages of some customers by a `customerId` header. To check only that a header is there, or has one exact value, `has-header-filter-action` is simpler, and to filter Kafka records by their topic, use `topic-name-matches-filter-action`.

Input: any message. The header named by `headerName` is read.

Output: the same message, unchanged, when the value of the header matches `regex`. Otherwise, and when the message does not have the header, the message is dropped and nothing is sent on.

Good to know: the expression must match the whole value, not only a part of it: `order-[0-9]+` matches `order-1` but not `x-order-1`, and it is case-sensitive. `headerName` must be set: the Kamelet does not start without it.

kamelets.name: hoist-field-action
kamelets.title: Hoist Field Action
kamelets.summary: Wraps the body of each message in a new JSON object, as the value of the one field you name.
kamelets.description:
Wraps the body of each message in a new JSON object, as the value of the one field you name.

Use it to nest the whole message under one name, for example to turn `{"id":1}` into `{"order":{"id":1}}` for a system that expects that shape. To do the opposite, and take the value out of a field, use `extract-field-action`.

Input: any body. JSON is nested as a JSON object or array when it is parsed JSON (a Map or a Jackson `JsonNode`), or JSON text with the `Content-Type` header `application/json`. Any other text, including JSON text with another `Content-Type`, becomes a text value: `hello` gives `{"order":"hello"}`.

Output: the body is the new JSON object, as JSON text, and the `Content-Type` header is set to `application/json`.

kamelets.name: http-sink
kamelets.title: HTTP Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message to a web service or REST API as an HTTP or HTTPS request, for example a POST of JSON to a webhook.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message to a web service or REST API as an HTTP or HTTPS request, for example a POST of JSON to a webhook.

Use it to push data to any service that accepts HTTP calls, such as a webhook, a REST API or a serverless function.

Input: the body is sent as the request body, as text, bytes or a stream. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The `Content-Type` header is sent as the content type of the request, and the other headers of the message, except the Camel ones and `Authorization` and `Proxy-Authorization`, are sent as HTTP headers.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the response of the service.

Good to know: a response with a status code outside `okStatusCodeRange`, which is `200-299` when it is not set, fails the message. The address, the method and the proxy come only from the options; headers on the message cannot change where it is sent. The login comes only from the options too: an `Authorization` or `Proxy-Authorization` header on the message is removed, so a credential that came with the message, such as the one of the caller of `webhook-source`, is not sent on. For a token that differs for each message, use the `http` component instead. Log in either with `authUsername` and `authPassword`, with a static token in `authBearerToken`, or with `oauth2ClientId`, `oauth2ClientSecret` and `oauth2TokenEndpoint`: the Kamelet then gets a token from that URL and sends it as a Bearer token. Without `authenticationPreemptive`, the user and password, or the static token, are sent only after the service asks for them with a 401 response. To go through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and `proxyUser` and `proxyPassword` when the proxy asks for a login; an `https://` address goes through the proxy too. The certificate of an `https://` service is checked against the certificate authorities that Java trusts. To trust a private one with Camel JBang or Camel Main, set the application properties `camel.ssl.enabled=true`, `camel.ssl.trustStore`, `camel.ssl.trustStorePassword` and `camel.component.https.useGlobalSslContextParameters=true`: that trust store then replaces the one of Java for every `https://` call of the application.

kamelets.name: http-source
kamelets.title: HTTP Source
kamelets.summary: Fetches a web address with an HTTP request, a GET unless `method` says otherwise, at a regular interval, and sends each response as a message.
kamelets.description:
Fetches a web address with an HTTP request, a GET unless `method` says otherwise, at a regular interval, and sends each response as a message.

Use it to poll a REST API, a feed or a status page for its current data, for example fetch the state of the orders every minute. To receive the requests that other systems send instead, use `webhook-source`.

Output: the body is the body of the response, as bytes. The headers of the response, such as `Content-Type`, are copied to the message, and `CamelHttpResponseCode` holds the status code.

Good to know: it fetches the address every `period` and sends a message for each response, even when the data has not changed. A response with a status code outside `okStatusCodeRange`, which is `200-299` when it is not set, sends no message: the error is logged, and the address is fetched again at the next period. Log in either with `authUsername` and `authPassword`, with a static token in `authBearerToken`, or with `oauth2ClientId`, `oauth2ClientSecret` and `oauth2TokenEndpoint`: the Kamelet then gets a token from that URL and sends it as a Bearer token. To go through an HTTP proxy, set `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`, and `proxyUser` and `proxyPassword` when the proxy asks for a login; an `https://` address goes through the proxy too. The certificate of an `https://` service is checked against the certificate authorities that Java trusts. To trust a private one with Camel JBang or Camel Main, set the application properties `camel.ssl.enabled=true`, `camel.ssl.trustStore`, `camel.ssl.trustStorePassword` and `camel.component.https.useGlobalSslContextParameters=true`: that trust store then replaces the one of Java for every `https://` call of the application.

kamelets.name: ibm-cos-sink
kamelets.title: IBM Cloud Object Storage Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file (object) to a bucket in IBM Cloud Object Storage.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file (object) to a bucket in IBM Cloud Object Storage.

Use it to store data for later use or for other systems, such as exported reports, archived events or files received from another system. To read the files of a bucket, use `ibm-cos-source`.

Input: the body is the content of the file, as text, bytes, a stream or a file. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The name of the file (its key) is `keyName` when it is set; otherwise the optional `file` header (or `ce-file`), with its folders, such as `reports/2024-06-01.csv`; otherwise a generated unique name.

Output: the message is unchanged, with the ETag of the uploaded file in the `CamelIBMCOSETag` header.

Good to know: a file with the same name is overwritten. With `deleteAfterWrite` set to true, a body that is a local file, such as the file of `file-watch-source`, is deleted from the local disk once it has been uploaded. The bucket must exist, unless `autoCreateBucket` is true. It logs in with an IBM Cloud API key.

kamelets.name: ibm-cos-source
kamelets.title: IBM Cloud Object Storage Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files (objects) in a bucket of IBM Cloud Object Storage, one message per file, and by default deletes each file once it has been read.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files (objects) in a bucket of IBM Cloud Object Storage, one message per file, and by default deletes each file once it has been read.

Use it to process files that another system drops into a bucket, such as uploaded documents, exported reports or log files. To upload files to a bucket, use `ibm-cos-sink`.

Output: the body is the content of the file, as a stream. The headers give the bucket name (`CamelIBMCOSBucketName`), the key, that is the path of the file in the bucket (`CamelIBMCOSKey`), the content type, the size and the ETag of the file.
