Good to know: files are deleted from the bucket after they are read, unless `deleteAfterRead` is set to false; then the same files are read again on every poll. `moveAfterRead` moves them to another bucket instead. To read one file only, set `fileName`. A file whose processing fails is kept, and read again on the next poll. It logs in with an IBM Cloud API key.

kamelets.name: ibm-watson-language-sink
kamelets.title: IBM Watson Natural Language Understanding Sink
kamelets.summary: Analyzes the text of each message with IBM Watson Natural Language Understanding and replaces the body with the results, such as the sentiment, the entities and the keywords.
kamelets.description:
Analyzes the text of each message with IBM Watson Natural Language Understanding and replaces the body with the results, such as the sentiment, the entities and the keywords.

Use it to find out what people write about and how they feel, for example to flag angry customer emails, tag support tickets with the products they mention, or measure the tone of reviews.

Input: the body is the text to analyze, as text. With `operation` set to `analyzeUrl`, the body is instead the address of a web page for Watson to fetch and analyze. The optional `CamelIBMWatsonLanguageText` or `CamelIBMWatsonLanguageUrl` header gives the text or the address instead of the body. An empty body fails.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the results as JSON text (bytes), with the `Content-Type` header set to `application/json`. The `CamelIBMWatsonLanguageSentimentLabel` and `CamelIBMWatsonLanguageSentimentScore` headers give the sentiment of the whole text, and `CamelIBMWatsonLanguageLanguage` its language.

Good to know: it logs in with the API key of a Natural Language Understanding instance in IBM Cloud; set `serviceUrl` when the instance is not in the US South region.

kamelets.name: infinispan-sink
kamelets.title: Infinispan Sink
kamelets.summary: Stores the body of each message under a key in a cache of a remote Infinispan server, or in Red Hat Data Grid, or removes the entry of the key.
kamelets.description:
Stores the body of each message under a key in a cache of a remote Infinispan server, or in Red Hat Data Grid, or removes the entry of the key.

Use it to share data between applications through an Infinispan cache, for example the latest status of each order or a lookup table that other services read, or to keep an entry only for a while, such as a session. To react to the changes in a cache, use `infinispan-source`.

Input: the body is the value to store, as text. The `key` header (or `ce-key`) is the key; without one, a new unique id is used as the key, so each message adds a new entry. What is done depends on `operation`. By default (`PUT`), a value that is already under the key is replaced. `PUTIFABSENT` keeps a value that is already there, and `REPLACE` stores the body only under a key that has a value. `REMOVE` deletes the entry of the key: with an empty body always, and with a body only when the value stored is equal to the body.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the message has no body afterwards. With `REMOVE` and a body, the body afterwards is `true` when the entry was deleted and `false` when it was not.

Good to know: the cache must already exist on the server. A body that the Infinispan client cannot store, such as a Map, fails the message; turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. With `lifespan` or `maxIdle`, the entries are removed after that time. Recent Infinispan servers do not accept the default `saslMechanism` of `DIGEST-MD5`: set it to `SCRAM-SHA-512`. The connection has TLS only when `sslTruststoreLocation` is set, together with `sslSniHostName`.

kamelets.name: infinispan-source
kamelets.title: Infinispan Source
kamelets.summary: Receives an event each time an entry of a cache on a remote Infinispan server, or Red Hat Data Grid, is created, changed, removed or expires, one message per event.
kamelets.description:
Receives an event each time an entry of a cache on a remote Infinispan server, or Red Hat Data Grid, is created, changed, removed or expires, one message per event.

Use it to react to changes in a shared cache, for example to update a search index or notify another service when a value changes. To write to a cache, use `infinispan-sink`.

Output: the message has no body: the event is in headers. `infinispan-event-type` is the kind of event, such as `CLIENT_CACHE_ENTRY_CREATED`, `infinispan-key` the key of the entry, `infinispan-cache-name` the name of the cache and `infinispan-entry-version` the version of the entry. The same values are in `ce-infinispaneventtype`, `ce-infinispankey`, `ce-infinispancachename` and `ce-infinispanentryversion`. To read the value, look up the key in the cache.

Good to know: only the changes made while the integration runs are received. The cache must already exist on the server. Recent Infinispan servers do not accept the default `saslMechanism` of `DIGEST-MD5`: set it to `SCRAM-SHA-512`. The connection has TLS only when `sslTruststoreLocation` is set, together with `sslSniHostName`.

kamelets.name: insert-field-action
kamelets.title: Insert Field Action
kamelets.summary: Adds a field with a value you choose to each message that is a JSON object, or replaces the value when the field is already there.
kamelets.description:
Adds a field with a value you choose to each message that is a JSON object, or replaces the value when the field is already there.

Use it to tag records with where they come from or which environment they passed through, or to add a value from a header or the current date. To add a header instead of a field, use `insert-header-action`.

Input: a JSON object, as JSON text or as parsed JSON (a Map or a Jackson `JsonNode`). When the body is a JSON array, the value is added at the end of the array and `field` is not used. A body that is not JSON fails.

Output: the object with the field. When the `Content-Type` header is `application/json`, the body is JSON text again; otherwise it is parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`), which `json-serialize-action` turns into JSON text.

Good to know: the value is always added as a JSON text value, in quotes, even when it looks like a number. The field is added at the top level of the object.

kamelets.name: insert-header-action
kamelets.title: Insert Header Action
kamelets.summary: Adds a header to each message, or replaces it, with a fixed text or a value taken from the message.
kamelets.description:
Adds a header to each message, or replaces it, with a fixed text or a value taken from the message.

Use it to give a sink the headers it reads, such as the `ce-projectKey` header of `jira-add-issue-sink`, to tag messages with where they come from, or to copy the body into a header for a later step. To set the key of a Kafka record, `set-kafka-key-action` is simpler.

Input: any message.

Output: the same body. The header named by `name` is set to `value`, and replaces a header of the same name.

Good to know: `value` is written in the Camel Simple language: plain text is used as it is, and the `${...}` parts are filled in from the message, such as `$\{body}` for the body, or `${header.source}` for the value of the header `source`.

kamelets.name: is-tombstone-filter-action
kamelets.title: Is Tombstone Filter Action
kamelets.summary: Drops the Kafka records that have no value, called tombstones, and passes on all other messages unchanged.
kamelets.description:
Drops the Kafka records that have no value, called tombstones, and passes on all other messages unchanged.

Use it to skip tombstones, which mark a key as deleted in a compacted topic, after `kafka-source` when the next step cannot handle a message without a body.

Input: any message.

Output: the same message, unchanged, when it has a body. A message with no body, or with empty text as its body, is dropped and nothing is sent on.

kamelets.name: jira-add-comment-sink
kamelets.title: Jira Add Comment Sink
kamelets.summary: Adds the text of each message as a new comment to an existing issue in Jira.
kamelets.description:
Adds the text of each message as a new comment to an existing issue in Jira.

Use it to record on a ticket what happened elsewhere, for example a deployment, the result of a build or a reply of a customer. To create issues use `jira-add-issue-sink`, to change their fields `jira-update-issue-sink`, and to change their status `jira-transition-issue-sink`.

Input: the body is the text of the comment, as text. The `ce-issueKey` header, the key of the issue such as `SHOP-42`, is required. Set it before this sink, for example with `insert-header-action`.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: a message without `ce-issueKey`, or for an issue that does not exist or that the user cannot see, fails. The comment is written in the name of the account the Kamelet logs in with. Log in either with `username` and `password`, or with `personal-token`.

kamelets.name: jira-add-issue-sink
kamelets.title: Jira Add Issue Sink
kamelets.summary: Creates a new issue, such as a bug or a task, in a Jira project for each message.
kamelets.description:
Creates a new issue, such as a bug or a task, in a Jira project for each message.

Use it to open a ticket automatically when something happens, for example when a monitoring alert fires, a form is submitted or an order fails.

Input: the body is the description of the issue, as text. The other fields come from headers. `ce-projectKey` (the key of the project, such as `SHOP`), `ce-issueTypeName` (such as `Bug` or `Task`) and `ce-issueSummary` (the title) are required. `ce-issueAssignee`, `ce-issuePriorityName` (such as `High`) and `ce-issueComponents` (a comma-separated list) are optional. Set them before this sink, for example with `insert-header-action`.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the issue that was created.

Good to know: a message without a project key, an issue type or a summary fails. Log in either with `username` and `password`, or with `personal-token`.

kamelets.name: jira-oauth-source
kamelets.title: Jira oauth Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each new Jira issue that matches a JQL query, such as every new bug of a project, by asking Jira at a regular interval, and logs in with OAuth 1.0a.
kamelets.description:
Receives each new Jira issue that matches a JQL query, such as every new bug of a project, by asking Jira at a regular interval, and logs in with OAuth 1.0a.

Use it to react to new tickets of a Jira Server or Data Center where an administrator has set up an application link with OAuth for your integration, for example to tell a team chat about a new bug. To log in with a user and an API token or a personal access token, which is simpler, use `jira-source`.

Output: the body is the issue as JSON text, with fields such as `key`, `summary`, `description`, `status`, `issueType`, `project`, `reporter`, `assignee` and `priority`.

Good to know: only the issues created after the Kamelet starts are sent; the issues that already exist are not, and neither are changes to an issue. It checks every 6 seconds. The four OAuth values come from the OAuth 1.0a authorization of the application link, see each option.

kamelets.name: jira-source
kamelets.title: Jira Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each new Jira issue that matches a JQL query, such as every new bug of a project, by asking Jira at a regular interval.
kamelets.description:
Receives each new Jira issue that matches a JQL query, such as every new bug of a project, by asking Jira at a regular interval.

Use it to react when a ticket is opened, for example to tell a team chat about a new bug or to copy new issues into another tracker. To log in with OAuth 1.0a instead of a password or a token, use `jira-oauth-source`.

Output: the body is the issue as JSON text, with fields such as `key`, `summary`, `description`, `status`, `issueType`, `project`, `reporter`, `assignee` and `priority`.

Good to know: only the issues created after the Kamelet starts are sent; the issues that already exist are not, and neither are changes to an issue. It checks every 6 seconds. `jql` must be set, or the Kamelet does not start. Log in either with `username` and `password`, or with `personal-token`.

kamelets.name: jira-transition-issue-sink
kamelets.title: Jira Transition Issue Sink
kamelets.summary: Moves an existing Jira issue to another status, such as from `In Progress` to `Done`, by running a transition of its workflow for each message.
kamelets.description:
Moves an existing Jira issue to another status, such as from `In Progress` to `Done`, by running a transition of its workflow for each message.

Use it to keep tickets in step with what happens elsewhere, for example to close an issue when its fix is deployed or to reopen it when a test fails again. To change other fields use `jira-update-issue-sink`, and to only add a comment `jira-add-comment-sink`.

Input: the `ce-issueKey` header (the key of the issue, such as `SHOP-42`) and the `ce-issueTransitionId` header (the ID number of the transition, such as `31`, not the name of the status) are required. The body, as text, is added to the issue as a comment after the transition.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: a message without one of the two headers fails, and so does a transition that the workflow does not allow from the current status of the issue. Jira lists the transitions possible for an issue, with their IDs, at `<jiraUrl>/rest/api/2/issue/<key>/transitions`. Log in either with `username` and `password`, or with `personal-token`.

kamelets.name: jira-update-issue-sink
kamelets.title: Jira Update Issue Sink
kamelets.summary: Changes the fields of an existing Jira issue, such as its summary, description, assignee or priority, for each message.
kamelets.description:
Changes the fields of an existing Jira issue, such as its summary, description, assignee or priority, for each message.

Use it to keep a ticket in step with another system, for example to assign an issue to the person on call or to raise its priority when an alert repeats. To change the status use `jira-transition-issue-sink`, and to create issues `jira-add-issue-sink`.

Input: the body becomes the new description of the issue, as text, and replaces the old one. When the body is empty, the `ce-issueDescription` header gives the description instead. The `ce-issueKey` header (the key of the issue, such as `SHOP-42`) is required. The other fields come from optional headers, and a field without a header is left as it is: `ce-issueSummary` (the title), `ce-issueTypeName` (such as `Bug`), `ce-issueAssignee`, `ce-issuePriorityName` (such as `High`) and `ce-issueComponents` (a comma-separated list, which replaces the components).

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: a message with a body always replaces the description, even when it also has the `ce-issueDescription` header. An issue type or a priority whose name Jira does not know is ignored. A message without `ce-issueKey` fails. Log in either with `username` and `password`, or with `personal-token`.

kamelets.name: jms-amqp-10-sink
kamelets.title: JMS - AMQP 1.0 Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message to a queue or a topic in a message broker that speaks AMQP 1.0, such as Apache ActiveMQ Artemis, through JMS and the Apache Qpid client.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message to a queue or a topic in a message broker that speaks AMQP 1.0, such as Apache ActiveMQ Artemis, through JMS and the Apache Qpid client.

Use it to hand work to another application through a queue, or to publish events on a topic, on any broker that supports the AMQP 1.0 protocol. For an Artemis broker, `jms-apache-artemis-sink` works too.

Input: text is sent as a JMS text message, bytes as a JMS bytes message, and a Map as a JMS map message; `jmsMessageType` sends text or bytes as the other kind. The headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent along as JMS properties of the message.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: Messages go to a queue unless `destinationType` is `topic`, and a message sent to a topic reaches only the receivers subscribed at that moment. Messages are persistent, with priority 4, and never expire, unless `deliveryPersistent`, `priority` and `timeToLive` say otherwise. It logs in with `username` and `password` when they are set; the TLS settings go in `remoteURI`. It opens a new connection to the broker for each message. It does not wait for a reply, even when the incoming message expects one, as one from `webhook-source` does.

kamelets.name: jms-amqp-10-source
kamelets.title: JMS - AMQP 1.0 Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each message from a queue or a topic in a message broker that speaks AMQP 1.0, such as Apache ActiveMQ Artemis, through JMS and the Apache Qpid client.
kamelets.description:
Receives each message from a queue or a topic in a message broker that speaks AMQP 1.0, such as Apache ActiveMQ Artemis, through JMS and the Apache Qpid client.

Use it to process work that other applications put on a queue, or to react to events published on a topic, on any broker that supports the AMQP 1.0 protocol. For an Artemis broker, `jms-apache-artemis-source` works too.

Output: the body is text for a JMS text message, bytes for a bytes message, and a Map for a map message. The JMS properties of the message become headers, along with the JMS headers such as `JMSMessageID`, `JMSDestination`, `JMSTimestamp`, `JMSPriority` and `JMSRedelivered`.

Good to know: From a queue, each message is removed when it is received, even when the rest of the flow then fails, unless `transacted` is true or `acknowledgementModeName` is `CLIENT_ACKNOWLEDGE`: then a message whose flow failed is delivered again. Several copies of this source share the messages of a queue, and `concurrentConsumers` processes several messages at the same time. From a topic (`destinationType` set to `topic`), it receives only the messages sent while it is connected, unless `subscriptionDurable` is true: then the broker keeps the messages sent while it is stopped, under `subscriptionName`. A durable subscription needs `clientId` unless it is shared (`subscriptionShared`, JMS 2.0), and only one connection may use a client ID at a time. With `selector`, it receives only the messages whose properties and headers match the selector. It logs in with `username` and `password` when they are set; the TLS settings go in `remoteURI`. When the broker cannot be reached, it starts anyway and tries again every 5 seconds.

kamelets.name: jms-apache-artemis-sink
kamelets.title: JMS - Apache Artemis Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message to a queue or a topic in an Apache ActiveMQ Artemis broker, through JMS.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message to a queue or a topic in an Apache ActiveMQ Artemis broker, through JMS.

Use it to hand work to another application through a queue, such as orders to process, or to publish events on a topic for every application that listens. For another broker that speaks AMQP 1.0, use `jms-amqp-10-sink`.

Input: text is sent as a JMS text message, bytes as a JMS bytes message, and a Map as a JMS map message; `jmsMessageType` sends text or bytes as the other kind. The headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent along as JMS properties of the message.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: Messages go to a queue unless `destinationType` is `topic`, and a message sent to a topic reaches only the receivers subscribed at that moment. Messages are persistent, with priority 4, and never expire, unless `deliveryPersistent`, `priority` and `timeToLive` say otherwise. It connects with no TLS unless `brokerURL` asks for it, and logs in with `username` and `password` when they are set. It keeps its connections to the broker in a pool and reuses them for the next messages. It does not wait for a reply, even when the incoming message expects one, as one from `webhook-source` does.

kamelets.name: jms-apache-artemis-source
kamelets.title: JMS - Apache Artemis Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each message from a queue or a topic in an Apache ActiveMQ Artemis broker, through JMS.
kamelets.description:
Receives each message from a queue or a topic in an Apache ActiveMQ Artemis broker, through JMS.

Use it to process work that other applications put on a queue, such as orders or jobs, or to react to events published on a topic. For another broker that speaks AMQP 1.0, use `jms-amqp-10-source`.

Output: the body is text for a JMS text message, bytes for a bytes message, and a Map for a map message. The JMS properties of the message become headers, along with the JMS headers such as `JMSMessageID`, `JMSDestination`, `JMSTimestamp`, `JMSPriority` and `JMSRedelivered`.

Good to know: From a queue, each message is removed when it is received, even when the rest of the flow then fails, unless `transacted` is true or `acknowledgementModeName` is `CLIENT_ACKNOWLEDGE`: then a message whose flow failed is delivered again. Several copies of this source share the messages of a queue, and `concurrentConsumers` processes several messages at the same time. From a topic (`destinationType` set to `topic`), it receives only the messages sent while it is connected, unless `subscriptionDurable` is true: then the broker keeps the messages sent while it is stopped, under `subscriptionName`. A durable subscription needs `clientId` unless it is shared (`subscriptionShared`, JMS 2.0), and only one connection may use a client ID at a time. With `selector`, it receives only the messages whose properties and headers match the selector. It connects with no TLS unless `brokerURL` asks for it, and logs in with `username` and `password` when they are set. When the broker cannot be reached, it starts anyway and tries again every 5 seconds.

kamelets.name: jms-ibm-mq-sink
kamelets.title: JMS - IBM MQ Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message to a queue or a topic of an IBM MQ queue manager, through JMS.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message to a queue or a topic of an IBM MQ queue manager, through JMS.

Use it to hand work or events to applications that read from IBM MQ, such as an existing enterprise or mainframe system. Use `jms-ibm-mq-source` to read from IBM MQ.

Input: text is sent as a JMS text message, and bytes as a JMS bytes message; `jmsMessageType` sends text or bytes as the other kind. The headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent along as JMS properties of the message.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: the IBM MQ client library is not included, as its licence is not the Apache one: add `mvn:com.ibm.mq:com.ibm.mq.jakarta.client` with a version to the dependencies of the integration (Camel JBang adds it by itself). It connects as a client over the network, with no TLS unless `sslCipherSuite` is set; the trust store and the key store for TLS are those of the Java runtime (`javax.net.ssl.trustStore`, `javax.net.ssl.keyStore`). For a multi-instance queue manager, list its instances in `connectionNameList`. Messages go to a queue unless `destinationType` is `topic`, and a message sent to a topic reaches only the receivers subscribed at that moment. Messages are persistent, with priority 4, and never expire, unless `deliveryPersistent`, `priority` and `timeToLive` say otherwise. It does not wait for a reply, even when the incoming message expects one, as one from `webhook-source` does.

kamelets.name: jms-ibm-mq-source
kamelets.title: JMS - IBM MQ Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each message from a queue or a topic of an IBM MQ queue manager, through JMS.
kamelets.description:
Receives each message from a queue or a topic of an IBM MQ queue manager, through JMS.

Use it to process work or events that other applications put on IBM MQ, such as an existing enterprise or mainframe system. Use `jms-ibm-mq-sink` to send to IBM MQ.

Output: the body is text for a JMS text message, and bytes for a bytes message. The JMS properties of the message become headers, along with the JMS headers such as `JMSMessageID` and `JMSTimestamp`, and IBM MQ details such as `JMSXUserID`, `JMS_IBM_PutDate` and `JMS_IBM_Format`.

Good to know: the IBM MQ client library is not included, as its licence is not the Apache one: add `mvn:com.ibm.mq:com.ibm.mq.jakarta.client` with a version to the dependencies of the integration (Camel JBang adds it by itself). From a queue, each message is removed when it is received, even when the rest of the flow then fails, unless `transacted` is true or `acknowledgementModeName` is `CLIENT_ACKNOWLEDGE`: then a message whose flow failed is delivered again. Several copies of this source share the messages of a queue, and `concurrentConsumers` processes several messages at the same time. From a topic (`destinationType` set to `topic`), it receives only the messages sent while it is connected, unless `subscriptionDurable` is true: then the queue manager keeps the messages sent while it is stopped, under `subscriptionName`. A durable subscription needs `clientId` unless it is shared (`subscriptionShared`, JMS 2.0), and only one connection may use a client ID at a time. With `selector`, it receives only the messages whose properties and headers match the selector. It connects with no TLS unless `sslCipherSuite` is set; the trust store and the key store for TLS are those of the Java runtime (`javax.net.ssl.trustStore`, `javax.net.ssl.keyStore`). For a multi-instance queue manager, list its instances in `connectionNameList`. When the queue manager cannot be reached, it starts anyway and tries again every 5 seconds.

kamelets.name: jolt-transformation-action
kamelets.title: Jolt Transformation Action
kamelets.summary: Reshapes each JSON message into other JSON, as a Jolt specification describes: moves, renames, removes fields or adds defaults.
kamelets.description:
Reshapes each JSON message into other JSON, as a Jolt specification describes: moves, renames, removes fields or adds defaults.

Use it to map the JSON of one system to the JSON another system expects, for example to rename fields or move them into a nested object, when you already have Jolt specifications. `jslt-action` does the same with a query language, and is often easier to write.

Input: parsed JSON, a Map (or a List). Since Camel 4.24, JSON text, bytes and a stream work too. With older versions they do not fail but give an empty body, and so does the parsed JSON of `json-deserialize-action`.

Output: the body is the result as parsed JSON, a Map (or a List), not JSON text. Add `json-serialize-action` after it to get JSON text. The headers are kept.

Good to know: the specification cannot read headers, only the body. It is loaded from a file, the classpath or a URL given by the `template` option; it cannot come from the message.

kamelets.name: jslt-action
kamelets.title: JSLT Action
kamelets.summary: Turns each JSON message into new JSON with a JSLT transformation, a query language for JSON that picks, renames and computes fields.
kamelets.description:
Turns each JSON message into new JSON with a JSLT transformation, a query language for JSON that picks, renames and computes fields.

Use it to map the JSON of one system to the JSON another system expects, for example to keep only some fields, rename them or count the items of an order. To build text rather than JSON, use `mustache-template-action`; `jolt-transformation-action` reshapes JSON with Jolt specifications instead.

Input: JSON text, bytes or a stream. The transformation sees the body as `.` and a header as `$headers.name`, for example `{"customer": .name, "items": size(.items), "source": $headers.origin}`.

Output: the body is the result as JSON text. The headers are kept.

Good to know: parsed JSON (a Map or a JsonNode, such as the output of `json-deserialize-action`) fails the message: give the JSON as text. A field whose value is missing, such as a header that is not set, is left out of the result. The transformation is loaded from a file, the classpath or a URL given by the `template` option; it cannot come from the message.

kamelets.name: json-deserialize-action
kamelets.title: Json Deserialize Action
kamelets.summary: Turns a body of JSON text into parsed JSON, a Jackson `JsonNode`, so that the next steps can work with its fields.
kamelets.description:
Turns a body of JSON text into parsed JSON, a Jackson `JsonNode`, so that the next steps can work with its fields.

Use it to prepare a message for a step that needs parsed JSON rather than text, such as `jsonata-action`, or to make sure that a body is well-formed JSON. To turn parsed data back into JSON text, use `json-serialize-action`, and to check JSON against a schema, use `json-schema-validator-action`.

Input: JSON text, as text or bytes: a JSON object or a JSON array.

Output: the body is parsed JSON, a Jackson `JsonNode`: an object node for a JSON object, an array node for a JSON array. The `Content-Type` header is removed.

Good to know: a body that is not valid JSON fails the message.

kamelets.name: json-schema-validator-action
kamelets.title: Json Schema Validator Action
kamelets.summary: Checks that each JSON message matches a JSON Schema, and fails the messages that do not.
kamelets.description:
Checks that each JSON message matches a JSON Schema, and fails the messages that do not.

Use it to stop bad data early, for example to reject the orders that miss a required field before they reach a database or another system. To keep or drop messages by a condition instead of failing them, use `predicate-filter-action`.

Input: JSON text, as text, bytes or a stream, or parsed JSON from `json-deserialize-action`. A Map fails.

Output: the same message, unchanged, when it matches the schema.

Good to know: a message that does not match the schema, or that is not JSON, fails with an error that lists what is wrong; it is not dropped silently, so the error handling of the integration decides what happens to it. The schema is loaded from the `template` location; it cannot come from the message.

kamelets.name: json-serialize-action
kamelets.title: Json Serialize Action
kamelets.summary: Turns a body of parsed data, such as a Map, a List or parsed JSON, into JSON text.
kamelets.description:
Turns a body of parsed data, such as a Map, a List or parsed JSON, into JSON text.

Use it to send parsed data to a sink that needs JSON text, for example after `jsonata-action` or `json-deserialize-action`, whose output is parsed JSON. To do the opposite, use `json-deserialize-action`.

Input: parsed data: a Map, a List, or parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`).

Output: the body is JSON text, as a stream of bytes. The `Content-Type` header is set to `application/json`.

Good to know: a body that is already text becomes one JSON string, in quotes: `hello` becomes `"hello"`, and JSON text is quoted the same way. Do not use it on a body that is already JSON text.

kamelets.name: jsonata-action
kamelets.title: Jsonata Action
kamelets.summary: Transforms each JSON message with a JSONata expression, to reshape it, pick out fields, or compute new values.
kamelets.description:
Transforms each JSON message with a JSONata expression, to reshape it, pick out fields, or compute new values.

Use it to turn the JSON of one system into the JSON another system expects, for example to rename fields, join a first and a last name, or add up the lines of an order. For other ways to reshape JSON, see `jslt-action` and `jolt-transformation-action`; to build text, such as an email, from a template, use `mustache-template-action`.

Input: parsed JSON, such as a Map, a List, or the output of `json-deserialize-action`.

Output: the body is the result of the expression, as parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`), not as text: add `json-serialize-action` after it to get JSON text. The headers are kept.

Good to know: put `json-deserialize-action` before it when the body is JSON text, as depending on the Camel version the expression sees JSON text as one string rather than as an object, and bytes or a stream fail. The expression is loaded from the `template` location; it cannot come from the message.

kamelets.name: kafka-apicurio-registry-not-secured-sink
kamelets.title: Kafka Not Secured with Apicurio Registry Sink
kamelets.summary: Deprecated, to be removed in a later release: sends each message as an Avro record to a topic in Apache Kafka, with the schema kept in an Apicurio Registry, and no login or TLS to either.
kamelets.description:
Deprecated, to be removed in a later release: sends each message as an Avro record to a topic in Apache Kafka, with the schema kept in an Apicurio Registry, and no login or TLS to either.

Use it to publish records that other applications read with the schema of the registry, on a Kafka and a registry that need no login, such as in development. When the registry is secured with Keycloak use `kafka-not-secured-apicurio-registry-sink`; for records without a schema use `kafka-sink`. This Kamelet is deprecated and will be removed in a later release, as the Kafka Kamelets are reduced to a few.

Input: the body must be an Avro object, such as an Avro `GenericRecord` or an object of a class generated from the schema; it is written as Avro binary. A body of text is written as an Avro string, and so fails unless the schema is a string. The optional `key` header (or `ce-key`) becomes the key of the record, and the optional `partition-key` header (or `ce-partitionkey`) is the number of the partition to write to. The other headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent as record headers.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: The schema must already be in the registry, as the artifact `<topic>-value` (such as `orders-value`) in the default group: the Kamelet does not register it, and a message whose schema is not found fails with `ArtifactNotFoundException`. Neither Kafka nor the registry is secured: there is no login and no TLS.

kamelets.name: kafka-apicurio-registry-not-secured-source
kamelets.title: Kafka Not Secured with Apicurio Registry Source
kamelets.summary: Deprecated, to be removed in a later release: receives each record written with a JSON Schema from topics in Apache Kafka, with the schema kept in an Apicurio Registry, and no login or TLS to either.
kamelets.description:
Deprecated, to be removed in a later release: receives each record written with a JSON Schema from topics in Apache Kafka, with the schema kept in an Apicurio Registry, and no login or TLS to either.

Use it to read JSON records that other applications write with a JSON Schema of the registry, on a Kafka and a registry that need no login, such as in development. For Avro records use `kafka-batch-apicurio-registry-not-secured-source`; when the registry is secured with Keycloak use `kafka-not-secured-apicurio-registry-json-source`; for records without a schema use `kafka-source`. This Kamelet is deprecated and will be removed in a later release, as the Kafka Kamelets are reduced to a few.

Output: the body is the value of the record as parsed JSON. The `kafka-topic`, `kafka-key`, `kafka-partition`, `kafka-offset` and `kafka-timestamp` (in milliseconds since 1970) headers say where the record came from. They are also set as `ce-kafkatopic`, `ce-kafkakey` and so on, and as the `CamelKafka*` headers that the Kafka actions read. The record headers become message headers, as text unless `deserializeHeaders` is false.

Good to know: it reads JSON Schema records only, not Avro: the sink of the same name writes Avro. Neither Kafka nor the registry is secured: there is no login and no TLS. A new consumer group starts at the newest records, unless `autoOffsetReset` is `earliest`. Without `consumerGroup`, every start uses a new group, so the records sent while the integration was stopped are skipped.

kamelets.name: kafka-batch-apicurio-registry-not-secured-source
kamelets.title: Kafka Batch Not Secured with Apicurio Registry Source
kamelets.summary: Deprecated, to be removed in a later release: receives Avro records from topics in Apache Kafka in batches, with the schema kept in an Apicurio Registry, and no login or TLS to either.
kamelets.description:
Deprecated, to be removed in a later release: receives Avro records from topics in Apache Kafka in batches, with the schema kept in an Apicurio Registry, and no login or TLS to either.

Use it to read many Avro records at once, as written by `kafka-apicurio-registry-not-secured-sink`, on a Kafka and a registry that need no login, such as in development. When the registry is secured with Keycloak use `kafka-batch-apicurio-registry-source`. This Kamelet is deprecated and will be removed in a later release, as the Kafka Kamelets are reduced to a few.

Output: the body is a List with one entry per record, up to `batchSize`. Each entry is a message of its own, with the value of the record as its body (an Avro `GenericRecord`, whose text form is JSON), and the key, offset and timestamp of the record in its `CamelKafkaKey`, `CamelKafkaOffset` and `CamelKafkaTimestamp` headers. The record headers are in the entries too, as bytes. The message itself has the `CamelKafkaTopic` and `CamelKafkaPartition` headers. The `kafka-topic`, `kafka-key` and other headers of `kafka-source` are not set.

Good to know: neither Kafka nor the registry is secured: there is no login and no TLS. To save the position in Kafka only once a batch was handled, set `allowManualCommit` to true and `autoCommitEnable` to false, and end the flow with `kafka-batch-manual-commit-action`.

kamelets.name: kafka-batch-manual-commit-action
kamelets.title: Kafka Batch Manual Commit Action
kamelets.summary: Saves in Kafka the position (offset) reached by a batch of records from `kafka-batch-source`, so that the batch is not received again after a restart.
kamelets.description:
Saves in Kafka the position (offset) reached by a batch of records from `kafka-batch-source`, so that the batch is not received again after a restart.

Use it to count the records of a batch as read only once the whole batch was handled, for example once it was written to a database: put it at the end of a flow that starts with `kafka-batch-source`. For single records from `kafka-source` use `kafka-manual-commit-action`.

Input: a batch from `kafka-batch-source`, or from one of the `kafka-batch-*-registry-*` sources, with `allowManualCommit` set to true and `autoCommitEnable` set to false. It uses the `CamelKafkaManualCommit` header of the message, or else that of the last entry of the list.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: without the `CamelKafkaManualCommit` header, for example when `allowManualCommit` is false, it does nothing and does not fail.

kamelets.name: kafka-batch-source
kamelets.title: Kafka Batch Source
kamelets.summary: Receives records from one or more topics in Apache Kafka in batches, as one message that holds a list of up to `batchSize` records.
kamelets.description:
Receives records from one or more topics in Apache Kafka in batches, as one message that holds a list of up to `batchSize` records.

Use it to handle many records at once, for example to write them to a database in one go, or to save the position in Kafka only once a whole batch was handled. To handle one record at a time use `kafka-source`.

Output: the body is a List with one entry per record, up to `batchSize`. Each entry is a message of its own, with the value of the record as its body (text), and the key, offset and timestamp of the record in its `CamelKafkaKey`, `CamelKafkaOffset` and `CamelKafkaTimestamp` headers. The record headers are in the entries too, as bytes. The message itself has the `CamelKafkaTopic` and `CamelKafkaPartition` headers. The `kafka-topic`, `kafka-key` and other headers of `kafka-source` are not set.

Good to know: `saslAuthType` has no default and must be set; `NONE` connects with no login and no TLS. To save the position in Kafka only once a batch was handled, set `allowManualCommit` to true and `autoCommitEnable` to false, and end the flow with `kafka-batch-manual-commit-action`. A new consumer group starts at the newest records, unless `autoOffsetReset` is `earliest`. Without `consumerGroup`, every start uses a new group, so the records sent while the integration was stopped are skipped.

kamelets.name: kafka-manual-commit-action
kamelets.title: Kafka Manual Commit Action
kamelets.summary: Saves in Kafka the position (offset) of the record that `kafka-source` received, so that the record is not received again after a restart.
kamelets.description:
Saves in Kafka the position (offset) of the record that `kafka-source` received, so that the record is not received again after a restart.

Use it to count a record as read only once it was handled, for example once it was written to a database: put it at the end of a flow that starts with `kafka-source`. The records after the last saved position are read again after a restart. For `kafka-batch-source` use `kafka-batch-manual-commit-action`.

Input: any message from `kafka-source` with `allowManualCommit` set to true and `autoCommitEnable` set to false. It uses the `CamelKafkaManualCommit` header that the source then sets.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: without the `CamelKafkaManualCommit` header, for example when `allowManualCommit` is false, it does nothing and does not fail. Saving the position of a record also counts the earlier records of its partition as read.

kamelets.name: kafka-sink
kamelets.title: Kafka Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message as a record to a topic in Apache Kafka, or in a Kafka-compatible service such as Amazon MSK, Confluent Cloud or Redpanda.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message as a record to a topic in Apache Kafka, or in a Kafka-compatible service such as Amazon MSK, Confluent Cloud or Redpanda.

Use it to publish events or data for other applications to read, such as orders, sensor readings or changes from a database. To write the records with a schema kept in a schema registry, such as Confluent Schema Registry, Redpanda or Apicurio Registry, set `schemaRegistryVendor`.

Input: the body becomes the value of the record, as text. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. With `schemaRegistryVendor` and `schemaFormat` `json`, the body must be JSON text (or a Map), and the record is written with a JSON Schema; with `avro`, `confluent` and `apicurio` write a text body as an Avro string, while `aws-glue` needs an Avro record. With `azure`, set `schemaGroup`. The optional `key` header (or `kafka-key`, `ce-key`, `ce-kafkakey`) becomes the key of the record, and the optional `partition-key` header (or `ce-partitionkey`) is the number of the partition to write to. The other headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent as record headers.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: `saslAuthType` has no default and must be set; `NONE` connects with no login and no TLS, as a local Kafka expects. A managed Kafka service needs one of the other types. With `schemaRegistryVendor`, the integration needs the serde jars of the vendor, which Camel JBang downloads by itself; for `confluent` add the Confluent Maven repository, as in `camel run --repos=confluent`. With `aws-glue` and `azure`, the serde logs in with the credentials of the environment the integration runs in: the AWS default credentials chain, or the Azure `DefaultAzureCredential` (such as the `AZURE_CLIENT_ID`, `AZURE_TENANT_ID` and `AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET` variables). A `confluent` or `apicurio` registry that requires a login is not supported yet. The sink registers a schema made from the message, which with `json` accepts any JSON object; it does not check the message against a schema that is already registered for the topic.

kamelets.name: kafka-source
kamelets.title: Kafka Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each record from one or more topics in Apache Kafka, or in a Kafka-compatible service such as Amazon MSK, Confluent Cloud or Redpanda.

With `schemaRegistryVendor`, the value is read with its schema from the registry and the body is JSON text, such as `{"id": 7, "item": "camel"}` for an Avro record. A record without a value (a tombstone) gives a message with no body. They are also set as `ce-kafkatopic`, `ce-kafkakey` and so on, and as the `CamelKafka*` headers that the Kafka actions read. The record headers become message headers, as text unless `deserializeHeaders` is false.

Without `consumerGroup`, every start uses a new group, so the records sent while the integration was stopped are skipped. With `schemaRegistryVendor`, the integration needs the serde jars of the vendor, which Camel JBang downloads by itself; for `confluent` add the Confluent Maven repository, as in `camel run --repos=confluent`. With `aws-glue` and `azure`, the serde logs in with the credentials of the environment the integration runs in: the AWS default credentials chain, or the Azure `DefaultAzureCredential` (such as the `AZURE_CLIENT_ID`, `AZURE_TENANT_ID` and `AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET` variables). kamelets.name: langchain4j-ingest-file-source
kamelets.title: LangChain4j Ingest File Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the documents in a directory and its subdirectories, one message per file, leaves them in place, and reads a file again when it changes.
kamelets.description:
Reads the documents in a directory and its subdirectories, one message per file, leaves them in place, and reads a file again when it changes.

Use it to feed a knowledge base for an AI assistant: put it in front of `langchain4j-ingest-sink`, with `tika-extract-text-action` or `docling-convert-action` in between for PDF or office documents.

Output: the body is the file, read as bytes unless `charset` is set. The `CamelLangChain4jIngestDocumentId` header is the path of the file relative to `directory`, such as `manuals/pump.pdf`, which `langchain4j-ingest-sink` uses as the document id. The usual file headers, such as `CamelFileName`, are set too.

Good to know: the files are never deleted or moved. A file is read again when its modification time or size changes, and `langchain4j-ingest-sink` then adds the new version next to the old one, unless it has an `idempotentRepository`, which skips it. The files already read are remembered in memory only, by default the last 1000, so after a restart every file is read again; set `idempotentRepository` to keep them. A file that is still being copied in is read only once it stops changing; for a slow copy, which can pause for more than a second, set `readLockMinAge`.

kamelets.name: langchain4j-ingest-sink
kamelets.title: LangChain4j Ingest Sink
kamelets.summary: Splits each document into small pieces of text, turns each piece into an embedding (a vector of numbers) with an AI embedding model, and writes them to a LangChain4j embedding store.
kamelets.description:
Splits each document into small pieces of text, turns each piece into an embedding (a vector of numbers) with an AI embedding model, and writes them to a LangChain4j embedding store.

Use it to load documents into a vector store, so that an AI assistant can later find the pieces that answer a question (RAG). Read PDF or office documents with `tika-extract-text-action` or `docling-convert-action` first, and a directory with `langchain4j-ingest-file-source`.

Input: the document, as text, bytes, a stream or a file, read as text. Every document needs an id, such as its file name, in the `CamelLangChain4jIngestDocumentId` header (or the one named in `documentIdHeader`); an id kept by `tika-extract-text-action` or `docling-convert-action` comes first.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is a result object with the pipeline name, the document id, the number of pieces written, and the outcome: `INGESTED`, `EMPTY` (an empty document, nothing written), `SKIPPED` (an id seen before, with `idempotentRepository`) or `FILTERED` (left out by `includeId`, `excludeId`, `minDocumentSize` or `documentFilter`).

Good to know: the embedding store and the embedding model are objects you define in the application, such as in the `beans` section of a YAML route; when there is one of each, the options can be left out. Writing a document again adds new pieces, and does not replace the ones written before. With `idempotentRepository`, only the first document with a given id is written, so a changed version of a file is skipped. A message without a document id, or larger than `maxDocumentSize`, fails.

kamelets.name: log-action
kamelets.title: Log Action
kamelets.summary: Writes each message to the log, with its body and optionally its headers, and passes it on unchanged.
kamelets.description:
Writes each message to the log, with its body and optionally its headers, and passes it on unchanged.

Use it to see what flows between two steps while you build or debug an integration, for example what a source really sends before a sink fails on it. To log at the end of a flow instead, use `log-sink`.

Input: any message.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: by default the log line shows the body and its Java type, but not the headers. The body is logged as it is, secrets included, unless `logMask` is true.

kamelets.name: log-sink
kamelets.title: Log Sink
kamelets.summary: Writes each message it receives to the log, with its body and optionally its headers.
kamelets.description:
Writes each message it receives to the log, with its body and optionally its headers.

Use it to see what a source sends while you build or try out an integration, or to end a flow during a test without a real system behind it. To log in the middle of a flow and pass the message on, use `log-action`.

Input: any message, with any kind of body.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: by default the log line shows the body and its Java type, but not the headers. The body is logged as it is, secrets included, unless `logMask` is true.

kamelets.name: mail-imap-source
kamelets.title: Mail IMAP Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the unread emails in a folder of a mailbox over IMAP, by default the inbox, one message per email, and marks each email as read.
kamelets.description:
Reads the unread emails in a folder of a mailbox over IMAP, by default the inbox, one message per email, and marks each email as read.

Use it to start a flow from incoming email, for example turn support requests into tickets, or process the orders and invoices that customers send by email. For a Microsoft 365 mailbox that needs an OAuth login, use `ms-exchange-online-imap-oauth-source`, and for Gmail through its API, use `google-mail-source`.

Output: the body is the text of the email. For an email with several parts, such as text and HTML or attachments, it is the text of the first part; attachments are not in the body. The `ce-subject`, `ce-from`, `ce-to` and `ce-cc` headers hold the subject and the addresses, and the headers of the email, such as `Subject`, `From`, `Date` and `Message-ID`, are copied too.

Good to know: by default it reads the `INBOX` folder, emails stay in the folder, marked as read, and emails that are already read are skipped. Set `delete` or `moveTo` to remove the emails once they are processed, `unseen` to false to read the emails that are already read too, and the search options, such as `searchFrom` or `searchSubject`, to read only some emails; an email must match every search option that is set. An email whose processing fails stays unread and is read again at the next check. An email that cannot be read at all, such as one with a broken format, fails every check of the mailbox until it is removed, unless `skipFailedMessage` is true. It always connects with TLS (IMAPS), and checks the certificate and the host name of the server against the certificate authorities that Java trusts. To trust a private one with Camel JBang or Camel Main, set the application properties `camel.ssl.enabled=true`, `camel.ssl.trustStore`, `camel.ssl.trustStorePassword` and `camel.component.imaps.useGlobalSslContextParameters=true`: that trust store then replaces the one of Java for every IMAPS connection of the application. It checks for new email once a minute by default (`delay`).

kamelets.name: mail-sink
kamelets.title: Mail Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message as an email through an SMTP server, with the body as the text of the email.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message as an email through an SMTP server, with the body as the text of the email.

Use it to send notifications, alerts or reports by email, for example tell a team when an order fails or send a daily summary.

Input: the body is the text of the email. It is sent as the type in `contentType`; when that is not set, as the type in the `Content-Type` header, such as `text/html` for an HTML email, and otherwise as plain text. The `ce-subject`, `ce-from`, `ce-to` and `ce-cc` headers set the subject, the sender, the recipients and the copy recipients of one email, each in place of its option; several addresses are separated by commas. Other mail headers on the message, such as `To`, `Bcc` or `Reply-To`, are removed and not used, so the blind copy recipients and the reply address come only from the `bcc` and `replyTo` options.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelMailMessageId` header holds the ID of the email that was sent.

Good to know: each email needs a sender, recipients and a subject, from the options or from the `ce-from`, `ce-to` and `ce-subject` headers. The default protocol, `smtps`, connects with TLS from the start, usually on port 465, and checks the certificate of the server. For a server that uses STARTTLS, usually on port 587, set `protocol` to `smtp` and `startTls` to true: the connection is then encrypted before the login, the certificate and the host name of the server are checked, and sending fails when the server does not offer STARTTLS. With `smtp` alone, the connection, the password and the emails are not encrypted. The certificate is checked against the certificate authorities that Java trusts. To trust a private one with Camel JBang or Camel Main, set the application properties `camel.ssl.enabled=true`, `camel.ssl.trustStore`, `camel.ssl.trustStorePassword`, and `camel.component.smtps.useGlobalSslContextParameters=true` for `smtps` or `camel.component.smtp.useGlobalSslContextParameters=true` for `smtp` with `startTls`: that trust store then replaces the one of Java for every connection of the application with that protocol.

kamelets.name: mariadb-sink
kamelets.title: MariaDB Sink
kamelets.summary: Runs an SQL statement, such as an INSERT, in a MariaDB database for each message, with values taken from the fields of the JSON object in the body.
kamelets.description:
Runs an SQL statement, such as an INSERT, in a MariaDB database for each message, with values taken from the fields of the JSON object in the body.

Use it to store records from another system as rows of a table, such as each order that arrives on a Kafka topic, or to update or delete rows. To read rows, use `mariadb-source`.

Input: the body is one JSON object, as text, such as `{"username":"oscerd","city":"Rome"}`. In `query`, write `:#username` where the value of the field `username` goes. When the object has no field of that name, the header of that name is used instead. Fields that `query` does not name are ignored. When `batch` is true, the body can also be a JSON array of such objects, and `query` runs once for each of them.

Output: the body afterwards is the JSON object as a Map, and the `CamelSqlUpdateCount` header holds the number of rows the statement changed. For a JSON array with `batch`, the body is a List of Maps, and the header holds the total for all of them. When `query` is a SELECT, the body is instead a List of the rows found, each a Map, and the `CamelSqlRowCount` header holds their number.

Good to know: a message fails when its body is not a JSON object (plain text, for example, or a JSON array when `batch` is not true), or when it has no value for a parameter of `query`. With `batch`, all the rows of one message are written in one transaction: when one of them fails, none is written. The values are sent to the database apart from the SQL text, so the content of a message cannot change the statement. Do not write `?` in `query`, not even in a quoted string: the Kamelet then fails to start. The JDBC driver of MariaDB is not included: add `mvn:org.mariadb.jdbc:mariadb-java-client` to the dependencies of the integration. Camel JBang (`camel run`) adds it by itself. Whether the connection uses TLS when `connectionProperties` is not set depends on the version of the MariaDB driver: set `sslMode=trust` in `connectionProperties` to insist on TLS.

kamelets.name: mariadb-source
kamelets.title: MariaDB Source
kamelets.summary: Runs an SQL query in a MariaDB database again and again, and sends each row it returns as a message, as a JSON object.
kamelets.description:
Runs an SQL query in a MariaDB database again and again, and sends each row it returns as a message, as a JSON object.

Use it to pick up the rows that another application adds to a table, such as new orders or events, and pass them on to another system. To write rows, use `mariadb-sink`.

Output: the body is one row as JSON text, an object with the column names as keys, such as `{"id":1,"username":"oscerd","city":"Rome"}`. When `useIterator` is false, the body is instead one JSON array with all the rows of a poll. The `Content-Type` header is `application/json`.

Good to know: the query runs again `delay` milliseconds after the previous run, so the same rows are sent again and again, unless `consumedQuery` marks or deletes each row once it is sent and `query` leaves such rows out: for example `SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE processed = false` with `UPDATE accounts SET processed = true WHERE id = :#id`. When the next step fails for a row, `consumedQuery` is not run for it, and the row is read again, unless `onConsumeFailed` marks it. A query that finds no rows sends nothing. `maxMessagesPerPoll` limits how many rows one poll sends. `query` cannot contain `?`. The format of date and time columns in the JSON depends on the Camel version. The JDBC driver of MariaDB is not included: add `mvn:org.mariadb.jdbc:mariadb-java-client` to the dependencies of the integration. Camel JBang (`camel run`) adds it by itself. Whether the connection uses TLS when `connectionProperties` is not set depends on the version of the MariaDB driver: set `sslMode=trust` in `connectionProperties` to insist on TLS.

kamelets.name: mask-field-action
kamelets.title: Mask Fields Action
kamelets.summary: Replaces the values of the fields you name in each message that is a JSON object with a fixed value, such as `XXXX`.
kamelets.description:
Replaces the values of the fields you name in each message that is a JSON object with a fixed value, such as `XXXX`.

Use it to hide card numbers, passwords or personal data before the messages are logged or sent to another system. To remove a field entirely, use `drop-field-action`, or `replace-field-action` for several fields.

Input: a JSON object, as JSON text or as parsed JSON (a Map or a Jackson `JsonNode`). Only the fields at the top level of the object are masked; nested objects are left as they are. A JSON array, or a body that is not JSON, fails.

Output: the object with the masked values; the order of its fields can change. When the `Content-Type` header is `application/json`, the body is JSON text again; otherwise it is parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`), which `json-serialize-action` turns into JSON text.

Good to know: the replacement must suit the value it replaces. A text value takes any replacement, but a number takes only a number, such as `0`, and a true or false value, an object or a list cannot be masked: such a message fails. A named field that the object does not have is ignored.

kamelets.name: message-timestamp-router-action
kamelets.title: Message Timestamp Router Action
kamelets.summary: Changes the topic that `kafka-sink` writes a record to, to a name made of the original topic name and a date read from a field of the JSON body.
kamelets.description:
Changes the topic that `kafka-sink` writes a record to, to a name made of the original topic name and a date read from a field of the JSON body.

Use it to spread the records over one topic per day or per month by a date in the data, such as the date of an order, in a flow from `kafka-source` to `kafka-sink`. To use the time the record was written to Kafka instead use `timestamp-router-action`.

Input: a JSON object as JSON text, with the `Content-Type` header set to `application/json`. The name of the topic is read from the `CamelKafkaTopic` header, which `kafka-source` sets.

Output: the same JSON object, as JSON text in a stream, with `Content-Type` set to `application/json`. When one of the `timestampKeys` fields is found, the `CamelKafkaOverrideTopic` header is set to the new name, and `kafka-sink` writes the record to that topic instead of its own `topic`.

Good to know: a field value that cannot be read as a date with `timestampKeyFormat` makes the message fail. The default `topicFormat` of `topic-$[timestamp]` gives names such as `topic-20240703`, without the original name: set it to `$[topic]-$[timestamp]` to keep it. The date is in UTC.

kamelets.name: minio-sink
kamelets.title: Minio Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file (object) to a bucket in MinIO, the S3-compatible object storage.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file (object) to a bucket in MinIO, the S3-compatible object storage.

Use it to store data in MinIO, such as reports, exports, images or received messages to keep as an archive. For Amazon S3 use `aws-s3-sink`, and for the S3 gateway of Ceph use `ceph-sink`.

Input: the body is the content of the file, as text, bytes or a stream. When `keyName` is set, every message is stored under that name. Otherwise the name of the file comes from the optional `file` header, or the `ce-file` header, and is a generated unique name when neither is set.

Output: the body is unchanged. The `CamelMinioObjectName` header holds the name the file was stored under, unless `keyName` is set.

Good to know: a file with the same name is overwritten, so with `keyName` set each message replaces the previous one. When `keyName` is set, the `file` and `ce-file` headers are ignored.

kamelets.name: minio-source
kamelets.title: Minio Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files (objects) in a MinIO bucket, one message per file, and by default deletes each file once it has been read.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files (objects) in a MinIO bucket, one message per file, and by default deletes each file once it has been read.

Use it to process files that another system drops into a MinIO bucket, such as uploaded documents, exported reports or log files. For Amazon S3 use `aws-s3-source`, and for the S3 gateway of Ceph use `ceph-source`.

Output: the body is the content of the file, as bytes. The headers give the bucket name, the name of the file (`CamelMinioObjectName`), and its content type, size, ETag and last modified date.

Good to know: files are deleted from the bucket after they are read, unless `deleteAfterRead` is set to false; then the same files are read again on every poll, about twice a second. Only the files at the top of the bucket are read: a file in a folder, such as `reports/january.csv`, is not.

kamelets.name: mongodb-changes-stream-source
kamelets.title: MongoDB Changes Stream Source
kamelets.summary: Sends a message for each change to a collection of a MongoDB database, such as a document inserted, updated or deleted, as it happens.
kamelets.description:
Sends a message for each change to a collection of a MongoDB database, such as a document inserted, updated or deleted, as it happens.

Use it to react to changes in MongoDB, for example to copy new orders to another system or to keep a cache or a search index up to date. To read the documents of a capped collection from the start, use `mongodb-source`. To write documents, use `mongodb-sink`.

Output: the body is JSON text. For an insert or a replace, it is the whole new document. For an update, it is the whole document as it is when the change is sent, read again from the collection, so it can already hold later changes, and it is the text `null` when the document was deleted meanwhile; `fullDocument` changes this. For a delete, it is an object with only the `_id` of the deleted document. The `CamelMongoDbStreamOperationType` header says what happened (`insert`, `update`, `replace` or `delete`), and the `_id` header holds the `_id` of the document.

Good to know: only changes made after the Kamelet starts are sent. It does not save where it stopped, so the changes made while it is stopped, such as during a restart, are never sent. The collection must exist when the Kamelet starts; otherwise it fails to start with `Collection ... does not exist on the database`. Reading the document again costs MongoDB one more read for each update; set `fullDocument` to `default` to send `null` for an update instead. MongoDB offers change streams only on a replica set or a sharded cluster, not on a single standalone server. Set either `hosts` or `connectionString`. With `hosts`, it connects with TLS by default; set `ssl` to false for a MongoDB without TLS, such as a local one. With `connectionString`, such as the `mongodb+srv://` string of MongoDB Atlas, it connects only as that string says, and `hosts`, `username`, `password`, `ssl` and `sslValidationEnabled` are not used. For a user defined in a database other than `admin`, use `connectionString` with `authSource`.

kamelets.name: mongodb-sink
kamelets.title: MongoDB Sink
kamelets.summary: Writes each message to a collection of a MongoDB database: inserts it as a new document, or, with `operation`, replaces or updates a stored document.
kamelets.description:
Writes each message to a collection of a MongoDB database: inserts it as a new document, or, with `operation`, replaces or updates a stored document.

Use it to store events, orders or other records as documents in MongoDB, for example each message that arrives on a Kafka topic, to keep a copy of records by their ID (`save`), or to change fields of a document, such as the stock of a product (`update`). To read documents, use `mongodb-source` or `mongodb-changes-stream-source`.

Input: with `insert` (the default) and `save`, the body is one document, as a JSON object in text, such as `{"item":"book","qty":2}`. When it has no `_id` field, MongoDB gives the document a new ObjectId. With `update`, the body is a JSON array in text of two objects: the filter that selects the document and the changes, such as `[{"sku":"A1"},{"$set":{"qty":3}}]`. An ObjectId is written as `{"$oid":"..."}`. Text that is not JSON fails.

Output: with `insert`, the body afterwards is the document that was stored, as a Map with its `_id`. With `save` and `update`, it is the result that MongoDB returns. With `insert` and `save`, the `CamelMongoOid` header holds the `_id` of the document. With `update`, the `CamelMongoDbRecordsMatched` and `CamelMongoDbRecordsAffected` headers say how many documents matched the filter and how many were changed.

Good to know: with `insert`, a document whose `_id` is already in the collection fails; `save` replaces it instead. `save` replaces the whole document, so fields that are not in the body are removed. `update` changes only the first document that matches, and nothing when none matches, unless `upsert` is true. The `db-upsert` and `ce-dbupsert` headers are not used. With `createCollection` false, the default, the Kamelet fails to start when the collection does not exist yet. Set either `hosts` or `connectionString`. With `hosts`, it connects with TLS by default; set `ssl` to false for a MongoDB without TLS, such as a local one. With `connectionString`, such as the `mongodb+srv://` string of MongoDB Atlas, it connects only as that string says, and `hosts`, `username`, `password`, `ssl` and `sslValidationEnabled` are not used. For a user defined in a database other than `admin`, use `connectionString` with `authSource`.

kamelets.name: mongodb-source
kamelets.title: MongoDB Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the documents of a capped collection in a MongoDB database, first those already there and then each new one as it is added, one message per document, as JSON text.
kamelets.description:
Reads the documents of a capped collection in a MongoDB database, first those already there and then each new one as it is added, one message per document, as JSON text.

Use it to pass on records that an application appends to a capped collection, such as log entries or events, as they arrive. For a normal collection, or to also see updates and deletes, use `mongodb-changes-stream-source`. To write documents, use `mongodb-sink`.

Output: the body is one document as JSON text. An `_id` that is an ObjectId comes out as an object with only its time (`timestamp` and `date`), not as the ID text, and the format of dates depends on the Camel version. The `CamelMongoDbDatabase` and `CamelMongoDbCollection` headers name where the document comes from.

Good to know: the collection must be capped (created with a fixed size), or the Kamelet fails to start. Each time the integration starts, it reads the whole collection again from the start, unless `persistentTailTracking` is true. It stores its place only when the integration stops, so after a crash it reads again the documents since the last stop. Set either `hosts` or `connectionString`. With `hosts`, it connects with TLS by default; set `ssl` to false for a MongoDB without TLS, such as a local one. With `connectionString`, such as the `mongodb+srv://` string of MongoDB Atlas, it connects only as that string says, and `hosts`, `username`, `password`, `ssl` and `sslValidationEnabled` are not used. For a user defined in a database other than `admin`, use `connectionString` with `authSource`. To read from a secondary member of a replica set, use `connectionString` with `readPreference=secondaryPreferred`.

kamelets.name: mqtt-sink
kamelets.title: MQTT Sink
kamelets.summary: Publishes each message to a topic on an MQTT broker, such as Eclipse Mosquitto or HiveMQ, with MQTT 3.1.1.
kamelets.description:
Publishes each message to a topic on an MQTT broker, such as Eclipse Mosquitto or HiveMQ, with MQTT 3.1.1.

Use it to send commands or data to IoT devices, or to publish readings and events for MQTT clients to receive. For a broker or clients that use MQTT 5, use `mqtt5-sink`.

Input: the body is the payload, as text or bytes, and is sent as it is. A Map fails: turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The headers of the message are not sent, as an MQTT 3 message has none.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: messages are published with quality of service 2 (exactly once) unless `qos` is set, and the broker does not keep them for clients that subscribe later unless `retained` is true. It connects with no TLS unless `brokerUrl` starts with `ssl://`. With TLS it checks the certificate and the host name of the broker, and trusts the certificate authorities that Java trusts by default, or instead the ones in `sslTruststoreLocation`. It connects when the integration starts, and the integration fails to start when the broker cannot be reached or fails these checks.

kamelets.name: mqtt-source
kamelets.title: MQTT Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each message published to a topic on an MQTT broker, such as Eclipse Mosquitto or HiveMQ, with MQTT 3.1.1.
kamelets.description:
Receives each message published to a topic on an MQTT broker, such as Eclipse Mosquitto or HiveMQ, with MQTT 3.1.1.

Use it to collect readings and events from IoT devices and other MQTT clients. A topic with wildcards, such as `sensors/#`, receives from many topics at once. For a broker or clients that use MQTT 5, use `mqtt5-source`.

Output: the body is the payload, as bytes. The `CamelMqttTopic` header is the topic the message was published to, and `CamelMqttQoS` its quality of service.

Good to know: it receives only the messages published while it is connected, plus, when it subscribes, the last retained message of each matching topic. It subscribes with quality of service 2 (exactly once) unless `qos` is set. Each running copy needs its own `clientId`: two clients with the same ID keep pushing each other off the broker and lose messages. When it is not set, a unique one is generated. It connects with no TLS unless `brokerUrl` starts with `ssl://`. With TLS it checks the certificate and the host name of the broker, and trusts the certificate authorities that Java trusts by default, or instead the ones in `sslTruststoreLocation`. The integration fails to start when the broker cannot be reached or fails these checks.

kamelets.name: mqtt5-sink
kamelets.title: MQTT v5 Sink
kamelets.summary: Publishes each message to a topic on an MQTT broker, such as Eclipse Mosquitto or HiveMQ, with MQTT 5.
kamelets.description:
Publishes each message to a topic on an MQTT broker, such as Eclipse Mosquitto or HiveMQ, with MQTT 5.

Use it to send commands or data to IoT devices, or to publish readings and events, when the broker or the clients use MQTT 5. For a broker that only speaks MQTT 3.1.1, use `mqtt-sink`.

Input: the body is the payload, as text or bytes, and is sent as it is. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The headers of the message are not sent, not even as MQTT 5 user properties.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: messages are published with quality of service 2 (exactly once) unless `qos` is set, and the broker does not keep them for clients that subscribe later unless `retained` is true. It connects with no TLS unless `brokerUrl` starts with `ssl://`. With TLS it checks the certificate and the host name of the broker, and trusts the certificate authorities that Java trusts by default, or instead the ones in `sslTruststoreLocation`. It connects when the integration starts, and the integration fails to start when the broker cannot be reached or fails these checks.

kamelets.name: mqtt5-source
kamelets.title: MQTT 5 Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each message published to a topic on an MQTT broker, such as Eclipse Mosquitto or HiveMQ, with MQTT 5.
kamelets.description:
Receives each message published to a topic on an MQTT broker, such as Eclipse Mosquitto or HiveMQ, with MQTT 5.

Use it to collect readings and events from IoT devices and other MQTT clients, when the broker or the clients use MQTT 5. A topic with wildcards, such as `sensors/#`, receives from many topics at once. For a broker that only speaks MQTT 3.1.1, use `mqtt-source`.

Output: the body is the payload, as bytes. The `CamelMqttTopic` header is the topic the message was published to, `CamelMqttQoS` its quality of service, and `CamelPahoMqtt5MsgProperties` holds the MQTT 5 properties of the message, such as its user properties.

Good to know: it receives only the messages published while it is connected, plus, when it subscribes, the last retained message of each matching topic. It subscribes with quality of service 2 (exactly once) unless `qos` is set. kamelets.name: mysql-sink

kamelets.description:
Runs an SQL statement, such as an INSERT, in a MySQL database for each message, with values taken from the fields of the JSON object in the body.

kamelets.name: nats-sink
kamelets.title: NATS Sink
kamelets.summary: Publishes each message to a subject on a NATS server, or to a JetStream stream that stores the messages.
kamelets.description:
Publishes each message to a subject on a NATS server, or to a JetStream stream that stores the messages.

Use it to send events or commands to services that listen on NATS, such as microservices or edge devices. Use `nats-source` to receive them.

Input: the body is the payload, as text or bytes. A Map is sent as its Java text form, such as `{a=1, b=x}`, so turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. Headers of the message, such as `Content-Type`, are sent as NATS headers.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: a plain NATS subject stores nothing: only the receivers subscribed at that moment get the message, unless a JetStream stream takes in the subject. With `jetstreamEnabled`, the sink waits until the stream that takes in the subject has stored the message, and sending fails with `503 No Responders Available For Request` when no stream takes it in. The stream must exist already, for example created by `nats-source`. On a server without JetStream, `jetstreamEnabled` is ignored and the message is published as plain NATS. It connects with TLS when `secure` is true. The certificate of the server is checked against the certificate authorities that Java trusts. To trust a private one with Camel JBang or Camel Main, set the application properties `camel.ssl.enabled=true`, `camel.ssl.trustStore`, `camel.ssl.trustStorePassword` and `camel.component.nats.useGlobalSslContextParameters=true`: that trust store then replaces the one of Java for every NATS connection of the application that has `secure` set. kamelets.name: nats-source
kamelets.title: NATS Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each message published to a subject on a NATS server, or stored in a JetStream stream.
kamelets.description:
Receives each message published to a subject on a NATS server, or stored in a JetStream stream.

Use it to react to events or commands that services publish on NATS. Use `nats-sink` to publish them.

A message is acknowledged once it has been processed. A message that fails is delivered again 5 seconds later, with no end unless `maxDeliver` is set. When an integration with a `durableName` stops abruptly, the messages it had not finished come back after 30 seconds, so the one in progress can be received twice. When several copies of the integration run, each copy receives every message, unless they share a `queueName` (without JetStream) or a `durableName` (with JetStream): then each message goes to only one of them. It connects with TLS when `secure` is true. The certificate of the server is checked against the certificate authorities that Java trusts. To trust a private one with Camel JBang or Camel Main, set the application properties `camel.ssl.enabled=true`, `camel.ssl.trustStore`, `camel.ssl.trustStorePassword` and `camel.component.nats.useGlobalSslContextParameters=true`: that trust store then replaces the one of Java for every NATS connection of the application that has `secure` set. kamelets.description:

kamelets.title: OpenSearch Index Sink
kamelets.summary: Stores each message, a JSON object, as a document in an index of OpenSearch, so that it can be searched.

kamelets.description:
