Input: Protobuf binary data, as bytes, such as `protobuf-serialize-action` writes.

Output: the body is parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`) with the fields found in the data. The `Content-Type` header is removed. Put `json-serialize-action` after this action to get JSON text.

Good to know: a body that is not Protobuf data, such as JSON text, fails. When `schema` is not set, the schema found by an earlier `resolve-pojo-schema-action` is used.

kamelets.name: protobuf-serialize-action
kamelets.title: Protobuf Serialize Action
kamelets.summary: Turns each message, a JSON object, into Protobuf binary data that follows the Protobuf schema you give.
kamelets.description:
Turns each message, a JSON object, into Protobuf binary data that follows the Protobuf schema you give.

Use it to send records in Protocol Buffers (Protobuf), a compact binary format described by a schema, to a system that expects it, such as a Kafka topic whose readers decode Protobuf. To turn Protobuf back into JSON, use `protobuf-deserialize-action`; for Avro, use `avro-serialize-action`.

Input: parsed JSON (a Map or a Jackson `JsonNode`) whose fields match the schema. Put `json-deserialize-action` before this action when the body is JSON text.

Output: the body is the Protobuf binary data, as bytes, and the `Content-Type` header is set to `application/protobuf`.

Good to know: JSON text is not turned into Protobuf: it is passed on as it is, yet the `Content-Type` header is set to `application/protobuf`. A message fails when it has a field the schema does not know or a value of the wrong type; a field of the schema that the message lacks is left out, even when it is marked `required`. When `schema` is not set, the schema found by an earlier `resolve-pojo-schema-action` is used.

kamelets.name: pulsar-sink
kamelets.title: Pulsar Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message to a topic in Apache Pulsar, named by its tenant, namespace and topic name.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message to a topic in Apache Pulsar, named by its tenant, namespace and topic name.

Use it to publish events or data for other applications to read from Pulsar, such as orders or sensor readings. Use `pulsar-source` to read them.

Input: the body is the payload, as text or bytes. A Map fails: turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The headers of the message are not sent as Pulsar properties; to set properties, put a Map in the `CamelPulsarProducerMessageProperties` header. The optional `key` header becomes the key of the message, as the `key` header that `pulsar-source` sets; the `CamelPulsarProducerMessageKey` header takes precedence over it.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: it connects with no TLS and no login, unless `serviceUrl` starts with `pulsar+ssl://` and `authenticationClass` is set. Over TLS, the certificate of Pulsar must be signed by an authority that the Java trust store of the integration trusts; for a private one, point `javax.net.ssl.trustStore` at a trust store with it, as the Kamelet has no trust store option. It connects when the integration starts, and the integration fails to start when Pulsar cannot be reached, unless `lazyStart` is true.

kamelets.name: pulsar-source
kamelets.title: Pulsar Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each message from a topic in Apache Pulsar, or from every topic whose name matches a pattern, through a named subscription.
kamelets.description:
Receives each message from a topic in Apache Pulsar, or from every topic whose name matches a pattern, through a named subscription.

Use it to process events or data that other applications publish to Pulsar. Several copies can share the work with a `SHARED` or `KEY_SHARED` subscription.

Output: the body is the payload, as bytes. The headers give the topic (`topic_name`), the key (`key`), the Pulsar properties as a Map (`properties`), the `message_id`, the `publish_time` and the `producer_name`.

Good to know: the subscription (`subscriptionName`, `subs` by default) remembers what was read, so messages sent while the source is stopped are read when it starts again. A new subscription starts at the newest message, unless `subscriptionInitialPosition` is `EARLIEST`. A message whose processing fails is delivered again after one minute, again and again, unless `maxRedeliverCount` is set with a `SHARED` or `KEY_SHARED` subscription. A message whose processing takes longer than `ackTimeoutMillis` (10 seconds when not set) is delivered again, and so processed twice. It connects with no TLS and no login, unless `serviceUrl` starts with `pulsar+ssl://` and `authenticationClass` is set. Over TLS, the certificate of Pulsar must be signed by an authority that the Java trust store of the integration trusts; for a private one, point `javax.net.ssl.trustStore` at a trust store with it, as the Kamelet has no trust store option.

kamelets.name: redis-sink
kamelets.title: Redis Sink
kamelets.summary: Runs a Redis command for each message, such as storing the body under a key with `SET`, adding it to a list with `RPUSH`, or publishing it on a channel with `PUBLISH`.
kamelets.description:
Runs a Redis command for each message, such as storing the body under a key with `SET`, adding it to a list with `RPUSH`, or publishing it on a channel with `PUBLISH`.

Use it to put values in a Redis cache for other applications to read, to push work items onto a Redis list, or to publish events on a Redis channel that `redis-source` or other subscribers listen to.

Input: the body is the value, as text. The `key` header (or `ce-key`) gives the key, for commands that work on a key such as `SET`, `GET` or `RPUSH`. The `channel` header (or `ce-channel`) gives the channel for `PUBLISH`; without it, the channel in `channels` is used.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is what Redis answered, such as the value for `GET` or the new length of the list for `RPUSH`; for `SET` the body is unchanged.

Good to know: the default `command` is `GET`, which reads and stores nothing, so set it to the command you need. A body that is not text, such as a Map, fails the message; turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. By default it connects with no password and no TLS, to database 0: set `password` (and `username` for an ACL user) for a Redis server that asks for a login, and `ssl` for one that needs TLS.

kamelets.name: redis-source
kamelets.title: Redis Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the messages published on one or more Redis channels, one message per publication, as a subscriber of Redis publish and subscribe.
kamelets.description:
Receives the messages published on one or more Redis channels, one message per publication, as a subscriber of Redis publish and subscribe.

Use it to react to events that other applications publish on Redis, such as notifications, cache invalidations or status changes. To publish on a channel, use `redis-sink` with the `PUBLISH` command.

Output: the body is the published message, as text. The `CamelRedis.Channel` header is the channel it was published on.

Good to know: only the messages published while the integration runs are received; Redis does not keep them for later. By default it connects with no password and no TLS: set `password` (and `username` for an ACL user) for a Redis server that asks for a login, and `ssl` for one that needs TLS. The channels are shared by all the databases of a Redis server, so there is no database to choose.

kamelets.name: regex-router-action
kamelets.title: Regex Router Action
kamelets.summary: Changes the topic that `kafka-sink` writes a record to, by applying a regular expression and a replacement to the name of the topic it was read from.
kamelets.description:
Changes the topic that `kafka-sink` writes a record to, by applying a regular expression and a replacement to the name of the topic it was read from.

Use it to copy records, in a flow from `kafka-source` to `kafka-sink`, to topics with related names, for example from `orders-eu` to `archive-eu`. To add the date to the name use `timestamp-router-action`.

Input: a message from `kafka-source`, with the name of the topic in the `CamelKafkaTopic` header. The same expression is also applied to the `ce-type` header, when there is one.

Output: the same body. When `regex` matches the whole topic name, the `CamelKafkaOverrideTopic` header is set to the name with the match replaced by `replacement`, and `kafka-sink` writes the record to that topic instead of its own `topic`. When `regex` matches the whole `ce-type` header, that header is replaced in the same way.

Good to know: the expression must match the whole name, not a part of it. When it does not match, nothing changes.

kamelets.name: replace-field-action
kamelets.title: Replace Field Action
kamelets.summary: Renames fields of each message that is a JSON object, and can also keep only some fields or remove others.
kamelets.description:
Renames fields of each message that is a JSON object, and can also keep only some fields or remove others.

Use it to match the field names another system expects, such as `name` to `fullName`, and to leave out the fields it should not get. To remove a single field, `drop-field-action` is simpler; to hide a value but keep the field, use `mask-field-action`.

Input: a JSON object, as JSON text or as parsed JSON (a Map or a Jackson `JsonNode`). Only the fields at the top level of the object are renamed, kept or removed; nested objects are left as they are. A JSON array, or a body that is not JSON, fails.

Output: the object with the renamed fields, without the removed ones; the order of its fields can change. When the `Content-Type` header is `application/json`, the body is JSON text again; otherwise it is parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`), which `json-serialize-action` turns into JSON text.

Good to know: `renames` is required, even when you only want to keep or remove fields. A rename of a field the object does not have is ignored. When `enabled` and `disabled` together would remove every field, the object is passed on unchanged.

kamelets.name: resolve-pojo-schema-action
kamelets.title: Resolve Schema Action
kamelets.summary: Attaches an Avro, Protobuf or JSON schema to each message, for the later steps that need one, and leaves the body unchanged.
kamelets.description:
Attaches an Avro, Protobuf or JSON schema to each message, for the later steps that need one, and leaves the body unchanged.

Use it to give the schema once, before `data-type-action` with a format such as `avro-binary` or `protobuf-binary`, which takes its schema only from here. `avro-serialize-action`, `avro-deserialize-action`, `protobuf-serialize-action` and `protobuf-deserialize-action` use it too when their own `schema` is not set.

Input: any body. The schema comes from `schema`, or else from the Java class named by `contentClass`.

Output: the body and the headers are unchanged. The schema is kept with the message in the properties `X-Content-Schema` and `X-Content-Schema-Type` (`avsc`, `proto` or `json`), which are not headers and are not sent to other systems.

Good to know: with the default `mimeType`, `application/json`, and no `schema` or `contentClass`, it does nothing. A `mimeType` it does not know makes every message fail with "Unsupported type".

kamelets.name: rest-openapi-sink
kamelets.title: REST OpenAPI Sink
kamelets.summary: Calls one operation of a REST API for each message, building the request (method, path, parameters and content type) from the OpenAPI specification of the API.
kamelets.description:
Calls one operation of a REST API for each message, building the request (method, path, parameters and content type) from the OpenAPI specification of the API.

Use it to call an API that publishes an OpenAPI (Swagger) document without writing its URLs by hand, for example to create a customer or look up an order in a service of your company. For a call to a fixed URL, use `http-sink`.

Input: the body is the request body, such as JSON text, and is sent with the content type the specification gives for the operation, or the one in `produces`. The path and query parameters of the operation come from headers of the same name: for `/pets/\{petId}`, set the `petId` header. The other headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent as HTTP headers.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the response of the API, as bytes, with the headers of the response and its status code in `CamelHttpResponseCode`.

Good to know: a missing path parameter is not an error; the request is sent with `\{petId}` in the path, unless `clientRequestValidation` is true. The address of the API is taken from the `servers` of the specification, unless `host` or `basePath` is set. The Kamelet has no login options. The Kamelet does not start when the specification has no operation with the ID in `operation`.

kamelets.name: salesforce-composite-upsert-sink
kamelets.title: Salesforce composite upsert Sink
kamelets.summary: Creates or updates many Salesforce records of one kind in a single call, matching each record to an existing one by an external ID field.
kamelets.description:
Creates or updates many Salesforce records of one kind in a single call, matching each record to an existing one by an external ID field.

Use it to copy a batch of customers, products or orders from another system into Salesforce without creating duplicates: a record whose external ID is already in Salesforce is updated, the others are created. To create or change one record at a time, use `salesforce-create-sink` or `salesforce-update-sink`.

Input: the body is JSON text with a `records` list. Each record gives its kind in `attributes`, such as `{"attributes": {"type": "Contact"}, "External_Id__c": "C-1", "LastName": "Lovelace"}`, and holds the external ID field named by `sObjectIdName` with its value, and the fields to set. Salesforce accepts up to 200 records in one call.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is a List with one result per record, in the same order, each with `id`, `success`, `created` (true for a new record) and `errors`.

Good to know: a record that Salesforce refuses does not fail the message, and the other records are still saved: check `success` in the results.

kamelets.name: salesforce-create-sink
kamelets.title: Salesforce Create Sink
kamelets.summary: Creates a new record, such as a contact, an account or a lead, in Salesforce for each message.
kamelets.description:
Creates a new record, such as a contact, an account or a lead, in Salesforce for each message.

Use it to add to Salesforce what happens in other systems, for example a contact for each web form sent or a lead from a marketing tool. To change existing records use `salesforce-update-sink`, and to create or update many records at once, matched by an external ID, `salesforce-composite-upsert-sink`.

Input: the body is the fields of the new record as JSON text, with the API names of the fields, such as `{"LastName": "Lovelace", "Email": "ada@example.com"}`. It is sent to Salesforce as it is. The kind of record comes from `sObjectName`.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the answer of Salesforce as JSON text, with the `id` of the new record, `success` and `errors`.

Good to know: a record that Salesforce refuses, for example because a required field is missing or a validation rule fails, fails the message. `sObjectName` must be set, or the Kamelet does not start.

kamelets.name: salesforce-delete-sink
kamelets.title: Salesforce Delete Sink
kamelets.summary: Deletes the Salesforce record that each message names by its ID, such as a contact or an account.
kamelets.description:
Deletes the Salesforce record that each message names by its ID, such as a contact or an account.

Use it to remove records from Salesforce when they are removed in another system, for example to delete a contact when a customer closes their account.

Input: the body is JSON text with two fields: `sObjectName`, the API name of the kind of record (such as `Contact`), and `sObjectId`, the ID of the record. For example `{"sObjectName": "Contact", "sObjectId": "003XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX"}`. Other fields are ignored.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is empty.

Good to know: Salesforce moves the deleted record to its Recycle Bin. A message without `sObjectName` or `sObjectId`, or for a record that does not exist, fails. The message decides which record is deleted, so place this sink only after a source you trust.

kamelets.name: salesforce-pubsub-source
kamelets.title: Salesforce Pub/Sub Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the events of a Salesforce channel, such as a Platform Event or the Change Data Capture events of a kind of record, through the Pub/Sub API, one message per event.
kamelets.description:
Receives the events of a Salesforce channel, such as a Platform Event or the Change Data Capture events of a kind of record, through the Pub/Sub API, one message per event.

Use it to react to what happens in Salesforce, for example to an `Order_Shipped__e` Platform Event that a Flow publishes, or to every change of an account through `/data/AccountChangeEvent`. To be told about records that match a SOQL query, through a PushTopic, use `salesforce-source`.

Output: by default (`deserializeType` `JSON`) the body is the event as JSON text, with the fields of the event. The `CamelSalesforcePubSubReplayId` header holds the replay ID of the event, and `CamelSalesforcePubSubEventId` its ID.

Good to know: by default only the events published after the start are received. The Kamelet does not remember where it stopped: to go on after a restart, set `replayPreset` to `CUSTOM` and `replayId` to the replay ID of the last event processed.

kamelets.name: salesforce-source
kamelets.title: Salesforce Source
kamelets.summary: Receives an event each time a Salesforce record that matches a SOQL query is created, updated, deleted or undeleted, through a PushTopic of the Streaming API.
kamelets.description:
Receives an event each time a Salesforce record that matches a SOQL query is created, updated, deleted or undeleted, through a PushTopic of the Streaming API.

Use it to react to changes in Salesforce, for example to copy each new contact to a mailing tool or to alert a team when an opportunity is won. For Platform Events and Change Data Capture through the newer Pub/Sub API, use `salesforce-pubsub-source`.

Output: the body is the record as JSON text, with the fields that the query selects. The `CamelSalesforceEventType` header says what happened: `created`, `updated`, `deleted` or `undeleted`. The `CamelSalesforceReplayId` header identifies the event.

Good to know: when it starts, it creates the PushTopic `topicName` in Salesforce with `query` and the notify options, or updates it when it exists, so the user needs the permission to create PushTopics. By default only new records send an event; turn on `notifyForOperationUpdate` and the others for more. Only the events after the start are received, unless `replayId` is set.

kamelets.name: salesforce-update-sink
kamelets.title: Salesforce Update Sink
kamelets.summary: Changes fields of an existing Salesforce record, such as the phone number of a contact, for each message; the message names the record and the new values.
kamelets.description:
Changes fields of an existing Salesforce record, such as the phone number of a contact, for each message; the message names the record and the new values.

Use it to keep Salesforce records in step with another system, for example to update the address of an account when it changes in the ERP. To create records use `salesforce-create-sink`, and to create or update many records matched by an external ID, `salesforce-composite-upsert-sink`.

Input: the body is JSON text with three fields: `sObjectName`, the API name of the kind of record (such as `Contact`); `sObjectId`, the ID of the record; and `payload`, an object with the fields to change and their new values. For example `{"sObjectName": "Contact", "sObjectId": "003XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX", "payload": {"Phone": "+45 1234 5678"}}`. The fields that are not in `payload` keep their values.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the `payload` as JSON text.

Good to know: a message without `sObjectName` or `sObjectId`, for a record that does not exist, or with a change that Salesforce refuses, fails. The message decides which record is changed, so place this sink only after a source you trust.

kamelets.name: scp-sink
kamelets.title: SCP Sink
kamelets.summary: Copies each message as a file to a directory on a remote server, with SCP (secure copy) over an SSH connection.
kamelets.description:
Copies each message as a file to a directory on a remote server, with SCP (secure copy) over an SSH connection.

Use it to copy files to a server you reach with SSH that does not offer SFTP, for example to drop a configuration or a report on a host. To append to or keep existing files, or to create the directory when it is missing, use `sftp-sink` instead.

Input: the body is the content of the file, as text, bytes or a stream. The name of the file comes from the `CamelFileName` header, which may hold subdirectories, such as `reports/data.csv`; without it, a unique name is generated.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: files are written in `directoryName`, or else in the home directory of `username`, with the rights of that user, and a file with the same name is replaced. `directoryName` must exist: when it does not, every file is written as a file with the name of the directory. A file name that points outside the directory fails the message. The key of the server is checked against the file in `knownHostsUri`, or else `~/.ssh/known_hosts` of the user that runs the integration, unless `strictHostKeyChecking` is `no`. Do not place it after messages from an untrusted source.

kamelets.name: set-body-action
kamelets.title: Set Body Action
kamelets.summary: Replaces the body of each message with a text you write, which can include values from the message, such as a header.
kamelets.description:
Replaces the body of each message with a text you write, which can include values from the message, such as a header.

Use it to send a fixed text or a small JSON document, such as a status message, or to build a short text from headers and the old body. For longer texts, a template Kamelet such as `mustache-template-action` is easier to maintain.

Input: any message. In the text, `$\{body}` is the old body and `${header.name}` the value of a header.

Output: the body is the text, with the values filled in. The headers are kept as they were, `Content-Type` too, so set it to match the new body when needed, for example with `insert-header-action`.

Good to know: up to Camel 4.23, two closing braces in a row are read as the end of a placeholder and make the Kamelet fail to start, so write nested JSON with a space between them, as `} }`.

kamelets.name: set-kafka-key-action
kamelets.title: Set Kafka Key Action
kamelets.summary: Sets the key of the Kafka record to the value of a header of the message.
kamelets.description:
Sets the key of the Kafka record to the value of a header of the message.

Use it before `kafka-sink` when the records need a key, for example so that all the records of one customer go to the same partition and stay in order.

Input: any message with the header named by `headerName`.

Output: the same body. The `CamelKafkaKey` header, which `kafka-sink` uses as the record key, is set to the value of that header.

Good to know: to build the key from fields of the body instead, use `value-to-key-action`.

kamelets.name: sftp-sink
kamelets.title: SFTP Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file to a directory on an SFTP server, which transfers files over an encrypted SSH connection.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file to a directory on an SFTP server, which transfers files over an encrypted SSH connection.

Use it to deliver exports, reports or data files to a server you reach with SSH, such as the SFTP drop box of a partner. For an FTP server use `ftp-sink` or `ftps-sink`.

Input: the body is the content of the file, as text, bytes or a stream. The name of the file comes from the `file` header, or from `ce-file` when `file` is not set; any directory in it is dropped, so `reports/data.csv` is written as `data.csv`. Without these headers, `CamelFileName` is used as it is, subdirectories included, and without any of them a unique name is generated.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelFileNameProduced` header is set to the path of the file on the server.

Good to know: a file with the same name is replaced, unless `fileExist` says otherwise. A file is uploaded under its real name from the start, so a reader that polls the directory can pick it up half-written. To prevent that, set `tempPrefix` to upload it under a temporary name and rename it once it is complete, or `doneFileName` to write an empty done file next to it once it is complete. Log in with `username` and either `password` or a private key. The key of the server must be in a known_hosts file, `knownHostsUri` or else `~/.ssh/known_hosts` of the user that runs the integration, or the connection fails. A file name that points outside `directoryName` fails the message.

kamelets.name: sftp-source
kamelets.title: SFTP Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files in a directory on an SFTP server, over an encrypted SSH connection, one message per file, and by default leaves them on the server.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files in a directory on an SFTP server, over an encrypted SSH connection, one message per file, and by default leaves them on the server.

Use it to collect the files that a partner or another system drops on a server you reach with SSH, such as orders, invoices or exports. For an FTP server use `ftp-source` or `ftps-source`.

Output: the body is the content of the file, as bytes, or as a stream when `streamDownload` is true. The `file` and `ce-file` headers hold the name of the file, with its path below `directoryName` when `recursive` is true, such as `2026/orders.csv`. `CamelFileName` holds the same name, and `CamelFileLength` the size of the file in bytes.

Good to know: files are not deleted or moved after they are read, unless `delete` is true or `move` is set. A file is read only once while the integration runs (`idempotent`), but the files left on the server are all read again after a restart; to read each file only once, also across restarts, set `move` to a directory such as `.done`, set `delete` to true, or keep the list of the files read in a file with `idempotentRepository`. To read only some of the files, set `include`, `exclude` or `antInclude`. To leave a file alone while another program is still writing it, set `readLock`. Log in with `username` and either `password` or a private key. The key of the server must be in a known_hosts file, `knownHostsUri` or else `~/.ssh/known_hosts` of the user that runs the integration, or the connection fails.

kamelets.name: simple-filter-action
kamelets.title: Simple Filter Action
kamelets.summary: Drops the messages for which a condition, written in the Camel Simple language, is true, and passes on all others.
kamelets.description:
Drops the messages for which a condition, written in the Camel Simple language, is true, and passes on all others.

Use it to leave out the messages you do not want, for example the test events, with the condition `${header.type} == 'test'`. To keep only the messages that match a condition instead, use `predicate-filter-action` (a condition on a JSON body), `has-header-filter-action` or `header-matches-filter-action`.

Input: any message.

Output: the same message, unchanged, when the condition is false. When it is true, the message is dropped and nothing is sent on.

Good to know: this is the opposite of the other filter actions of the catalog, which keep the messages that match. A condition on a header the message does not have is false, so such a message is passed on.

kamelets.name: slack-sink
kamelets.title: Slack Sink
kamelets.summary: Posts each message as a text message to a Slack channel, through an incoming webhook of a Slack app.
kamelets.description:
Posts each message as a text message to a Slack channel, through an incoming webhook of a Slack app.

Use it to tell a team in Slack when something happens, such as a monitoring alert, a failed build, a new order or a daily report. To read the messages of a channel instead, use `slack-source`.

Input: the body is the text of the Slack message, as text; another kind of body is turned into text first. JSON text is posted as it is, as the text of the message, not as a Slack message structure. The text can use Slack's own formatting, such as `*bold*`. Headers are not read.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: the webhook decides where the message goes. The webhook of a Slack app posts only to the channel chosen when the webhook was created, whatever `channel` says. When Slack does not answer with a success status, the message fails.

kamelets.name: slack-source
kamelets.title: Slack Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the new messages posted in a public Slack channel, by asking Slack at a regular interval, one message per Slack message.
kamelets.description:
Reads the new messages posted in a public Slack channel, by asking Slack at a regular interval, one message per Slack message.

Use it to react to what people write in a channel, for example to turn a message in `#support` into a ticket, to archive a channel, or to start a job when someone posts a command. To post to Slack instead, use `slack-sink`.

Output: the body is the Slack message as JSON text, with fields such as `text` (what was written), `user` (the ID of the author) and `ts` (the time stamp that identifies the message). The `Content-Type` header is `application/json`.

Good to know: when it starts, it also sends the most recent message already in the channel, then only the messages posted after it. It does not remember where it stopped: after a restart it starts again from the most recent message. It reads public channels only, by their name, and needs a token of a Slack app, see `token`.

kamelets.name: smpp-sink
kamelets.title: SMPP Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message as an SMS text message to a mobile phone, through an SMS center (SMSC) that speaks the SMPP protocol.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message as an SMS text message to a mobile phone, through an SMS center (SMSC) that speaks the SMPP protocol.

Use it to send alerts, one-time codes or notifications by SMS, through an SMS provider or operator that offers SMPP access. Use `smpp-source` to receive SMS replies and delivery receipts.

Input: the body is the text of the SMS. The phone number to send it to comes from the `CamelSmppDestAddr` header when it is set, and from `destAddr` otherwise. A text longer than one SMS (160 characters, or 70 with `alphabet` `8`) is split, cut or refused, as `splittingPolicy` says.

Output: the message is unchanged, with the IDs that the SMSC gave the SMS in the `CamelSmppId` header (a List), and how many SMS were sent in `CamelSmppSentMessageCount`.

Good to know: the defaults of `sourceAddr` (1616) and `destAddr` (1717) are test numbers: set them, or set `CamelSmppDestAddr` on each message. It asks the SMSC for a delivery receipt of each SMS, which `smpp-source` receives: set `registeredDelivery` to `0` to not ask for them. The text is encoded with `encoding`, so characters it cannot hold, such as Cyrillic or emoji in ISO-8859-1, are sent as `?`: for text in any language, set `alphabet` and `dataCoding` to `8`. It logs in to the SMSC when the integration starts, and the integration fails to start when the SMSC cannot be reached. It connects with no TLS unless `usingSSL` is true.

kamelets.name: smpp-source
kamelets.title: SMPP Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each SMS sent to your numbers, and the delivery receipts of the SMS you sent, from an SMS center (SMSC) that speaks the SMPP protocol.
kamelets.description:
Receives each SMS sent to your numbers, and the delivery receipts of the SMS you sent, from an SMS center (SMSC) that speaks the SMPP protocol.

Use it to process SMS replies from customers, such as a STOP or a YES, or to follow whether the SMS sent with `smpp-sink` reached the phone.

Output: the body is the text of the SMS. The `CamelSmppSourceAddr` header is the phone number of the sender, `CamelSmppDestAddr` the number it was sent to, and `CamelSmppMessageType` is `DeliverSm` for an SMS and `DeliveryReceipt` for a delivery receipt, whose body is the text of the receipt and whose fields are in other `CamelSmpp` headers.

Good to know: it logs in to the SMSC as a receiver when the integration starts, and the integration fails to start when the SMSC cannot be reached. The SMSC sends a delivery receipt for each SMS that `smpp-sink` sent with `registeredDelivery` `1` (its default), or `2` when the SMS failed: the `CamelSmppId` header of the receipt is the ID that `smpp-sink` got for the SMS, and `CamelSmppStatus` its final state, such as `DELIVRD`. The SMSC decides which messages it gets, from `systemId` and `addressRange`. It connects with no TLS unless `usingSSL` is true.

kamelets.name: snmp-source
kamelets.title: SNMP Source
kamelets.summary: Reads values, such as uptime or interface counters, from a network device over SNMP at a regular interval, or receives the SNMP traps that devices send, one message per reading or trap.
kamelets.description:
Reads values, such as uptime or interface counters, from a network device over SNMP at a regular interval, or receives the SNMP traps that devices send, one message per reading or trap.

Use it to monitor routers, switches, printers or servers that speak SNMP, for example to store their counters over time, or to forward their alarms (traps) to a ticketing or chat system.

Output: the body is XML text with one `entry` per value, each with its `oid` (the identifier of the value, such as `1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0` for the uptime) and its `value`, inside an `snmp` element. For a trap, the `peerAddress` header is the address of the device that sent it.

Good to know: with `type` set to `TRAP`, `host` and `port` are the address to listen on, not a device; traps are usually sent to port 162, but `port` is 161 by default, and a port below 1024 needs administrator rights on most systems. A device that does not answer a poll gives no message: it is sent again `retries` times, each time after waiting `snmpTimeout` for the answer; when they are not set, that is 2 more times, after 1.5 seconds each. SNMP v1 and v2c send the community string in clear text; prefer v3 when the device supports it.

kamelets.name: snowflake-sink
kamelets.title: Snowflake Sink
kamelets.summary: Runs an SQL statement, such as an INSERT, in a Snowflake database for each message, with values taken from the fields of the JSON object in the body.
kamelets.description:
Runs an SQL statement, such as an INSERT, in a Snowflake database for each message, with values taken from the fields of the JSON object in the body.

Use it to store records from another system as rows of a table, such as each order that arrives on a Kafka topic, or to update or delete rows. To read rows, use `snowflake-source`.

Input: the body is one JSON object, as text, such as `{"username":"oscerd","city":"Rome"}`. In `query`, write `:#username` where the value of the field `username` goes. When the object has no field of that name, the header of that name is used instead. Fields that `query` does not name are ignored.

Output: the body afterwards is the JSON object as a Map, and the `CamelSqlUpdateCount` header holds the number of rows the statement changed. When `query` is a SELECT, the body is instead a List of the rows found, each a Map, and the `CamelSqlRowCount` header holds their number.

Good to know: a message fails when its body is not a JSON object (a JSON array or plain text, for example), or when it has no value for a parameter of `query`. The values are sent to the database apart from the SQL text, so the content of a message cannot change the statement. Do not write `?` in `query`, not even in a quoted string: the Kamelet then fails to start. Log in with `password`, or with a key pair in `privateKey` or `privateKeyFile`: a Snowflake user of type SERVICE, meant for applications, cannot log in with a password. When a key is set, the password is not used. `warehouse`, `schema` and `role` choose what the session uses; when they are not set, the defaults of the user apply, and a user with no default warehouse cannot run a query that needs one. Each message logs in to Snowflake anew, as the Kamelet keeps no connection open between messages.

kamelets.name: snowflake-source
kamelets.title: Snowflake Source
kamelets.summary: Runs an SQL query in a Snowflake database again and again, and sends each row it returns as a message, as a JSON object.
kamelets.description:
Runs an SQL query in a Snowflake database again and again, and sends each row it returns as a message, as a JSON object.

Use it to pick up the rows that another application adds to a table, such as new orders or events, and pass them on to another system. To write rows, use `snowflake-sink`.

Output: the body is one row as JSON text, an object with the column names as keys, such as `{"id":1,"username":"oscerd","city":"Rome"}`. The `Content-Type` header is `application/json`.

Good to know: the query runs again `delay` milliseconds after the previous run, so the same rows are sent again and again, unless `consumedQuery` marks or deletes each row once it is sent and `query` leaves such rows out: for example `SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE processed = false` with `UPDATE accounts SET processed = true WHERE id = :#id`. When the next step fails for a row, `consumedQuery` is not run for it, and the row is read again. A query that finds no rows sends nothing. `query` cannot contain `?`. The format of date and time columns in the JSON depends on the Camel version. Log in with `password`, or with a key pair in `privateKey` or `privateKeyFile`: a Snowflake user of type SERVICE, meant for applications, cannot log in with a password. When a key is set, the password is not used. `warehouse`, `schema` and `role` choose what the session uses; when they are not set, the defaults of the user apply, and a user with no default warehouse cannot run a query that needs one. Each poll logs in to Snowflake anew, as the Kamelet keeps no connection open between polls.

kamelets.name: solr-sink
kamelets.title: Solr Sink
kamelets.summary: Adds each message, a JSON object or a JSON array of objects, as one or more documents to a collection or core of Apache Solr, so that they can be searched.
kamelets.description:
Adds each message, a JSON object or a JSON array of objects, as one or more documents to a collection or core of Apache Solr, so that they can be searched.

Use it to make records searchable in Solr, such as products, articles or orders. To run a query on a schedule, use `solr-source`.

Input: the body is JSON text: an object for one document, such as `{"id": "order-42", "status_s": "shipped"}`, or an array of objects for several. A document with the same `id` as one already stored replaces it.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the answer of Solr, as a Map-like object with its `responseHeader`.

Good to know: a body that is not JSON fails the message. With `autocommit` false, the default, the documents become searchable only when Solr commits them, as set in the configuration of the collection. It connects with plain HTTP by default; set `enableSSL` to true for a Solr that is reached with HTTPS, and give the certificate in `certificate` when Solr uses a self-signed certificate. The documents go to the `/update` handler of the collection, or to the one in `requestHandler`. When Solr does not answer, a message fails only after 10 minutes, and the first one over plain HTTP after twice as long; set `requestTimeout` to fail sooner.

kamelets.name: solr-source
kamelets.title: Solr Source
kamelets.summary: Runs the same query on a collection or core of Apache Solr at a regular interval, and sends the result of each query as one message.
kamelets.description:
Runs the same query on a collection or core of Apache Solr at a regular interval, and sends the result of each query as one message.

Use it to watch a Solr collection on a schedule, for example to send the documents that match a query to another system. To add documents to Solr, use `solr-sink`.

Output: the body is JSON text, the answer of Solr: `responseHeader`, and under `response` the list of the documents found, each with its fields. The `Content-Type` header is `application/json`.

Good to know: every query returns all the matching documents again, not only the new ones; filter on a date in the query to get only new documents. Each query returns only the first documents found: as many as `size`, or 10 with the usual Solr settings when `size` is not set. It connects with plain HTTP by default; set `enableSSL` to true for a Solr that is reached with HTTPS, and give the certificate in `certificate` when Solr uses a self-signed certificate. The query runs on the `/select` handler of the collection, or on the one in `requestHandler`. When Solr does not answer, the query fails only after 10 minutes; set `requestTimeout` to fail sooner. A query that fails is logged, and the next one runs at the next period.

kamelets.name: splunk-hec-sink
kamelets.title: Splunk HEC Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message as an event to Splunk through its HTTP Event Collector (HEC), for searching, dashboards and alerts in Splunk.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message as an event to Splunk through its HTTP Event Collector (HEC), for searching, dashboards and alerts in Splunk.

Use it to send application logs, audit records, metrics or business events from any flow into a Splunk index.

Input: the body is the event, as text or as structured data such as a Map, which is sent as a JSON object. By default the event sent to Splunk is a JSON object with the headers of the message under `headers` and the body under `body`; `bodyOnly` sends the body alone, and `headersOnly` the headers alone.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: when `index`, `source` and `sourceType` are not set, the events go to the index `camel` with the source and source type `camel`, so set them for your Splunk. The `host` field of the event is the IP address of the machine that runs the integration, unless `hostPayload` is set. It connects with HTTPS and checks the certificate of the server, unless `https` or `skipTlsVerify` say otherwise. It sends to the event endpoint `/services/collector/event`; with `splunkEndpoint` set to `/services/collector/raw`, Splunk stores the whole JSON object as raw text instead, and `index`, `source` and `sourceType` no longer apply. A response other than 200, such as a wrong path, fails the message.

kamelets.name: spring-rabbitmq-sink
kamelets.title: RabbitMQ Sink
kamelets.summary: Publishes each message to an exchange in a RabbitMQ broker, which routes it to queues by its routing key.
kamelets.description:
Publishes each message to an exchange in a RabbitMQ broker, which routes it to queues by its routing key.

Use it to hand work or events to applications that read from RabbitMQ queues. Use `spring-rabbitmq-source` to read from them.

Input: the body is the payload, as text or bytes. Text is sent with the content type `text/plain`, and bytes with `application/octet-stream`, unless `contentType` says otherwise. A Map fails: turn structured data into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`, and set `contentType` to `application/json`. A message with no body fails, unless `allowNullBody` is true. The headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent as headers of the RabbitMQ message.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: it does not create the exchange, unless `autoDeclareProducer` is true. A message sent to an exchange that does not exist is lost without an error, unless publisher confirms are on (`publisherConfirmType` and `confirm`), and RabbitMQ drops a message that no queue is bound to take. It connects with no TLS unless `protocol` is `amqps`. With `amqps`, the certificate of the broker must be trusted by Java, or by the trust store in `sslTruststoreLocation`, and must name the host in `host`; otherwise it cannot connect. It does not wait for a reply, even when the incoming message expects one, as one from `webhook-source` does.

kamelets.name: spring-rabbitmq-source
kamelets.title: RabbitMQ Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each message from a queue in a RabbitMQ broker, and can create that queue and bind it to an exchange with a routing key.
kamelets.description:
Receives each message from a queue in a RabbitMQ broker, and can create that queue and bind it to an exchange with a routing key.

Use it to process work or events that other applications publish to RabbitMQ. Use `spring-rabbitmq-sink` to publish them.

Output: the body is text when the content type of the message starts with `text`, and bytes otherwise. The headers of the RabbitMQ message become headers, along with `CamelSpringRabbitmqExchangeName`, `CamelSpringRabbitmqRoutingKey` and `CamelSpringRabbitmqContentType`.

Good to know: with `autoDeclare` false, the default, the queue must exist already, bound to the exchange; until it does, the source keeps trying again. With `autoDeclare` true, it creates the exchange, as a `direct` exchange unless `exchangeType` says otherwise, the queue in `queues` and the binding with `routingKey`; when the exchange or the queue exists already with other settings, such as another type or another dead letter exchange, the source fails to start. Without `queues`, it reads from a new queue with a generated name. A message whose processing fails is tried 6 times, one second apart (see `maximumRetryAttempts` and `retryDelay`), and then dropped, or sent to the dead letter exchange of the queue when it has one, such as the one in `deadLetterExchange`. One consumer processes one message at a time; `concurrentConsumers` processes several in parallel, so not in order. It connects with no TLS unless `protocol` is `amqps`. With `amqps`, the certificate of the broker must be trusted by Java, or by the trust store in `sslTruststoreLocation`, and must name the host in `host`; otherwise it cannot connect.

kamelets.name: sqlserver-sink
kamelets.title: Microsoft SQL Server Sink
kamelets.summary: Runs an SQL statement, such as an INSERT, in a Microsoft SQL Server database for each message, with values taken from the fields of the JSON object in the body.
kamelets.description:
Runs an SQL statement, such as an INSERT, in a Microsoft SQL Server database for each message, with values taken from the fields of the JSON object in the body.

Use it to store records from another system as rows of a table, such as each order that arrives on a Kafka topic, or to update or delete rows. To read rows, use `sqlserver-source`.

Input: the body is one JSON object, as text, such as `{"username":"oscerd","city":"Rome"}`. In `query`, write `:#username` where the value of the field `username` goes. When the object has no field of that name, the header of that name is used instead. Fields that `query` does not name are ignored. When `batch` is true, the body can also be a JSON array of such objects, and `query` runs once for each of them.

Output: the body afterwards is the JSON object as a Map, and the `CamelSqlUpdateCount` header holds the number of rows the statement changed. For a JSON array with `batch`, the body is a List of Maps, and the header holds the total for all of them. When `query` is a SELECT, the body is instead a List of the rows found, each a Map, and the `CamelSqlRowCount` header holds their number.

Good to know: a message fails when its body is not a JSON object (plain text, for example, or a JSON array when `batch` is not true), or when it has no value for a parameter of `query`. With `batch`, all the rows of one message are written in one transaction: when one of them fails, none is written. The values are sent to the database apart from the SQL text, so the content of a message cannot change the statement. Do not write `?` in `query`, not even in a quoted string: the Kamelet then fails to start. The connection is encrypted and the certificate of the server is checked: for a self-signed certificate, as a new installation has, set `trustServerCertificate` to true. The JDBC driver of SQL Server is not included: add `mvn:com.microsoft.sqlserver:mssql-jdbc` to the dependencies of the integration. Camel JBang (`camel run`) adds it by itself.

kamelets.name: sqlserver-source
kamelets.title: Microsoft SQL Server Source
kamelets.summary: Runs an SQL query in a Microsoft SQL Server database again and again, and sends each row it returns as a message, as a JSON object.
kamelets.description:
Runs an SQL query in a Microsoft SQL Server database again and again, and sends each row it returns as a message, as a JSON object.

Use it to pick up the rows that another application adds to a table, such as new orders or events, and pass them on to another system. To write rows, use `sqlserver-sink`.

Output: the body is one row as JSON text, an object with the column names as keys, such as `{"id":1,"username":"oscerd","city":"Rome"}`. When `useIterator` is false, the body is instead one JSON array with all the rows of a poll. The `Content-Type` header is `application/json`.

Good to know: the query runs again `delay` milliseconds after the previous run, so the same rows are sent again and again, unless `consumedQuery` marks or deletes each row once it is sent and `query` leaves such rows out: for example `SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE processed = false` with `UPDATE accounts SET processed = true WHERE id = :#id`. When the next step fails for a row, `consumedQuery` is not run for it, and the row is read again, unless `onConsumeFailed` marks it. A query that finds no rows sends nothing. `maxMessagesPerPoll` limits how many rows one poll sends. `query` cannot contain `?`. The format of date and time columns in the JSON depends on the Camel version. The connection is encrypted and the certificate of the server is checked: for a self-signed certificate, as a new installation has, set `trustServerCertificate` to true. The JDBC driver of SQL Server is not included: add `mvn:com.microsoft.sqlserver:mssql-jdbc` to the dependencies of the integration. Camel JBang (`camel run`) adds it by itself.

kamelets.name: ssh-sink
kamelets.title: SSH Sink
kamelets.summary: Runs the text of each message as a command on a remote server over SSH, and returns what the command prints.
kamelets.description:
Runs the text of each message as a command on a remote server over SSH, and returns what the command prints.

Use it to run a script or a maintenance command on a server when something happens, for example restart a service after a deployment or clear a cache when data changes. To run a fixed command on a schedule and read its output, use `ssh-source`; to run a command on the machine of the integration, use `exec-sink`.

Input: the body is the command to run, as text, such as `systemctl restart myapp`. It runs in the shell of `username`, so it can hold several commands separated by `;`.

Output: the body afterwards is what the command printed on its standard output, as a stream. The `CamelSshExitValue` header holds the exit code of the command, and `CamelSshStderr` what it printed on its standard error, as a stream.

Good to know: it runs whatever command it receives, with the rights of `username`. Never send it messages from an untrusted source, and log in with an account that may do only what is needed. A command that ends with an exit code other than 0 does not fail the message: check `CamelSshExitValue`. Log in with `password`, or with a private key in `privateKeyResource` when the server does not take passwords; when a key is set, the password is not used. The key of the server is checked only when `knownHostsResource` is set; without it, any server is accepted. A server that is not listed in that file is still accepted, unless `failOnUnknownHost` is true.

kamelets.name: ssh-source
kamelets.title: SSH Source
kamelets.summary: Runs a command on a remote server over SSH again and again, at a regular interval, and sends what the command prints as a message each time.
kamelets.description:
Runs a command on a remote server over SSH again and again, at a regular interval, and sends what the command prints as a message each time.

Use it to watch a server without installing anything on it, for example check the free disk space, the state of a service or the last lines of a log file every minute. To run a command for each incoming message instead, use `ssh-sink`.

Output: the body is what the command printed on its standard output, as text. The `CamelSshExitValue` header holds the exit code of the command, and `CamelSshStderr` what it printed on its standard error, as a stream.

Good to know: it runs `pollCommand` with the rights of `username`, so log in with an account that may do only what is needed. It runs it every half second by default; set `delay` to how often you need it. A command that fails still sends a message, with its exit code in `CamelSshExitValue`. Log in with `password`, or with a private key in `privateKeyResource` when the server does not take passwords; when a key is set, the password is not used. The key of the server is checked only when `knownHostsResource` is set; without it, any server is accepted. A server that is not listed in that file is still accepted, unless `failOnUnknownHost` is true.

kamelets.name: string-template-action
kamelets.title: String Template Action
kamelets.summary: Builds a new message body from a StringTemplate template, filling in values from the incoming message.
kamelets.description:
Builds a new message body from a StringTemplate template, filling in values from the incoming message.

Use it to turn data into text for people or for another system, such as the text of an email or a small XML or JSON document, when you already have StringTemplate templates. For simple templates, `mustache-template-action` is an alternative; to reshape JSON into other JSON, `jslt-action` is often simpler.

Input: any body. The template sees the body as `<body>` and a header as `<headers.name>`, for example `Dear <headers.customer>, your order <body> has shipped.`

Output: the body is the text the template produced. The headers are kept, and a `CamelStringTemplateResourceUri` header is added with the location of the template.

Good to know: a header the template uses that is not set gives nothing in the text. A template file that cannot be found fails the message. The template is loaded from a file, the classpath or a URL given by the `template` option; it cannot come from the message.

kamelets.name: telegram-sink
kamelets.title: Telegram Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message as a text message, or as a photo, from your Telegram bot to a Telegram chat, group or channel.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message as a text message, or as a photo, from your Telegram bot to a Telegram chat, group or channel.

Use it to notify a person or a group on Telegram, for example with an alert, an order update or a daily report, or to answer the messages your bot receives with `telegram-source`.

Input: the body is the text of the message, as text; another kind of body is turned into text first, and the text is sent as it is, without Markdown or HTML formatting. When the `Content-Type` header is `image/png` or `image/jpeg`, the body is sent as a photo instead, as bytes, and the `text` or `ce-text` header is its caption. The `chat-id` or `ce-chatid` header chooses the chat, instead of the `chatId` option; `telegram-source` sets both, so a reply goes back to the chat a message came from.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the answer of Telegram as JSON text, with the message that was sent.

Good to know: a message fails when no chat is given, neither in a header nor in `chatId`, and when Telegram refuses it, for example because the bot is not a member of the group or the person never started a chat with the bot.

kamelets.name: telegram-source
kamelets.title: Telegram Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the messages that people send to your Telegram bot, in private chats and in the groups the bot is in, one message per Telegram message.
kamelets.description:
Receives the messages that people send to your Telegram bot, in private chats and in the groups the bot is in, one message per Telegram message.

Use it to build a chat bot, for example to answer questions, take orders or run commands sent on Telegram; send the answers with `telegram-sink`.

Output: the body is the Telegram message as JSON text, with fields such as `text` (what was written), `chat` (with the `id` of the chat), `from` (the sender) and `message_id`. A photo or a document comes without `text`. The `chat-id` and `ce-chatid` headers hold the ID of the chat, so that `telegram-sink` can answer in the same chat.

Good to know: it asks Telegram for new messages all the time, and each message is received once. Telegram keeps the messages that arrive while the Kamelet is stopped for up to 24 hours. It does not work while a webhook is set for the bot, and only one application at a time can read the messages of a bot. In a group, Telegram gives a bot only the commands and the replies to the bot, unless its privacy mode is turned off with @BotFather.

kamelets.name: throttle-action
kamelets.title: Throttle Action
kamelets.summary: Lets through at most a set number of messages per period of time, such as 10 per second, and holds back the rest for a later period.
kamelets.description:
Lets through at most a set number of messages per period of time, such as 10 per second, and holds back the rest for a later period.

Use it to protect a sink or a service that cannot take more than a certain rate, for example an API that allows 100 calls per minute. To hold every message for a fixed time instead, use `delay-action`.

Input: any message.

Output: the same message, unchanged. The messages over the limit are not dropped: they wait, and are passed on in a later period.

kamelets.name: tika-extract-text-action
kamelets.title: Tika Extract Text Action
kamelets.summary: Turns each document, such as an HTML page, a text file or a PDF, into its plain text, or into XHTML, with Apache Tika, inside the integration.
kamelets.description:
Turns each document, such as an HTML page, a text file or a PDF, into its plain text, or into XHTML, with Apache Tika, inside the integration.

Use it to get the text of documents before searching, indexing or summarising them, for example in front of `langchain4j-ingest-sink` to load documents into a vector store for an AI assistant. For a richer conversion to Markdown that keeps headings and tables, use `docling-convert-action`, which needs a Docling server.

Input: the document, as bytes, a stream, a file or text. The header named in `documentIdHeader` (by default `CamelLangChain4jIngestDocumentId`) is the id of the document, if any; it is kept for `langchain4j-ingest-sink` further on.

Output: the body is the plain text of the document, as text in UTF-8, with its blocks on separate lines; with `outputFormat` set to `html` or `xml`, it is the document as XHTML text instead. All the headers of the message are removed, except the Camel ones, such as the file name headers of `langchain4j-ingest-file-source`.

Good to know: only HTML and plain text are read out of the box. For PDF, add the Tika PDF parser module (`org.apache.tika:tika-parser-pdf-module`, in the Tika version of your Camel) to the integration, and add the other Tika parser modules for other formats; without the module, a PDF gives an empty text, and does not fail. With `maxDocumentSize`, a larger document fails the message without being read.

kamelets.name: timer-source
kamelets.title: Timer Source
kamelets.summary: Sends the same fixed message again and again at a regular interval, such as once every second.
kamelets.description:
Sends the same fixed message again and again at a regular interval, such as once every second.

Use it to try out a sink or an action without a real system behind it, to trigger a flow on a schedule (for example, call an HTTP service every minute), or to send a heartbeat. For a calendar schedule such as "every weekday at 9:00" use `cron-source` instead, and for a message that counts up use `counter-source`.

Output: the body is the `message` option as text, the same on every message. The `Content-Type` header is set to the `contentType` option.

Good to know: it keeps sending until the integration is stopped, unless `repeatCount` is set.

kamelets.name: timestamp-router-action
kamelets.title: Timestamp Router Action
kamelets.summary: Changes the topic that `kafka-sink` writes a record to, to a name made of the original topic name and the date of the record, such as `orders-20240703`.
kamelets.description:
Changes the topic that `kafka-sink` writes a record to, to a name made of the original topic name and the date of the record, such as `orders-20240703`.

Use it to spread the records over one topic per day or per month, in a flow from `kafka-source` to `kafka-sink`, for example to keep or delete them by period. To take the date from a field of a JSON body instead use `message-timestamp-router-action`.

Input: a message from `kafka-source`, with the name of the topic in the `CamelKafkaTopic` header and the time of the record, in milliseconds since 1970, in the `CamelKafkaTimestamp` header. `topicHeaderName` and `timestampHeaderName` choose other headers.

Output: the same body. The `CamelKafkaOverrideTopic` header is set to the new name, and `kafka-sink` writes the record to that topic instead of its own `topic`.

Good to know: the default `topicFormat` of `topic-$[timestamp]` gives names such as `topic-20240703`, without the original name: set it to `$[topic]-$[timestamp]` to keep it. The date is in UTC. Without a time header, nothing changes.

kamelets.name: topic-name-matches-filter-action
kamelets.title: Kafka Topic Name Matches Filter Action
kamelets.summary: Keeps only the Kafka records whose topic name matches a regular expression, and drops all others.
kamelets.description:
Keeps only the Kafka records whose topic name matches a regular expression, and drops all others.

Use it to handle the records of only some topics, after a `kafka-source` whose `topic` lists several topics or is a pattern, for example only those of `orders-eu`. To keep or drop messages by another header use `header-matches-filter-action`.

Input: a message from `kafka-source`, with the name of the topic in the `CamelKafkaTopic` header.

Output: the same message, unchanged, when `regex` matches the whole topic name. Otherwise the message is dropped and nothing is sent on.

Good to know: the expression must match the whole name: `orders` does not keep the records of `orders-eu`, but `orders.*` does. A message without the `CamelKafkaTopic` header is dropped.

kamelets.name: value-to-key-action
kamelets.title: Value to Key Action
kamelets.summary: Sets the key of the Kafka record to some fields of the JSON body, so that records with the same values in those fields get the same key.
kamelets.description:
Sets the key of the Kafka record to some fields of the JSON body, so that records with the same values in those fields get the same key.

Use it to take the key of the record from the data, before `kafka-sink`, for example the customer of an order, so that all the records of one customer go to the same partition and stay in order. To take the key from a header instead use `set-kafka-key-action`.

Input: a JSON object as JSON text, with the `Content-Type` header set to `application/json`.

Output: the same JSON object, as JSON text in a stream, with `Content-Type` set to `application/json`. The `CamelKafkaKey` header, which `kafka-sink` uses as the key of the record, is set to a Map of the fields named in `fields` and their values.

Good to know: `kafka-sink` writes the key as text such as `{id=7, customer=acme}`, not as JSON, and not necessarily with the fields in the order of `fields`. A field that is not in the body is left out of the key.

kamelets.name: velocity-template-action
kamelets.title: Velocity Template Action
kamelets.summary: Builds a new message body from an Apache Velocity template, filling in values from the incoming message.
kamelets.description:
Builds a new message body from an Apache Velocity template, filling in values from the incoming message.

Use it to turn data into text for people or for another system, such as an email, a report or a small XML or JSON document, when you already have Velocity templates or need its loops and conditions. For simple templates, `mustache-template-action` is an alternative; to reshape JSON into other JSON, `jslt-action` is often simpler.

Input: any body. The template sees the body as `$\{body}` and a header as `${headers.name}`, for example `Dear ${headers.customer}, your order $\{body} has shipped.`

Output: the body is the text the template produced. The headers are kept.

Good to know: a value the template uses that is missing, such as a header that is not set, stays in the text as written, for example `${headers.customer}`; write `$!{headers.customer}` to get nothing instead. A template file that cannot be found fails the message. The template is loaded from a file, the classpath or a URL given by the `template` option; it cannot come from the message.

kamelets.name: webhook-source
kamelets.title: Webhook Source
kamelets.summary: Receives HTTP requests on a path of its own, such as `/webhook`, and sends each request on as a message, with its body and headers.
kamelets.description:
Receives HTTP requests on a path of its own, such as `/webhook`, and sends each request on as a message, with its body and headers.

Use it to receive the webhook calls of an online service, such as a payment, form or code hosting service, or to let another system push data with a simple HTTP POST. To fetch a URL at a regular interval instead, use `http-source`.

Output: the body is the body of the request, as a stream, and is empty for a request without a body, such as a GET. The HTTP headers of the request become headers of the message, and so does each query parameter. `CamelHttpMethod` gives the method (such as `POST`), `CamelHttpPath` the path and `CamelHttpQuery` the query string. A form (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`) arrives as a Map of its fields instead.

Good to know: there is no login, so anyone who can reach the address can send messages; protect it with network rules or a gateway in front, and treat the content as untrusted. It accepts every HTTP method, on the exact path only. It listens on the HTTP port of the application, 8080 by default with Camel JBang. The caller gets back the message as it is at the end of the flow: by default the body it sent, with status 200, or status 204 when there is no body.

kamelets.name: xj-identity-action
kamelets.title: XJ Identity Action
kamelets.summary: Converts each message from XML to JSON, or from JSON to XML, with a fixed mapping and no template to write.
kamelets.description:
Converts each message from XML to JSON, or from JSON to XML, with a fixed mapping and no template to write.

Use it to pass XML to a system that expects JSON, or the other way round, when the default mapping is good enough. To control the result, such as the names of the elements or which fields to keep, use `xj-template-action` with an XSLT stylesheet.

Input: XML or JSON as text, bytes or a stream, as `direction` says. Parsed JSON, such as a Map, fails the message.

Output: the body is JSON text or XML text. From XML, the root element is dropped, its attributes and child elements become fields, repeated elements become an array, and all values are text: `<order id="7"><qty>2</qty></order>` gives `{"id":"7","qty":"2"}`. To XML, each JSON value becomes an `object` element that keeps its name and type in `xj:name` and `xj:type` attributes, such as `<object xj:name="qty" xj:type="int">2</object>`. The headers are kept.

kamelets.name: xj-template-action
kamelets.title: XJ Template Action
kamelets.summary: Converts each message from XML to JSON, or from JSON to XML, with an XSLT stylesheet that decides what the result looks like.
kamelets.description:
Converts each message from XML to JSON, or from JSON to XML, with an XSLT stylesheet that decides what the result looks like.

Use it to map the XML of one system to the JSON of another, or the other way round, when the fixed mapping of `xj-identity-action` does not give the shape you need.

Input: XML or JSON as text, bytes or a stream, as `direction` says. With `JSON2XML` the stylesheet sees the JSON as XML in which each value is an `object` element with its name and type in `xj:name` and `xj:type` attributes, such as `<object xj:name="qty" xj:type="int">2</object>`; select a field with `object[@xj:name='qty']`.

Output: the body is JSON text or XML text. With `XML2JSON` the stylesheet must write that same form, which becomes JSON: `<object xj:type="object"><object xj:name="qty" xj:type="int">2</object></object>` gives `{"qty":2}`. The prefix `xj` stands for the namespace `http://camel.apache.org/component/xj`. The headers are kept.

Good to know: the stylesheet is loaded from a file, the classpath or a URL given by the `template` option; it cannot come from the message.
